子，鼠殹。以亡，盜者中人。取之，臧（藏）穴中、糞土中，為人面、 小目，然、扁然，名曰輒、曰耳、曰芯、曰聲，賤人殹，得。
丑，牛殹。以亡，其盜從北方入，憙大息，盜不遠，旁桑殹，得。
寅，虎殹。以亡，盜從東方入，有從出，臧（藏）山谷中，其為人方面、面廣頰、瞏目，盜它所人殹，不得。
卯，兔殹。以亡，盜從東方入，復從出，臧野林草茅中，為人短面，出， 不得。
辰，虫殹。以亡，盜者從東方入，有從出，取者臧谿谷窌內中，外人殹， 其為人長頸、小首、小目，女子為巫，男子為祝。名……
巳，雞殹。以亡，盜者中人殹。臧囷、屋、屒、糞土中、蹇木下，其為人 小面、長赤目，賤人殹，得。
午，馬殹。盜從南方入，有從之出，爯才（在）廄廡芻槀中，為人長面、 大目，喜疾行，外人，不遠。
未，羊殹。大復、出目。盜者從南方入，有從出，爯在牢圈中，其為人小頸、 必得。
申，石殹。 遠所殹。盜從西方入，爯在山谷，為人美，不牷。名曰“環”， 不得。
酉，雞殹。盜從西方入，復從西方出，爯在囷屋、東屒、水旁，名曰“灌”， 有黑子矦。
戌，犬殹。爯在責薪糞蔡中，黑、單、多言，旬月當得。
亥，豕殹。盜者中人殹，爯在屏圂方及矢，其為人長面、折鞮、赤目、長 髪，得。
——《十二地支占盗》
en:
Zi (Rat): The thief is of average build, hiding in a burrow or a rubbish heap. He has a small, flat face and small eyes. His name might be Zhe, Er, Xin, or Sheng. He is of low social standing and will be caught.
Chou (Ox): The thief came from the north. He sighs frequently and has not fled far, hiding among the mulberry trees. He will be caught.
Yin (Tiger): The thief struck from the east and fled back east, taking refuge in a valley. He has a square face, broad cheeks, and round eyes. He is a foreigner and will evade capture.
Mao (Rabbit): The thief struck from the east and fled east, hiding in wild woods or tall grass. He has a short face. He will eventually show himself, but you will not catch him.
Chen (Dragon): The thief struck from the east and fled east, hiding in a ravine or a cellar. He has a long neck, a small head, and small eyes. He is an outsider. If a woman, she is a shaman; if a man, a priest. Their name is unknown.
Si (Snake): The thief is of average build, hiding in a granary, a house, a latrine, a refuse pile, or under a tree. He has a small face and long, red eyes. He is of low status and will be caught.
Wu (Horse): The thief struck from the south and fled south, hiding in a stable or in the hay. He has a long face and large eyes, and walks with a brisk stride. He is an outsider but has not gone far.
Wei (Sheep): The thief struck from the south and fled south, hiding in a livestock pen. He has a short neck and will undoubtedly be caught.
Shen (Monkey): The thief came from the west and is hiding in a valley. He is handsome but has a physical defect. His name is Huan; he hails from a distant land and cannot be caught.
You (Rooster): The thief struck from the west and fled west, hiding in a granary, an eastern latrine, or near the water. His name is Guan, and he has a dark mole on his face.
Xu (Dog): The thief is hiding among firewood or refuse. He has a dark complexion, a slender build, and talks too much. He will be caught within ten days to a month.
Hai (Pig): The thief is of average build, hiding in a latrine, a pigsty, or near a cache of arrows. He has a long face, an upturned nose, red eyes, and long hair. He will be caught.
— Divination of Thieves by Twelve Earthly Branches

zh:
【梁惠王章句上】

孟子见梁惠王，王曰：叟，不远千里而来，亦将有以利吾国乎？
孟子对曰：王何必曰利？亦有仁义而已矣。王曰：何以利吾国？大夫曰：何以利吾家？士庶人曰：何以利吾身？上下交征利，而国危矣。万乘之国，弑其君者，必千乘之家；千乘之国，弑其君者，必百乘之家。万取千焉，千取百焉，不为不多矣。苟为后义而先利，不夺不餍。未有仁而遗其亲者也，未有义而后其君者也。王亦曰仁义而已矣，何必曰利？
孟子见梁惠王，王立于沼上，顾鸿雁麋鹿，曰：贤者亦乐此乎？
孟子对曰：贤者而后乐此，不贤者虽有此，不乐也。诗云：经始灵台，经之营之。庶民攻之，不日成之。经始勿亟，庶民子来。王在灵囿，麀鹿攸伏，麀鹿濯濯，白鸟鹤鹤。王在灵沼，于牣鱼跃。文王以民力为台为沼，而民欢乐之，谓其台曰灵台，谓其沼曰灵沼，乐其有麋鹿鱼鳖。古之人与民偕乐，故能乐也。汤誓曰：时日害丧？予及女皆亡。民欲与之皆亡，虽有台池鸟兽，岂能独乐哉？
梁惠王曰：寡人之于国也，尽心焉耳矣。河内凶，则移其民于河东，移其粟于河内。河东凶亦然。察邻国之政，无如寡人之用心者。邻国之民不加少，寡人之民不加多，何也？
孟子对曰：王好战，请以战喻。填然鼓之，兵刃既接，弃甲曳兵而走，或百步而后止，或五十步而后止。以五十步笑百步，则何如？
曰：不可。直不百步耳，是亦走也。
曰：王如知此，则无望民之多于邻国也。
不违农时，谷不可胜食也。数罟不入洿池，鱼鳖不可胜食也。斧斤以时入山林，材木不可胜用也。谷与鱼鳖不可胜食，材木不可胜用，是使民养生丧死无憾也。养生丧死无憾，王道之始也。
五亩之宅，树之以桑，五十者可以衣帛矣。鸡豚狗彘之畜，无失其时，七十者可以食肉矣。百亩之田，勿夺其时，数口之家可以无饥矣。谨庠序之教，申之以孝悌之义，颁白者不负戴于道路矣。七十者衣帛食肉，黎民不饥不寒，然而不王者，未之有也。
狗彘食人食而不知检，涂有饿莩而不知发。人死，则曰：非我也，岁也。是何异于刺人而杀之，曰：“非我也，兵也？”王无罪岁，斯天下之民至焉。
梁惠王曰：寡人愿安承教。
孟子对曰：杀人以梃与刃，有以异乎？曰：无以异也。
以刃与政，有以异乎？曰：无以异也。
曰：庖有肥肉，廏有肥马，民有饥色，野有饿莩，此率兽而食人也。兽相食，且人恶之。为民父母，行政不免于率兽而食人，恶在其为民父母也？仲尼曰：始作俑者，其无后乎？为其象人而用之也。如之何其使斯民饥而死也？
梁惠王曰：晋国，天下莫强焉，叟之所知也。及寡人之身，东败于齐，长子死焉，西丧地于秦七百里，南辱于楚，寡人耻之。愿比死者壹洒之，如之何则可？
孟子对曰：地方百里而可以王，王如施仁政于民，省刑罚，薄税敛，深耕易耨，壮者以暇日修其孝悌忠信，入以事其父兄，出以事其长上，可使制梃以挞秦、楚之坚甲利兵矣。
彼夺其民时，使不得耕耨以养其父母，父母冻饿，兄弟妻子离散。彼陷溺其民，王往而征之，夫谁与王敌？故曰：仁者无敌。王请勿疑。
孟子见梁襄王，出，语人曰：望之不似人君，就之而不见所畏焉。卒然问曰：天下恶乎定？吾对曰：定于一。孰能一之？
对曰：不嗜杀人者能一之。孰能与之？对曰：天下莫不与也。王知夫苗乎？七八月之间旱，则苗槁矣。天油然作云，沛然下雨，则苗渤然兴之矣。其如是，孰能御之？今夫天下之人牧，未有不嗜杀人者也。如有不嗜杀人者，则天下之民皆引领而望之矣。诚如是也，民归之，由水之就下，沛然谁能御之？
齐宣王问曰：齐桓、晋文之事，可得闻乎？
孟子对曰：仲尼之徒，无道桓、文之事者，是以后世无传焉。臣未之闻也。无以，则王乎？
曰：德何如则可以王矣？
曰：保民而王，莫之能御也。
曰：若寡人者，可以保民乎哉？曰：可。曰：何由知吾可也？
曰：臣闻之胡龁曰：王坐于堂上，有牵牛而过堂下者，王见之，曰：牛何之？对曰：将以衅钟。王曰：舍之，吾不忍其觳觫，若无罪而就死地。对曰：然则废衅钟与？曰：何可废也？以羊易之。不识有诸？曰：有之。
曰：是心足以王矣。百姓皆以王为爱也，臣固知王之不忍也。
王曰：然。诚有百姓者，齐国虽褊小，吾何爱一牛？即不忍其觳觫，若无罪而就死地，故以羊易之也。
曰：王无异于百姓之以王为爱也。以小易大，彼恶知之？王若隐其无罪而就死地，则牛羊何择焉？
王笑曰：是诚何心哉！我非爱其财而易之以羊也，宜乎百姓之谓我爱也。
曰：“无伤也，是乃仁术也，见牛未见羊也。君子之于禽兽也，见其生不忍见其死，闻其声不忍食其肉，是以君子远庖厨也。
王说，曰：诗云：他人有心，予忖度之，夫子之谓也。夫我乃行之，反而求之，不得吾心。夫子言之，于我心有戚戚焉。此心之所以合于王者，何也？
曰：有复于王者，曰：吾力足以举百钧，而不足以举一羽，明足以察秋豪之末，而不见舆薪。则王许之乎？曰：否。
今恩足以及禽兽，而功不至于百姓者，独何与？然则一羽之不举，为不用力焉；舆薪之不见，为不用明焉；百姓之不见保，为不用恩焉。故王之不王，不为也，非不能也。
曰：不为者与不能者之形何以异？
曰：挟大山以超北海，语人曰：我不能。是诚不能也。为长者折枝，语人曰：我不能。是不为也，非不能也。故王之不王，非挟大山以超北海之类也；王之不王，是折枝之类也。
老吾老，以及人之老；幼吾幼，以及人之幼，天下可运于掌。诗云：刑于寡妻，至于兄弟，以御于家邦。言举斯心加诸彼而已，故推恩足以保四海，不推恩无以保妻子。古之人所以大过人者，无他焉，善推其所为而已矣。
今恩足以及禽兽，而功不至于百姓者，独何与？
权，然后知轻重；度，然后知长短。物皆然，心为甚。王请度之。
抑王兴甲兵，危士臣，搆怨于诸侯，然后快于心与？
王曰：否。吾何快于是？将以求吾所大欲也。
曰：王之所大欲，可得闻与？王笑而不言。
曰：为肥甘不足于口与？轻暖不足于体与？抑为采色不足视于目与？声音不足听于耳与？便嬖不足使令于前与？王之诸臣皆足以供之，而王岂为是哉？曰：否，吾不为是也。
曰：然则王之所大欲可知已。欲辟土地，朝秦、楚，莅中国而抚四夷也。以若所为，求若所欲，犹缘木而求鱼也。王曰：若是其甚与？
曰：殆有甚焉。缘木求鱼，虽不得鱼，无后灾。以若所为，求若所欲，尽心力而为之，后必有灾。曰：可得闻与？
曰：邹人与楚人战，则王以为孰胜？曰：楚人胜。
曰：然则小固不可以敌大，寡固不可以敌众，弱固不可以敌强。海内之地，方千里者九，齐集有其一，以一服八，何以异于邹敌楚哉？盖亦反其本矣。
今王发政施仁，使天下仕者皆欲立于王之朝，耕者皆欲耕于王之野，商贾皆欲藏于王之市，行旅皆欲出于王之涂，天下之欲疾其君者皆欲赴诉于王。其若是，孰能御之？
王曰：吾惛，不能进于是矣，愿夫子辅吾志，明以教我。我虽不敏，请尝试之。
曰：无恒产而有恒心者，惟士为能。若民则无恒产，因无恒心。苟无恒心，放辟邪侈，无不为已。及陷于罪，然后从而刑之，是罔民也。焉有仁人在位，罔民而可为也？是故明君制民之产，必使仰足以事父母，俯足以畜妻子，乐岁终身饱，凶年免于死亡，然后驱而之善，故民之从之也轻。
今也制民之产，仰不足以事父母，俯不足以畜妻子，乐岁终身苦，凶年不免于死亡。此惟救死而恐不赡，奚暇治礼义哉？
王欲行之，则盍反其本矣。
五亩之宅，树之以桑，五十者可以衣帛矣。鸡豚狗彘之畜，无失其时，七十者可以食肉矣。百亩之田，勿夺其时，八口之家可以无饥矣。谨庠序之教，申之以孝悌之义，颁白者不负戴于道路矣。老者衣帛食肉，黎民不饥不寒，然而不王者，未之有也。
en:
[King Hui of Liang, Part I]

Mencius went to see King Hui of Liang. The king said, "Venerable sir, since you have not counted it far to come here, a distance of a thousand li, may I presume that you are provided with counsels to profit my kingdom?"
Mencius replied, "Why must your Majesty use that word 'profit'? What I am provided with, are counsels to benevolence and righteousness, and these are my only topics. If your Majesty say, 'What is to be done to profit my kingdom?' the great officers will say, 'What is to be done to profit our families?' and the inferior officers and the common people will say, 'What is to be done to profit our persons?' Superiors and inferiors will try to snatch this profit the one from the other, and the kingdom will be endangered. In the kingdom of ten thousand chariots, the murderer of his sovereign shall be the chief of a family of a thousand chariots. In a kingdom of a thousand chariots, the murderer of his prince shall be the chief of a family of a hundred chariots. To have a thousand in ten thousand, and a hundred in a thousand, cannot be said not to be a large allotment, but if righteousness be put last, and profit be put first, they will not be satisfied without snatching all. There never has been a benevolent person who neglected one's parents. There never has been a righteous person who made one's sovereign an after consideration. Let your Majesty also say, 'Benevolence and righteousness, and let these be your only themes.' Why must you use that word—'profit'?"
Mencius, another day, saw King Hui of Liang. The king went and stood with him by a pond, and, looking round at the large geese and deer, said, "Do wise and good princes also find pleasure in these things?"
Mencius replied, "Being wise and good, they have pleasure in these things. If they are not wise and good, though they have these things, they do not find pleasure. It is said in the Book of Poetry, 'He measured out and commenced his marvellous tower; He measured it out and planned it. The people addressed themselves to it, And in less than a day completed it. When he measured and began it, he said to them—Be not so earnest: But the multitudes came as if they had been his children. The king was in his marvellous park; The does reposed about, The does so sleek and fat: And the white birds shone glistening. The king was by his marvellous pond; How full was it of fishes leaping about!' King Wen used the strength of the people to make his tower and his pond, and yet the people rejoiced to do the work, calling the tower 'the marvellous tower,' calling the pond 'the marvellous pond,' and rejoicing that he had his large deer, his fishes, and turtles. The ancients caused the people to have pleasure as well as themselves, and therefore they could enjoy it. In the Declaration of Tang it is said, 'O sun, when wilt thou expire? We will die together with thee.' The people wished for Jie's death, though they should die with him. Although he had towers, ponds, birds, and animals, how could he have pleasure alone?"
King Hui of Liang said, "Small as my virtue is, in the government of my kingdom, I do indeed exert my mind to the utmost. If the year be bad on the inside of the river, I remove as many of the people as I can to the east of the river, and convey grain to the country in the inside. When the year is bad on the east of the river, I act on the same plan. On examining the government of the neighbouring kingdoms, I do not find that there is any prince who exerts his mind as I do. And yet the people of the neighbouring kingdoms do not decrease, nor do my people increase. How is this?"
Mencius replied, "Your Majesty is fond of war—let me take an illustration from war. The soldiers move forward to the sound of the drums; and after their weapons have been crossed, on one side they throw away their coats of mail, trail their arms behind them, and run. Some run a hundred paces and stop; some run fifty paces and stop. What would you think if those who run fifty paces were to laugh at those who run a hundred paces?"
The king said, "They should not do so. Though they did not run a hundred paces, yet they also ran away."
"Since your Majesty knows this," replied Mencius, "you need not hope that your people will become more numerous than those of the neighbouring kingdoms."
"If the seasons of husbandry be not interfered with, the grain will be more than can be eaten. If close nets are not allowed to enter the pools and ponds, the fishes and turtles will be more than can be consumed. If the axes and bills enter the hills and forests only at the proper time, the wood will be more than can be used. When the grain and fish and turtles are more than can be eaten, and there is more wood than can be used, this enables the people to nourish their living and mourn for their dead, without any feeling against any. This condition, in which the people nourish their living and bury their dead without any feeling against any, is the first step of royal government."
"Let mulberry trees be planted about the homesteads with their five mu, and persons of fifty years may be clothed with silk. In keeping fowls, pigs, dogs, and swine, let not their times of breeding be neglected, and persons of seventy years may eat flesh. Let there not be taken away the time that is proper for the cultivation of the farm with its hundred mu, and the family of several mouths that is supported by it shall not suffer from hunger. Let careful attention be paid to education in schools, inculcating in it especially the filial and congenial duties, and grey-haired men will not be seen upon the roads, carrying burdens on their backs or on their heads. It never has been that the ruler of a State, where such results were seen—persons of seventy wearing silk and eating flesh, and the black-haired people suffering neither from hunger nor cold—did not attain to the royal dignity."
"Your dogs and swine eat the food of people, and you do not make any restrictive arrangements. There are people dying from famine on the roads, and you do not issue the stores of your granaries for them. When people die, you say, 'It is not owing to me; it is owing to the year.' In what does this differ from stabbing a person and killing one, and then saying—'It was not I; it was the weapon?' Let your Majesty cease to lay the blame on the year, and instantly from all the nation the people will come to you."
King Hui of Liang said, "I wish quietly to receive your instruction."
Mencius replied, "Is there any difference between killing a person with a stick and with a sword?" The king said, "There is no difference."
"Is there any difference between doing it with a sword and with the style of government?" "There is no difference," was the reply.
Mencius then said, "In your kitchen there is fat meat; in your stables there are fat horses. But your people have the look of hunger, and on the wilds there are those who have died of famine. This is leading on beasts to devour people. Beasts devour one another, and people hate them for doing so. When a prince, being the parent of his people, administers his government so as to be chargeable with leading on beasts to devour people, where is his parental relation to the people? Zhongni said, 'Was he not without posterity who first made wooden images to bury with the dead?' So he said, because that person made the semblances of people, and used them for that purpose—what shall be thought of him who causes his people to die of hunger?"
King Hui of Liang said, "There was not in the nation a stronger State than Jin, as you, venerable Sir, know. But since it descended to me, on the east we have been defeated by Qi, and then my eldest son perished; on the west we have lost seven hundred li of territory to Qin; and on the south we have sustained disgrace at the hands of Chu. I have brought shame on my departed predecessors, and wish on their account to wipe it away, once for all. What course is to be pursued to accomplish this?"
Mencius replied, "With a territory which is only a hundred li square, it is possible to attain to the royal dignity."
"If your Majesty will indeed dispense a benevolent government to the people, being sparing in the use of punishments and fines, and making the taxes and levies light, so causing that the fields shall be ploughed deep, and the weeding of them be carefully attended to, and that the strong-bodied, during their days of leisure, shall cultivate their filial piety, congenial respectfulness, sincerity, and truthfulness, serving thereby, at home, their fathers and elder brothers, and, abroad, their elders and superiors—you will then have a people who can be employed, with sticks which they have prepared, to oppose the strong mail and sharp weapons of the troops of Qin and Chu. The rulers of those States rob their people of their time, so that they cannot plough and weed their fields, in order to support their parents. Their parents suffer from cold and hunger. Brothers, wives, and children are separated and scattered abroad. Those rulers, as it were, drive their people into pit-falls, or drown them. Your Majesty will go to punish them. In such a case, who will oppose your Majesty? In accordance with this is the saying—'The benevolent has no enemy.' I beg your Majesty not to doubt what I say."
Mencius went to see the King Xiang of Liang. On coming out from the interview, he said to some persons, "When I looked at him from a distance, he did not appear like a sovereign; when I drew near to him, I saw nothing venerable about him. Abruptly he asked me, 'How can the kingdom be settled?' I replied, 'It will be settled by being united under one sway.' 'Who can so unite it?'"
I replied, "He who has no pleasure in killing people can so unite it." "Who can give it to him?" I replied, "All the people of the nation will unanimously give it to him. Does your Majesty understand the way of the growing grain? During the seventh and eighth months, when drought prevails, the plants become dry. Then the clouds collect densely in the heavens, they send down torrents of rain, and the grain erects itself, as if by a shoot. When it does so, who can keep it back? Now among the shepherds of people throughout the nation, there is not one who does not find pleasure in killing people. If there were one who did not find pleasure in killing people, all the people in the nation would look towards him with outstretched necks. Such being indeed the case, the people would flock to him, as water flows downwards with a rush, which no one can repress."
The King Xuan of Qi asked, saying, "May I be informed by you of the transactions of Huan of Qi, and Wen of Jin?"
Mencius replied, "There were none of the disciples of Zhongni who spoke about the affairs of Huan and Wen, and therefore they have not been transmitted to these after-ages—your servant has not heard them. If you will have me speak, let it be about royal government."
The king said, "What virtue must there be in order to attain to royal sway?"
Mencius answered, "The love and protection of the people; with this there is no power which can prevent a ruler from attaining to it."
The king asked again, "Is such an one as I competent to love and protect the people?" Mencius said, "Yes." "How do you know that I am competent for that?"
I heard the following incident from Hu He: "The king," said he, "was sitting aloft in the hall, when a person appeared, leading an ox past the lower part of it. The king saw him, and asked, 'Where is the ox going?' The person replied, 'We are going to consecrate a bell with its blood.' The king said, 'Let it go. I cannot bear its frightened appearance, as if it were an innocent person going to the place of death.' The person answered, 'Shall we then omit the consecration of the bell?' The king said, 'How can that be omitted? Change it for a sheep.'" I do not know whether this incident really occurred.
The king replied, "It did," and then Mencius said, "The heart seen in this is sufficient to carry you to the royal sway. The people all supposed that your Majesty grudged the animal, but your servant knows surely, that it was your Majesty's not being able to bear the sight, which made you do as you did."
The king said, "You are right. And yet there really was an appearance of what the people condemned. But though Qi be a small and narrow State, how should I grudge one ox! Indeed it was because I could not bear its frightened appearance, as if it were an innocent person going to the place of death, that therefore I changed it for a sheep."
Mencius pursued, "Let not your Majesty deem it strange that the people should think you were grudging the animal. When you changed a large one for a small, how should they know the true reason? If you felt pained by its being led without guilt to the place of death, what was there to choose between an ox and a sheep?"
The king laughed and said, "What really was my mind in the matter! I did not grudge the expense of it, and changed it for a sheep! There was reason in the people's saying that I grudged it."
"There is no harm in their saying so," said Mencius. "Your conduct was an artifice of benevolence. You saw the ox, and had not seen the sheep. So is the superior person affected towards animals, that, having seen them alive, one cannot bear to see them die; having heard their dying cries, one cannot bear to eat their flesh. Therefore one keeps away from one's slaughter-house and cook-room."
The king was pleased, and said, "It is said in the Book of Poetry, 'The minds of others, I am able by reflection to measure;' this is verified, my Master, in your discovery of my motive. I indeed did the thing, but when I turned my thoughts inward, and examined into it, I could not discover my own mind. When you, Master, spoke those words, the movements of compassion began to work in my mind. How is it that this heart has in it what is equal to the royal sway?"
Mencius replied, "Suppose a person were to make this statement to your Majesty:—'My strength is sufficient to lift three thousand catties, but it is not sufficient to lift one feather; my eyesight is sharp enough to examine the point of an autumn hair, but I do not see a waggon-load of faggots;' would your Majesty allow what he said?" "No," was the answer, on which Mencius proceeded,
"'Now here is kindness sufficient to reach to animals, and no benefits are extended from it to the people—How is this? Is an exception to be made here? The truth is, the feather is not lifted, because strength is not used; the waggon-load of firewood is not seen, because the eyesight is not used; and the people are not loved and protected, because kindness is not employed. Therefore your Majesty's not exercising the royal sway, is because you do not do it, not because you are not able to do it."
The king asked, "How may the difference between the not doing a thing, and the not being able to do it, be represented?"
Mencius replied, "In such a thing as taking the Tai mountain under your arm, and leaping over the north sea with it, if you say to people—'I am not able to do it,' that is a real case of not being able. In such a matter as breaking off a branch from a tree at the order of a superior, if you say to people—'I am not able to do it,' that is a case of not doing it, it is not a case of not being able to do it. Therefore your Majesty's not exercising the royal sway, is not such a case as that of taking the Tai mountain under your arm, and leaping over the north sea with it. Your Majesty's not exercising the royal sway is a case like that of breaking off a branch from a tree."
"Treat with the reverence due to age the elders in your own family, so that the elders in the families of others shall be similarly treated; treat with the kindness due to youth the young in your own family, so that the young in the families of others shall be similarly treated—do this, and the kingdom may be made to go round in your palm. It is said in the Book of Poetry, 'His example affected his wife. It reached to his brothers, and his family of the State was governed by it.'—The language shows how King Wen simply took his kindly heart, and exercised it towards those parties. Therefore the carrying out his kindness of heart by a prince will suffice for the love and protection of all within the four seas, and if he do not carry it out, he will not be able to protect his wife and children. The way in which the ancients came greatly to surpass other people, was no other but this:—simply that they knew well how to carry out, so as to affect others, what they themselves did."
Now your kindness is sufficient to reach to animals and no benefits are extended from it to reach the people. How is this? Is an exception to be made here?
"By weighing, we know what things are light, and what heavy. By measuring, we know what things are long, and what short. The relations of all things may be thus determined, and it is of the greatest importance to estimate the motions of the mind. I beg your Majesty to measure it."
"You collect your equipments of war, endanger your soldiers and officers, and excite the resentment of the other princes—do these things cause you pleasure in your mind?"
The king replied, "No. How should I derive pleasure from these things? My object in them is to seek for what I greatly desire."
Mencius said, "May I hear from you what it is that you greatly desire?" The king laughed and did not speak.
Mencius resumed, "Are you led to desire it, because you have not enough of rich and sweet food for your mouth? Or because you have not enough of light and warm clothing for your body? Or because you have not enough of beautifully coloured objects to delight your eyes? Or because you have not voices and tones enough to please your ears? Or because you have not enough of attendants and favourites to stand before you and receive your orders? Your Majesty's various officers are sufficient to supply you with those things. How can your Majesty be led to entertain such a desire on account of them?" "No," said the king; "my desire is not on account of them."
Mencius added, "Then, what your Majesty greatly desires may be known. You wish to enlarge your territories, to have Qin and Chu wait at your court, to rule the Middle Kingdom, and to attract to you the barbarous tribes that surround it. But doing what you do to seek for what you desire is like climbing a tree to seek for fish." The king said, "Is it so bad as that?"
"It is even worse," was the reply. "If you climb a tree to seek for fish, although you do not get the fish, you will not suffer any subsequent calamity. But doing what you do to seek for what you desire, doing it moreover with all your heart, you will assuredly afterwards meet with calamities." The king asked, "May I hear from you the proof of that?"
Mencius said, "If the people of Zou should fight with the people of Chu, which of them does your Majesty think would conquer?" "The people of Chu would conquer."
"Yes; and so it is certain that a small country cannot contend with a great, that few cannot contend with many, that the weak cannot contend with the strong. The territory within the four seas embraces nine divisions, each of a thousand li square. All Qi together is but one of them. If, with one part you try to subdue the other eight, what is the difference between that and Zou's contending with Chu? For, with such a desire, you must turn back to the proper course for its attainment."
"Now, if your Majesty will institute a government whose action shall be benevolent, this will cause all the officers in the kingdom to wish to stand in your Majesty's court, and all the farmers to wish to plough in your Majesty's fields, and all the merchants, both travelling and stationary, to wish to store their goods in your Majesty's market-places, and all travelling strangers to wish to make their tours on your Majesty's roads, and all throughout the kingdom who feel aggrieved by their rulers to wish to come and complain to your Majesty. And when they are so bent, who will be able to keep them back?"
The king said, "I am stupid, and not able to advance to this. I wish you, my Master, to assist my intentions. Teach me clearly; although I am deficient in intelligence and vigour, I will essay and try to carry your instructions into effect."
Mencius replied, "They are only people of education, who, without a certain livelihood, are able to maintain a fixed heart. As to the people, if they have not a certain livelihood, it follows that they will not have a fixed heart. And if they have not a fixed heart, there is nothing which they will not do, in the way of self-abandonment, of moral deflection, of depravity, and of wild license. When they thus have been involved in crime, to follow them up and punish them—this is to entrap the people. How can such a thing as entrapping the people be done under the rule of a benevolent person? Therefore an intelligent ruler will regulate the livelihood of the people, so as to make sure that, for those above them, they shall have sufficient wherewith to serve their parents, and, for those below them, sufficient wherewith to support their wives and children; that in good years they shall always be abundantly satisfied, and that in bad years they shall escape the danger of perishing. After this he may urge them, and they will proceed to what is good, for in this case the people will follow after it with ease."
"Now, the livelihood of the people is so regulated, that, above, they have not sufficient wherewith to serve their parents, and, below, they have not sufficient wherewith to support their wives and children. Notwithstanding good years, their lives are continually embittered, and, in bad years, they do not escape perishing. In such circumstances they only try to save themselves from death, and are afraid they will not succeed. What leisure have they to cultivate propriety and righteousness?"
"If your Majesty wishes to effect this regulation of the livelihood of the people, why not turn to that which is the essential step to it?"
"Let mulberry-trees be planted about the homesteads with their five mu, and persons of fifty years may be clothed with silk. In keeping fowls, pigs, dogs, and swine, let not their times of breeding be neglected, and persons of seventy years may eat flesh. Let there not be taken away the time that is proper for the cultivation of the farm with its hundred mu, and the family of eight mouths that is supported by it shall not suffer from hunger. Let careful attention be paid to education in schools, the inculcation in it especially of the filial and congenial duties, and grey-haired men will not be seen upon the roads, carrying burdens on their backs or on their heads. It never has been that the ruler of a State where such results were seen—the old wearing silk and eating flesh, and the black-haired people suffering neither from hunger nor cold—did not attain to the royal dignity."

zh:
当年墨门之中，有一长老前后收下五名弟子。因五人皆研习精微机关之法，多造奇物，被门中其他弟子并称“五奇”。其中最末一位，是在山外战火中侥幸逃脱，碰巧流亡入的不见山。其心中恨欲难息，以所学精微机关术，制造各类毒虫，意图学成后出山复仇。长老见其心术难正，始终未倾囊相授。
四位师兄师姐游学在际，出山前，做毒虫机关，以奇音诱杀山中毒物。只为向师父证明，毒虫机关亦可为有益之事。并在共制五毒过程中，悄然将精微机关术的最后法门传授师弟。
拏云蛇为当年五毒虫之一，为二师兄叶卓所作。
但愿清商复为假，拔去万累云间翔。
en:
Years ago, a Mohist elder took five disciples. Because all five studied the art of precision mechanisms and created many strange objects, they were known as the "Five Wonders" by the other disciples. The last of them had escaped the war outside and happened to flee into Hidden Mountain. His heart was filled with unquenchable hatred, and he used his knowledge to create various venomous insects, intending to seek revenge once his studies were complete. Seeing his improper intent, the elder never taught him his full knowledge.
Before the four senior disciples left on their travels, they created venomous mechanism insects to lure and kill the venomous creatures in the mountains using special sounds. They did this to prove to their master that venomous mechanisms could also be used for good. While co-creating the Five Venoms, they quietly passed the final secrets of precision mechanisms to their junior brother.
The Cloudclutch Serpent was one of the Five Venoms, created by the second brother, Ye Zhuo.
May the pure sound return as truth, casting off ten thousand burdens to soar among the clouds.

zh:
这里本该有多美啊，她真希望遍地都是红枫叶。
可现实留给她的，只有满地染血的盔甲。
她孤零零地伫立在这片血色焦土，当真也有一瞬怀疑过，墨山道要寻的桃源可在这世上？
想要找，就真能找到吗。即使找到了，到那时，还有人能够欣享吗。
人命如枯叶，连秋天都过不了。
她从不落败的心里竟生出一丝寂寞的凉意。
师父和她说，生如四季，秋天总是最短。
即使难过，也总会很快过去。
她抬头望着千里之外的方向，不知那不见山中的秋天会是怎样。
他们此刻，在真正的红枫下，像从前那样，等着自己吗？
想到这里，她又觉得能熬过这个秋天了。
en:
How beautiful this place should have been. She truly wished the ground were covered in red maple leaves.
But reality left her with nothing but blood-stained armor scattered across the earth.
Standing all alone upon this scorched earth, for a fleeting moment, she genuinely doubted: Does the Haven sought by the Mohist Hill truly exist in this world?
If one seeks it, can it actually be found? And even if it is, by then, will there be anyone left to share in the joy?
Human lives felt as fragile as withered leaves, unable to even survive the autumn.
A quiet, lonely chill crept into her otherwise unyielding heart.
Master once told her that life is like the four seasons, and autumn is always the shortest.
No matter how bitter, it will always pass swiftly.
She raised her head and gazed toward a place thousands of miles away, wondering what autumn must look like in the Hidden Mountain.
Were they, at this very moment, standing beneath real red maples, waiting for her just as they always did?
With that thought, she felt she could endure this autumn after all.

zh:
一个人为了弥补一生的遗憾，愿意付出什么？——沈义伦的答案是：倾尽所能。
他也的确是这样做的。他朝着“天下常平”的方向踽踽独行，慢慢走过了十二年的光阴。直到常平仓高高地耸立在金色的麦田上、直到八方粮草逐渐将其填满，他终于开始觉得故友们的约定不再那般遥不可及。可紧接着，朝廷宣布将平野原托与非人、又将粮草仅供军用……现实的冷雨很快便将理想的心火浇了个所剩无几。
沈义伦没有放弃。他在南巡归来的途中计划着奏疏、谏策、赈济……可一切又都被一场突如其来的劫持打断。再被擒捉的那一刻，他以为这便是终结了，心中不由生出许多的不甘来。但是紧接着，巨大的惊愕瞬间击中了他，因为他认出了“故友”。

自离开开封的那一刻，沈义伦便从未奢想过自己与阿郑的再见。于是当最初的震惊淡去后，他的心底除却难以遏制的、对好友走上歧路的悲痛，在一处隐秘的角落，竟有一股细小的喜悦，在偷偷蔓延。这喜悦既因好友的意外生还而生，却也关乎他自己。因为他前所未有地发觉，自己竟然有机会获得救赎、有机会挽回那个从十二年前便延续至今的错。
可惜事情的发展，很快便超出了沈义伦的想象。那株幕天席地的朝生暮落花直截了当地向他诉说了一个无比残忍的事实：他记忆中的故友，还是被乱世、被恶人，还有……他自己，埋葬了。可沈义伦无法接受约定的破灭，——尤其是被长大后的故友亲手摧毁。所以在那暗无天日的时日里，他调查着、祈祷着，直到他真的如十二年前那般，再度遇到了一个正直而善良的少年。
于是冲天的烈焰再度燃起。十二年前，烈火将郑家主宅、将少年们的天真与善意统统烧成灰烬；十二年后，愈发炽热的火焰将如今的罪业和过去的执念尽数化为乌有。沈义伦望着眼前失魂落魄的故友，发觉他的身影终究与曾经的少年再度重叠起来。
——“从今以后，你是真正的常平使了。”
缓缓吐出最后一口气、说出最后一句话，沈义伦明白，这便是真正的终结了。在踏上这条路时，他坚定地认为自己必将倾尽所有、绝无二念。可真到了心愿得偿的这一刻，除了欣慰，更多的不甘和歉意从心底里涌出来。
因为在阖上双眼的那一刻，沈义伦恍惚觉得自己似乎是回到了久远前的过去，又像是去往了不知名的未来。在那里，“常平使”独自一人望着一望无际的麦田，稚嫩而善良的少年们嬉笑着从麦浪里穿梭而过，漫山遍野都是香甜又温柔的麦香。
en:
What will a man sacrifice to atone for a lifetime of regrets?
For Shen Yilun, the answer was simple: Everything.
And so he did. For twelve solitary years, he trudged toward that vision of "Ever-Normal for All". Until the Ever-Normal Granary rose tall over golden wheat fields. Until carts of grain from all directions filled them to the brim. For a fleeting moment, his friends' long-ago vow seemed almost within reach. Then the court handed Plainfield to monsters and rationed the grain for war. Cold reality doused the flames of idealism, leaving only embers. Still, he persisted. On his return from a southern inspection, he plotted memorials, strategies, and relief efforts until a sudden kidnapping interrupted everything. As he was seized, he braced for death, consumed by regret. Then, shocked, he recognized his "old friend".

From the moment he left Kaifeng, Shen Yilun had never dared to hope for a reunion with A'zheng. So when the initial shock faded, his heart was overwhelmed by grief at his friend's descent into darkness. But in a hidden corner, a tiny flicker of joy began to grow. Part of this joy came from the sheer miracle of A'zheng's survival, but another part was selfishly personal: for the first time, he saw a chance at redemption, a way to undo the mistakes that had haunted him for twelve long years.
Unfortunately, events soon spiraled beyond Shen Yilun's control. The towering Dawn-to-Dusk Blossom laid bare a cruel truth: the friend he remembered had been buried by chaos, by villains, and... by himself. Shen Yilun refused to accept the shattered promise, especially when it was his grown friend who'd destroyed it. So in those endless dark days, he sought and prayed, until fate led him to another honest, kind-hearted boy, just as it had twelve years before.
And so the towering flames rose again. Twelve years prior, fire had reduced the Zheng family mansion and the teenagers' innocence and kindness to ash. Twelve years later, an even hotter blaze consumed both present-day sins and past obsessions. Gazing at his disoriented old friend, Shen Yilun found that the man's shadow at last overlapped with the boy he had once known.
"From now on, you are the true Master of Grain."
With those final words, exhaled on his final breath, Shen Yilun knew: This is the end. When he'd begun this path, he'd been certain he'd give everything without hesitation. Yet now, with his wish fulfilled, what surged up wasn't peace, but regret. Regret and apology.
For as his eyes closed, he thought he'd stepped back into the past or forward into an unknown future. There, the "Master of Grain" stood alone in endless wheat fields, while young, kind boys laughed and raced through the golden waves, the air thick with the sweet, gentle scent of grain.

而今年岁渐长，更觉时不我待。此生须臾间，诚专于机巧仍寸进之功，憾矣！


一日温书，忽有所感：昔愚公不以石厚而止志，日抡其凿，世继其功，而山终改易。一如耕种事，培土浇灌、日日复之，亦终有所获。

——墨门隐山千载，其所求何日可得？旧址烛火照吾，吾亦可照后来者。
兴雨祈祈，西出天弓；东风有幸，得谷芃芃 。
云槎日后改轨更易，或创制“星槎”于天，可尽托于后世。
en:
The sect's affairs are burdensome, and I am constantly called away from the mountain on our master's errands to visit old friends at Dragonbend Academy. Though you returned years ago, we have not once had the chance for a long conversation. The days of our youth feel as distant as the fading starlight.

The Sky Shuttle is now complete; it awaits only your finished water rails to be set in motion. Yet, though we bestow upon it the name "Sky Shuttle," it possesses no true ability to fly. I must confess, my aptitude for the mechanical arts has always been dull.

As my years increase, I feel the pressing weight of time. Life is but a fleeting moment. It is my deepest regret that even with a lifetime devoted to these mechanisms, true progress remains merely an inch out of reach!

While reviewing some texts the other day, a sudden realization struck me: In ancient times, the Foolish Old Man was not deterred by the sheer mass of the mountain. He struck with his chisel day after day, his descendants continuing his labor, until the mountain's shape was finally altered. It is much like farming. One turns the soil, waters the seeds, and repeats the toil daily, until the harvest is inevitably reaped.

Our sect has hidden in these mountains for a thousand years. When will our ultimate pursuit be realized? Just as the candlelight of this old sanctuary illuminates my present, so too can I become the light for those who follow.

Rain and prayers, a rainbow in the west... Blessed by the east wind, may the harvest flourish.

Whether the Sky Shuttle is one day rebuilt along a new course, or a true "Star Raft" is fashioned to cross the heavens, these things I must leave to those who follow.
Han Jiangliu

生意……莫不如设个耀武堂，能接我五十招的，送个木雕像，立在堂前。论回合排座次，只留前五十。谁打上去，谁就把人挤下来。那些好武之人，想必乐意争这个彩头。
可惜那木雕师傅不肯离山……我还在磨他，事成再叙。
en:
On my latest wanderings, I ran into a master woodcarver. His craft is unbelievable. The figures he carves look practically alive. I stood staring at his stall for ages, and suddenly remembered something the guys back at the hall used to say: "Business has to move with the times."
Speaking of business... I was thinking, why not set up a fighting arena? Anyone who can last fifty moves against me gets a custom wooden statue of themselves displayed right in the front hall. We'd rank the top fifty based on how many rounds they last. If a new challenger makes the cut, the one at the bottom gets bumped off the leaderboard. I bet the martial arts crowd would go crazy for that kind of bragging rights.
The only problem is the carver absolutely refuses to leave the mountain... I'm still working on him, though. I'll keep you posted if I pull it off.

zh:
自萧关古道南行，过松树湾，见一庐坐落烟柳中，门前清溪绕过，风中散有药香。
有诸人聚于檐下，或眉含愁绪，或捂身嚎哭。相传庐中有一神医，可活死人，肉白骨，此间人物皆慕名而来。
细观往来众人，有不少江湖客，面色红润，伤势又轻，不求医者垂怜，却游走于病者之间，似是窥探何事。
既无病痛，又不寻宝，无须多待。然此地药香隐隐，间有重疾得救者嘤咛笑语，令人不禁莞尔展颜，觉人间疾苦，随水逝也。
en:
South along the Xiao Pass Old Road, past Pine Tree Bend, I came upon a cottage nestled in misty willows. A clear stream ran before its door, and on the breeze rode the faint scent of herbs.
Beneath the eaves, some furrowed with worry, while others clutched themselves and wailed. Legend says a divine physician dwells here, one who can restore the dead and regrow the bone. The desperate flock here from far and wide.
Among them were many jianghu wanderers, healthy, lightly injured. They sought no cure but drifted through the sick, eyes sharp, as if gathering intelligence.
For the healthy and those not hunting treasure, there was little reason to linger. Yet the soft aroma of medicine and the occasional laughter of the healed brought a smile. For a moment, it seemed the sorrows of the world had slipped away with the stream.

zh: 萧萧是一只细犬，价值千金。但对于这四季宅邸的主人来说，千金与万金无甚区别。见过萧萧的人都会夸赞它细长而骨感的身形，夸赞公子眼光独到，能觅得这样一只疾如烈风的细犬。如今，这一阵来自西北的烈风，只是安安静静卧在江南豪宅中的秋天里。萧萧抬起头，看着四四方方的天。天底下是它看不懂的亭台楼阁，身边是步履匆匆的人们。萧萧记得，它小时候的天不是这样的。那时候，天好高好高，天边覆盖着黄黄的尘土，和远方的大地连在一起，怎么都跑不到尽头。它记得太阳大剌剌挂在正当空，阳光直直地洒下来，照得它身上热乎乎。它记得风路过它，吹迷它的视线，把它刮得生疼，却又托着它，让它越跑越快、越跑越快，它喜欢那种感觉。萧萧站起身，恰好园中风起，凄凄瑟瑟，吹散一地秋叶。江南的风太柔了，托不起小狗的自由。
en: Gale is a slender hound worth a thousand gold. But to the master of the Four Seasons Residence, a thousand gold and ten thousand make no difference. Everyone who sees Gale praises his lean, sinewy frame, and praises the master's discerning eye for finding a hound as swift as the high wind. Now, that gale from the northwest lies quietly in the autumn of a grand Jiangnan mansion. Gale lifts his head, gazing up at the small square of sky above. Beneath that sky are pavilions and towers he can't make sense of, and all around him, people are always in a hurry. Gale remembers that the sky wasn't like this when he was small. Back then it went up and up, edges dusted with yellow earth where it met the distant land, and no matter how he ran, he never reached the end of it. He remembers the sun hanging bold overhead, the light coming straight down, warm all over him. He remembers the wind going past, blurring his eyes, scouring him raw, and yet holding him up all the same, so he ran faster and faster still. He loved that. Gale gets to his feet, just as the wind comes through the garden, cold and mournful, scattering the autumn leaves. Jiangnan's wind is too soft. It can't lift a dog's freedom.

zh:
天资太过，便生疲懒。
叶卓总是眯着眼睛，打着哈欠，像一只永远睡不醒的狐狸。
门中弟子都喜欢叫他叶半仙，这半仙之名背后，其实没什么筹算天地的伟业，不过是帮着山中弟子解决些小的疑难。或是逃课被抓如何应对，或是师父留下的问题该当何解，或是面见长老可能会考校何物。他总是优哉游哉，三言两语便将困扰少年们许久的问题全都解决，将省事偷懒之道发扬光大。

至于师父那精微簧机之术，他其实也早掌握。只是师父不催，那便不急着说，免得又有新的东西要学。
天地万物，皆有其理。不必窥见太多，够用就行。山中之理，悟个七八，则足度余生。
天下第一等大事，还是好好睡觉才是。以半仙之名，居山水之间，岂不美哉！
只是当师兄向他嘱托山中诸事时，他觉察出了异样。
师兄不擅说谎，叶卓则不擅受骗。

师父曾特意叮嘱：“师兄弟五人之中，你处事最灵活。老大正气有余，却少变通，你要帮为师多看着些他。”叶卓终是将这叮嘱当了耳旁风。
嗯，出山，那便须知时局人心。如今诸将猜忌，恩怨久积；各方势力盘根错节，野心之人藏于暗地……要理清楚，当真是天下最麻烦的事！

不过离了我，要你们理清不更是够呛，能成事么？也罢也罢，便再小小地，辛苦一下吧。他伸了个懒腰，打起了些精神：
“你若要出山救楚国百姓，算我一个。”
“将军”出山，怎可无“军师”？蜉蝣之人，将拏云而去。

只是出山那年，内丘的雨太冷太长。
那山中半仙再无半刻偷闲，殚精竭虑，沥尽所学，终究未能以弱胜强到最后。
光阴流转，山外天地改换，那场战役与无数前事并无两样，不过化作飞烟，无数名姓就此掩埋，如不曾存在；山中“五奇”之名也已不闻，空余机括，结尘山间。
“契丹主将数万骑入寇，攻内丘，五日不克，死伤甚众。有戍兵五百叛应契丹，引契丹入城，屠之，又陷饶阳。”
这青史太硬太冷，多少飞蛾扑火，才能换来，一笔镌改？
en:
Excessive talent often breeds a spirit of sloth. Ye Zhuo had a habit of narrowing his eyes whenever he smiled, giving him the appearance of a perpetually drowsy, cunning fox.
The other disciples affectionately called him "Ye the Half-Immortal." Yet this nickname did not stem from any grand ambition to shape the cosmos. He simply helped his peers with their mundane troubles: how to talk their way out of being caught skipping class, how to unravel the puzzles their master had left behind, or what topics the elders might quiz them on.

He always seemed unhurried. With just a few casual words, he could untangle problems that had left the younger disciples in knots for days, elevating the art of saving effort to absolute perfection.
As for his master's intricate arts of springs and clockwork, he had mastered them long ago. Yet since his master never pressed him, he saw no reason to show it off, as boasting would only invite more lessons to learn.

All things in this world carry their own truths. There is no need to pry too deeply; knowing enough to get by is enough. To grasp but seventy percent of the wisdom hidden within the mountain is more than sufficient to weather a lifetime.
The greatest priority in this world, after all, is a good night's sleep. To dwell among mountains and streams carrying the title of "Half-Immortal" is surely the height of bliss!

But when his Eldest Brother came to entrust him with the affairs of the sect, he sensed a ripple in the still waters. His brother had always been a poor liar, and Ye Zhuo had never been an easy man to deceive.
His master had once warned him: "Among the five of you, you are the most adaptable. The Eldest is overflowing with righteousness but lacks flexibility. You must help me keep watch over him."

In the end, Ye Zhuo had let those words drift past his ears like the wind.
Fine. To descend the mountain is to be swept into the currents of the age.
The generals harbor deep suspicions, and old grudges have calcified. Factions intertwine like twisted roots, and the ambitious lurk in the shadows. To untangle such a web is truly the most vexing chore under Heaven!
But without me, I doubt any of you could even begin to sort out this mess. Could you truly prevail? Very well. I suppose I can endure a little more hardship.

"If you intend to descend the mountain and save the commoners of Chu, count me in."
How could a "General" march onto the battlefield without his "Strategist"? A mere mayfly of a man, reaching out to grasp the clouds.

Yet in the year they left the mountain, the rains of Neiqiu were far too cold, and far too long.
That Half-Immortal found not a single moment of rest. He exhausted his mind and poured out every ounce of his knowledge, yet in the end, he could not turn the tide for the weak against the strong.
Time flowed onward, and the world changed. That battle became no different from countless others before it, fading into smoke. Countless names were buried in the earth as though they had never drawn breath. The mountain's "Five Wonders" were spoken of no more, leaving their ingenious mechanisms to gather dust beneath the pines.

The historical chronicles, blunt and unforgiving, record it only thus:
"The Khitan general led tens of thousands of cavalry to invade the borders, assaulting Neiqiu. After five days, they failed to capture the city and suffered heavy casualties. Five hundred garrison soldiers rebelled, opening the gates to the Khitan forces. The garrison was slaughtered, and Raoyang fell."
History is a hard, cold stone. How many moths must fling themselves into the flames just to alter a single line carved upon it?
Militiaman

zh:
昔在明皇帝，召叶尊师。当新岁月圆之夜，是上元灯设之时。帝谓京洛，他处固难比也；师言良夜，今宵亦可观之。
于是请宸游，凭妙术。将越天宇，俄辞宣室。扶凤辇以云举，揭翠华而飙疾。不假御风之道，倏忽乘虚；如因缩地之方，逡巡驻跸。已觉夫关陇途尽，河湟景新。
到遝杂繁华之地，见骈阗游看之人。千条银烛，十里香尘。红楼逦迤以如昼，清夜荧煌而似春。
郡实武威，事同仙境。彩摇金像之色，光夺玉蟾之影。一游一豫，忽此地以微行；不识不知，竟何人而望幸。于时有露沾草，无云在天。
金鸭扬辉而光散，冰荷含耀以星连。乐异梨园，徒笙歌之满听；人非别馆，空罗绮以盈前。既而斗转玉绳，漏深银箭。周回未惬于睿旨，历览尚劳于宸眷。
莫不混迹尊卑，和光贵贱。亦由凤隐形于众鸟，众鸟莫知；龙匿影于群鱼，群鱼不见。
俄而归思潜轸，皇情不留。仿佛而方离边郡，斯须而已在神州。稍异穆王，至自瑶池之会；非同汉武，来从柏谷之游。
一自风灭兰釭，云迎羽客。尘昏蕃塞之草，烟暝秦陵之柏。空令思唐德之遗民，最悲凉于此夕。
en:
In the reign of Emperor Ming of Tang, the Master Ye Fashan was summoned. It was the night of the first full moon of the new year, the very hour when the Lantern Festival lights were displayed. The emperor remarked that the capital Luoyang was beyond compare elsewhere, yet the master said that even on this fine night, the spectacle could still be witnessed. 
Thereupon, he invited the emperor on a celestial journey, relying on wondrous arts. They were about to traverse the heavens when, in an instant, they departed the palace. The imperial phoenix carriage rose upon clouds, its emerald banners fluttering swift as a gale. Without relying on the art of riding the wind, they soared through the void in a flash. As if using the art of shrinking the earth, they halted in a moment. Soon, they felt the journey through Guanlong end, and the scenery of Hehuang unfold anew. 
Arriving at a bustling, prosperous place, they saw crowds of sightseers. A thousand silver lanterns glowed, fragrant dust filled ten miles of roads. Red mansions stretched endlessly, as bright as daytime, the clear night shimmered, as warm as spring. 
This prefecture was indeed Wuwei, its scenery like a fairyland. Colors flickered, reflecting the golden Buddha statues; light dazzled, outshining the jade toad in the sky. Wandering and enjoying, they wandered incognito here. No one recognized them, who could have expected the imperial visit? At that time, dew moistened the grass, and not a cloud dotted the sky. 
Golden duck-shaped incense burners radiated light, ice-like lotus lanterns held glow, connected like stars. The music was different from the Masked Troupe, yet flutes and songs filled the ears. The people were not from the imperial villa, yet silk and brocade filled the sight. Soon, the dipper shifted, and the silver arrow of the water clock marked the late hour. Wandering around did not fully satisfy the emperor's wish, viewing all still tired his royal attention. 
They mingled with people of high and low status, blending light with the common. Just as a phoenix hides its form among birds, and birds do not know it, a dragon conceals its shadow among fish, and fish do not see it. 
Soon homesickness crept in, and the emperor did not detain him. In a trance, he left the frontier, and in an instant, returned to the central plains. Unlike King Mu returning from the Jade Pool feast, or Emperor Wu coming back from the Bogu trip. 
Since lanterns died and immortals departed, weeds on frontier forts dim with dust, cypresses by Qin Mausoleums veiled in dusk. Only survivors mourning Tang's grace feel deepest sorrow on this night.

zh: 和其他猫一样，西米起得晚，总要到了日上三竿，才会悠悠转醒，小爪子开花，伸个大大的懒腰，最后晃晃猫头站起身。和其他猫不一样，西米用毛茸茸的前爪洗了洗猫脸，每天的悠闲时间基本也就结束了。当年小会首慧眼识猫，从仓库角落里刚出生的一窝小猫仔中一眼相中了它，取名西米。猫儿长得快，小会首好生喂了几个月，它就成了能独当一面的平粟仓“小管家”。仓库里人员往来频繁，各家管着各家的事，矛盾摩擦总是一波未平一波又起。西米爱操心，若是见着几人吵起来，就翘着尾巴从几个人中间跃过，喵喵几声，分别蹭蹭两侧的衣角。西米不明白，人为什么要吵架呢？明明每日的事情忙都忙不完。脑袋灵光的小猫当然也忙着自家事，这“小管家”并不是浪得虚名。西米目光如炬、身手敏捷，没有一只老鼠能逃出它的小爪心。
en: Like any other cat, Ximi rose late, never stirring from sleep until the sun stood high in the sky. Only then would it slowly awaken, little paws blossoming open, back arching in a great stretch, and at last the cat would sway its head and rise to its feet. Unlike other cats, Ximi would wash its furry face with its front paws, and with that, its daily leisure would come to an end. Years ago, the young Guild Leader, with a keen eye for cats, picked this one right out of a litter of newborn kittens tucked in a corner of the warehouse, and named it Ximi. Cats grow quickly, and after a few months of careful feeding by the young Guild Leader, it became the warehouse's very own "Little Steward." With so many people coming and going through the granary, each minding their own affairs, disputes and frictions never ceased, one quarrel settling only for another to rise. Ximi, ever the worrier, would leap between quarreling people whenever it saw them arguing, tail held high, mewing a few times before rubbing against the hems on either side. Ximi could never understand why people quarreled so. After all, there was already barely enough time to finish the day's work. This clever little cat, of course, was also busy with its own affairs; the title of "Little Steward" was no idle boast. With eyes sharp as embers and paws swift as lightning, not a single mouse could ever escape its little claws.

“因遭风雪拦路，只得暂时借宿山脚下的一家客栈。未料数日后风雪散去，这客栈中却遍地尸首，无一人得存。”
“因死状凄惨，见之生怖，便有了传闻，说他们是撞上了那魔头破山而出的日子、遭其屠戮。”
“我稽考旧卷，深觉此中似有隐情，故而闭关在此，制成了这一局“琴宫”，以再现当日情境，破障求真。”
“只是未料……罢了，既被你误触，那便交与你了。传闻那魔头最后现身之处，正是这家客栈。查清此案，便可追知其去向。”
“尔为声之弦，我为琴之身。助此一曲，应律天地。”
en:
"The man you saw was my senior brother, Jian Xingzhi. About 160 years ago, he traveled to Mount Tai for a case."
"Trapped by a blizzard, he took shelter in an inn at the foot of the mountain. But when the snow cleared days later, everyone inside was found dead."
"Their deaths were so gruesome that rumors spread, saying that the fiend had broken free and slaughtered them all."
"I studied the old records and felt something was amiss, so I made this Gong-Note Zither to recreate that day and uncover the truth. I just didn't expect..."
"Well, no matter. Since you've stumbled into this, it's yours to finish now. They say the fiend was last seen at this inn. Solve the case, and you'll learn where she went."
"You are the string. I, the zither. Together, we will harmonize with heaven and earth, and learn the truth."

zh:
范芗芗识字不多，她跟着文津馆的弟子学过几天，歪歪扭扭画了好久。
练得最熟的却不是自己的名字，而是油盐酱醋几个大字。
她有个习惯，路过乐安浦的外乡人，只要吃了她的饭，她都会塞上一张纸，那是她自己写的食谱。
纸是从文津馆弟子那儿讨来的，上头的字，有的描重了，黑乎乎一团。有的写轻了，得凑近看。但每道菜的调料和火候，她都写得很仔细。
旁人看了她的字，笑说跟鸡扒的似的。范芗芗也不恼，把食谱往怀里一揣，说能看懂就成。
她不认得几个字，却把每一个会写的字都用上了。
有人问她，为啥非要写这玩意儿，人家流民连下顿饭在哪儿都不知道，哪有心思想着做菜？
范芗芗擦擦手，说你不懂。
她记得小时候，她娘炖过一锅野菜汤，里头放了点盐和野葱，喝得她浑身暖洋洋的。那是她关于“家”唯一的味道。后来她逃到乐安浦，第一口热粥入嘴，差点哭出来——不是粥多好喝，是那个味道，让她想起了那锅野菜汤。
“往后他们走到哪儿，想吃这口了，照着做就是了。”
范芗芗把食谱叠好，塞到流民的手里，拍了拍她的手背。
“日子总得过下去。有口热乎的，就不算太难。”
en:
Fan Xiangxiang can barely read. She once spent a few days trailing after the Inkbound Order disciples, awkwardly tracing characters until her hand cramped.
Oddly enough, the words she mastered first weren't her own name, but oil, salt, soy sauce, and vinegar.
Over the years, she's developed a quirk: any traveler or refugee who eats at her stall in Tranquil Pier gets a slip of paper pressed into their hands before they leave. It's a handwritten recipe.
The paper is usually scrap she begged off the Inkbound Order disciples, and her handwriting is a complete mess. Some strokes are pressed so hard they bleed into inky blobs, while others are so faint you have to squint. But if you look closely, you'll see that the seasonings and heat levels for every dish are recorded with painstaking precision.
Folks tease her for it, joking that it looks like chicken scratch. Xiangxiang never takes offense. She just tucks the recipes into her apron and shrugs. "As long as it makes sense," she says. She might not know many words, but she puts the few she does know to good use.
Someone once asked her why she even bothered. "These refugees don't even know where their next meal is coming from," they pointed out. "Who has the luxury of worrying about recipes?"
Xiangxiang just wiped her hands on her apron. "You don't get it."
She thought back to when she was a little girl. She remembered her mother boiling a pot of foraged greens, seasoning it with nothing but a pinch of salt and some wild leeks. It warmed her to the bone. To this day, it remains her only memory of what "home" tastes like. Years later, when she finally stumbled into Tranquil Pier and took her first bite of that life-saving porridge, she nearly burst into tears. It wasn't because the food was a culinary masterpiece. It was because that comforting warmth brought her right back to her mother's soup.
"Wherever they end up," Xiangxiang said, "if they ever crave this taste, they'll know how to make it."
Carefully folding a recipe, she pressed it into a passing refugee's hand and gave it a gentle pat.
"Life has to go on. And as long as you've got a hot meal waiting for you, things are never too hard."

有一次村里人怎么都找不到它。就在大家以为快失去它的时候，一声惨叫从柴火堆里传来，一只被烧着尾巴的猫窜了出来。原是它为了暖和，睡在熄了的炭火里，猫猫黑炭差点变成真黑炭啦！
喵喵，喵喵！谁也听不懂它在说什么，许是也被快活的氛围感染了吧。
en:
"Hey! Over here!"

Sooty is a cat often lost, though not by choice. Its ebony fur blends seamlessly with the night. Once it closes its eyes, it vanishes completely into the darkness.
Still, the villagers adore their little shadow, and the nightly search for Sooty has become one of the town's few pastimes.
One time, they couldn't find it anywhere. Just as everyone began to fear the worst, a yowl erupted from a woodpile, and out shot a cat with a singed tail! Sooty had been napping in the warm embers, and almost turned into actual charcoal.
Meow, meow! No one knows what it's saying, but perhaps it's just caught up in the cheerful mood.

zh:
余家共有五个兄弟姐妹。虽说都顶着个“余”字，内里却并无半点血缘，全是已故父母早年间收养的流民孤儿。虽非亲生骨肉，这五个异姓兄妹却在烟火气里处得亲如一家。

二哥颠不来大勺，却生了张和气生财的巧嘴。他干起迎来送往的跑堂营生，活似个永远不知疲倦的陀螺。只是有一点教人头疼：他有个从小玩到大的发小，如今在湖东的“耸翠楼”当差。两人暗地里较着劲，非要在钱塘的跑堂行当里争个“天下第一”。

三妹是个天生的厨痴，那份对火候味道的悟性，大姐自叹不如。索性，余一美便将后厨的掌勺大权全权交托给了她，退居柜台安心盘算账目、做个八面玲珑的掌柜。

四弟脑筋活络，却总爱剑走偏锋，成日里琢磨些新奇菜式，近来正闭门死磕一道“至尊西湖醋鱼”。也不知他从哪路客商那儿学来的黑话，成天念叨着做菜也得“速速更新换代”，新菜谱一张接一张地出，苦了全家人夜夜被他拉着试菜。

五妹年纪最小，却是个闲不住的机灵鬼，成日在店里跑前跑后。偶尔跟着去市集采买，那张小嘴讨价还价的功夫堪称余家之最，连西马塍最精明的菜贩子见了她都得头疼。

对余一美来说，一日里最疲惫的时刻，便是夜深人静时挑灯盘账；可最安心的，往往也是此刻。昏黄的灯火映着窗外湖水的粼粼波光，待到天光破晓，又是一派朝霞晨雾。这日复一日的鲜活盼头，正应了当年父母为酒楼起名的念想——
山穷水尽疑无路，柳暗花明“又一楼”。
en:
All five siblings in Yu Yimei's family bear the name Yu, though none are related by blood. Their late parents adopted them years ago as orphaned refugees. Life together has made them a family through and through.

Her brother is next in age. He can't handle a wok, but he can charm any customer. He greets guests and waits tables with an energy that never seems to run out. The only headache is a private rivalry with a childhood friend who now works at Verdant Tavern, east of the lake. Each is determined to be the finest waiter in all Qiantang.

Her younger sister, the third eldest, lives for cooking. Even Yu Yimei admits she can't match her feel for heat and flavor. So she put her sister in full charge of the kitchen and settled behind the counter, where she now keeps the books and runs the place with easy charm.

The younger of her two brothers is quick-witted and forever trying something unconventional. He spends his days dreaming up new dishes. Lately, he's been holed up trying to perfect "Supreme West Lake Fish in Vinegar Gravy." No one knows which traveling merchant he picked the jargon up from, but he keeps insisting that cooking needs "rapid upgrades," too. New recipes follow one after another, and every night he drags the whole family in to taste them.

Their youngest sister is bright and full of energy, forever dashing about the tavern. Sometimes she tags along to the market for supplies. No one in the family can match her haggling, and even the shrewdest vegetable sellers in West Macheng dread seeing her coming.

Yu Yimei is at her weariest late at night, balancing the books by lamplight after everything has fallen quiet. Yet this is often when she feels most at ease. The dim yellow lamplight mingles with the shimmer of the lake outside her window. Dawn will bring rosy clouds and morning mist once more. The fresh hope each day brings is just what her parents had in mind when they named the tavern:
The road seems lost among hills and streams, until willow shade and bright blossoms reveal "Another Tavern."
Wang Zhushun

朱邪骨勒来自一个遥远的地方。
他记得，那里常年风沙漫天，而到了夜里，风中会传来孩童的嬉笑，妇人的歌唱，还有烛火摇曳声。
他想念那儿。虽然那的人，也和中原人一样，惧他，恨他。但那也有人，护他，爱他。
可惜长沙漫漫，他终是无法再回故土，也再不能见得故人。

在那个阴暗潮湿的地下牢笼里，他来回徘徊，日夜嘶吼，难觅归处。
直到有一日，他听见风声里，传来翅膀的扑棱声，还有清脆的、细弱的，鸟啼声。

不知道神灵是不是听见了他的不安和狂躁，所以派来了这只脆弱的小生命。
他将它捧于掌心，日夜呵护，将所能碰触到的一切美好，尽数奉上。
他在等它长大。
他希望它能飞出去。去替他看看遥远的地方，去听听，风声里的欢笑和烛火摇曳。
en:
Zhuxie Gule came from a distant land.
He remembered endless sandstorms by day, and at night, the wind carrying children's laughter, women's songs, and the flicker of candle flames.
He ached for it. Though its people, like those in the Central Plains, feared and hated him, there had been those who shielded and loved him.
But the vast desert stretched eternally. He could never return, never see those dear faces again.

In that damp, lightless prison beneath the earth, he paced and roared, a creature with no path back.
Until one day, a new sound threaded through the moaning wind: the flutter of wings, followed by a high, fragile chirp.

Had the gods heard his turmoil, sending this delicate creature as a salve?
He cradled the bird in his palm, nurturing it day and night, offering every scrap of beauty he could find.
He waited for it to grow strong.
He hoped it would soar free, to see the distant horizon for him, to hear the laughter and the flicker of flames in the wind.

有人念了首出律的歪诗，它连叫三声，还跳下石栏，抓掉了那人的帽子。

Sonnet likes springs, but it dislikes the tourists gathered around them. Every day, it sits by the spring, listening to them drink wine and compose poetry.

If they get the rhyme wrong, it meows. If the tonal patterns are off, it meows twice. Once, when someone recited a poorly metered, crooked poem, it let out three loud yowls, jumped off the stone railing, and swatted the man's hat right off his head.

"Go pretend to be cultured elsewhere, and stop disturbing my peace," Sonnet thought to itself.

倍倍不知道发生了什么，直到有一日，它见到有个人在桥上插了白色的旗，又对前来的人挥手，是让他们回去，别再经过此地。
这下倍倍听懂了，若是有一脸凶相的坏人路过，它就会乖乖地躲进草里，不让坏人发现自己。
可是倍倍不懂，为什么那么多人看到了白旗，听见了劝告，还是没转身，一股劲地向前冲。它记得住那些前行人的面孔，几乎没有几个还能回来的。
倍倍不明白，为什么猫都懂的道理，这群人却不明白呢？
en:
In Watcher's eyes, many people are big fools.
Watcher had lived by the bridge for a very long time and seen many people in a hurry. But lately, she noticed that everyone passing by carried weapons, which was terrifying, and many were covered in blood, barely able to walk straight.
Watcher didn't know what was happening until one day, she saw a man plant a white flag on the bridge and wave at those approaching, telling them to go back and not pass through.
Watcher understood then. If a fierce-looking villain passed by, she would hide obediently in the grass so they wouldn't find her.
But Watcher didn't understand that why so many people did see the white flag and hear the warning, yet still refuse to turn back, charging forward instead? She remembered the faces of those who went ahead; hardly any of them ever returned.
Watcher didn't understand: why don't these people understand the logic that even a cat knows?

Some say that certain powers in the jianghu are cultivating it in great quantities, though their motives remain unclear. Symptoms of poisoning begin with dry mouth and intense thirst, flushed and dry skin, sometimes accompanied by red rashes, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. This progresses to agitation, panic, delirium, auditory and visual hallucinations, and loss of coordination. In severe cases, symptoms escalate to stupor, convulsions, cyanosis, and ultimately respiratory failure and death.

zh: 火爆破碎即火爆法。用火加热岩石，使岩石内部结构受到破坏。有时用火烧热岩石，泼冷水或醋使岩石在热胀冷缩的作用下破裂，或在醋的作用下变酥。宋祝穆《方舆胜览》卷30说：“辰州府沅陵光明山，一名龙门山，有砂（指辰砂）井，土人采取……烧石取之。”“僚（指少数民族）以薪竹燔火爆石以取之。”
en: Fire-setting was a mining method in which rock was heated until its internal structure weakened and cracked. In some cases, cold water or vinegar was poured over the heated rock, causing it to split through rapid expansion and contraction, or to soften under the action of the vinegar. In Volume 30 of Zhu Mu's Territory Gazetteer from the Song dynasty, it is recorded that on Guangming Mountain in Yuanling, Chenzhou, where cinnabar was mined, the locals "burned the stone to extract it." It also notes that certain tribes "used wood and bamboo as fuel to fire-crack the rock and extract the ore."

原来此地不止藏书，更是皇家宴射之所。想来也是，天子的近臣禁军，当然是既要能文，也需善武！
看着他们射箭的样子，让我也不禁有些手痒！可惜今日守备森严，武德司的察子和监礼的内侍都盯得死紧，不好混入。且先记下此地，改日定要寻个机会，来此地射上几箭，顺道尝尝宴席上的御酒！
en:
No sooner had I drawn near than I heard the twang of bowstrings ringing out beside Purity Tower, mingled with bursts of applause. I found a high spot and stole a look. What a sight. On the archery ground, a band of elites was drilling with the bow, and several feathered arrows were clustered tightly around the bull's-eyes. Clearly, every last one of them was a skilled shot.

So this place not only stores books, but also serves as a ground for royal archery contests. It makes sense enough. The Son of Heaven's close attendants and palace guards must be accomplished in the written word, yet no less proficient in arms.

Watching them shoot made me itch to have a go myself. A pity the place is tightly guarded today. The Imperial Service agents and the eunuchs overseeing the rites are watching the place like hawks, so there is no easy way to slip in. I shall mark this place down for now. I will find a chance to try my hand another day, and perhaps even sample some of the wine being served while I'm at it.

zh: 酒令是饮酒娱戏的产物，筹令是酒令中的主流，筹子则是筹令必用之物。筹，本为算具，多以竹木制作，起初在饮酒中用以计数行酒，渐渐发展为行令的工具，制作时在筹子上刻写好各色令约酒约，行令时按照摇出的筹子所规定的令约行酒，常见酒令如：“劝意到”，意为每个人都喝一些聊表心意；“请人伴五分”，意为找同伴陪饮半杯；“放”，意为本轮无人罚酒，皆大欢喜。
en: Drinking games originated from drinking entertainment, with chip-based games as the mainstream. Chips, originally counting tools mostly made of bamboo or wood, were initially used to count drinks during drinking parties and gradually developed into tools for drinking games. Various rules and regulations were carved on the chips; during the game, drinks were served according to the rules on the drawn chips. Common rules included: "Toast with sincerity", everyone drinks a little to express goodwill; "Invite a companion for half a cup", find a partner to drink half a cup together; "Let it pass", no one is punished in this round, and everyone is happy.

zh:
记录人：丁小柳
监查对象：鸿胪寺少卿 吕从善
事由：前朝留用官员，需观察可有异心。

二月初四
今日起盯梢吕从善。头儿说怕他心里有鬼，我看他心里没鬼，是有病。
今日他在枢密院王大人跟前伺候。王大人嫌茶烫，随口骂了一句。这吕从善跟被火烧了尾巴似的，冲上去就用自己的袖子给茶碗扇风。
扇得太急，袖子上的灰都飘碗里了。
王大人看了一眼那碗茶，脸都绿了，猛地甩了下袖子，却不想吕从善贴得这么近，一下子被掀倒在地。
吕从善非但不怒，反而在地上打了个滚，爬起来赞道：“大人臂力雄浑，这一把挥出了我大宋的国威！”
王大人像看傻子一样看了他一眼，走了。

二月十四
早上眼见着吕从善把家里祖传的玉佩当了，换了一幅画，送去翰林学士李明远府上。
他在门口等了两个时辰，冻得鼻涕直流。
结果李大人看了一眼便说是“不入流之作”，“俗不可耐”。
吕从善愣在那，想夸这画好，又不敢反驳李大人，支支吾吾半天说不出话。
最后人家嫌他碍事，把他赶出来了。
我在房梁上看着都替他累。

三月初一
今天这事更绝。
吕从善在孙羊酒肆碰见殿前司的教头。教头喝多了，在那吹牛说自己靴子脏了没人擦。
吕从善二话不说，蹲下去就给人家擦靴子。
那是大庭广众啊，周围全是人看着。要不是我得猫着，我都想上去把他拉开。
教头酒醒了一半，想来是觉得丢人，一脚把他蹬开，骂他是个软骨头，丢我大宋的脸面。
我觉得骂得在理。

三月十五
跟了差不多俩月了，大约可以确认：此人无谋反之心，亦无做官之能。
他这么拼命巴结，无非是想活命，所以拼命想找根绳子拴住自己，觉得有了主子才安全。
除了看着闹心，倒也没什么大碍。不必再盯了。
en:
Recorded by: Ding Xiaoliu

Subject: Lyu Congshan, Deputy Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial

Reason: A holdover from the previous dynasty. Watch for any sign of disloyalty.



Second Month, Day 4

Started tailing Lyu Congshan today. The chief says he might be hiding something.

From what I can tell, he is not hiding anything. He is just sick in the head.



Today he was attending Lord Wang at the Privy Council. Lord Wang thought the tea was too hot and snapped a curse under his breath.

Lyu Congshan jumped like his tail was on fire and started fanning the teacup with his sleeve.

He fanned so hard the dust flew right into the tea.



Lord Wang took one look and his face went green. He flicked his sleeve in disgust.

Lyu Congshan was standing so close he got knocked flat.



Did he get mad? No.

He rolled once on the ground, popped right back up, and praised, "My lord, what power in your arm. One sweep like that, and you show the might of Great Song!"

Lord Wang stared at him like he was an idiot and walked off.



Second Month, Day 14

This morning I watched Lyu Congshan pawn a family jade pendant, all to buy a painting.

He carried it to the residence of Hanlin Academician Li Mingyuan.



He waited at the gate for two hours in the freezing cold, nose running the whole time.

Lord Li glanced at it and called it "third-rate" and "vulgar beyond measure."



Lyu Congshan froze on the spot. He clearly wanted to praise the thing, but he did not dare argue with Lord Li.

He stammered for ages and could not squeeze out a single proper sentence.

In the end, they got tired of him and threw him out.

I was up on a roof beam watching, and even I felt exhausted for him.



Third Month, Day 1

Today was even worse.



At Sun Yang Tavern, Lyu Congshan ran into an instructor from the Palace Guard.

The man was drunk, bragging that his boots were filthy and no one ever wiped them for him.



Lyu Congshan did not hesitate. He squatted down and started polishing the man’s boots.

In broad daylight. With people staring from all sides.

If I did not have to stay hidden, I would have dragged him away myself.



The instructor sobered up halfway, probably realized how it looked, and kicked Lyu Congshan off.

Then he cursed him for being spineless and a disgrace to Great Song.

I cannot say he was wrong.



Third Month, Day 15

Nearly two months of watching is enough.

Conclusion: no treason in him, and no ability for office either.



He claws at every powerful sleeve for one reason only: to stay alive.

He wants a master to tie himself to, because he thinks that is the only way to be safe.

Annoying to watch, but not dangerous.



Further surveillance unnecessary.

zh:
“南烛公子”是大约十年前，忽现江湖的传奇。
广顺三年，金陵国宴上，契丹使者当席发难，掳了前来献艺的醉花阴美人一路北上。幸而美人在辽周交界偶遇一名前朝儿郎，他一怒之下拔刀斩尽契丹贼子，这才保全了这只芙蓉牡丹。
后南烛与二人驿站邂逅，他感佩“英雄”义行，遂填词一折。其诗文精妙，令人叫绝，不出数旬，“前朝儿郎冲关一怒斩辽使”的故事便在美人的弹唱中传遍南北。
然不久后，契丹竟以此事为由，大举攻周。“英雄”战死疆场，南烛与美人离奇失踪，整件事也因而多了许多阴谋猜想。有人说此三人背后是一盘驱虎吞狼、渔翁得利的大戏，还有人说他们实则皆是与当今武林、朝堂息息相关之辈。
猜想没有结论。只让南烛诗文中烟水迷离的江南风韵，愈发清远悠扬地飘荡九州。
en:
The Shimmer of South is a legend that appeared in jianghu nearly a decade ago.
In the third Guangshun Era, during a royal banquet in Jinling, a Khitan envoy suddenly rebelled, abducting the famed performer from Velvet Shade and fleeing north. But fate intervened at the border between Liao and Zhou, where they encountered a youth from a fallen dynasty. Enraged, he drew his blade and cut down the Khitan raiders. rescuing the lotus from the mire.
Later, at a courier station, the Shimmer of the South crossed paths with the pair. Moved by the young man's valor, he penned a stirring verse. elegant and resounding. Within weeks, the tale of the lone hero who slew the Khitan envoy spread far and wide, carried on the beauty's song and lute.
But the tale soon turned grim. The Khitan used the incident as a pretext for war, launching a full-scale invasion of Zhou. "The young hero" fell on the battlefield. The Shimmer of the South and the beauty vanished without a trace. What remained was rumor and doubt. Some said they were mere pawns in a deeper game; others believed they were linchpins in the tangled fates of court and jianghu alike.
No one ever finds the truth. Only the Shimmer's poems remain, drifting like mist across the rivers of Jiangnan, endlessly sung through the Nine Prefectures.

On the day the Khitans marched into the city, Hong was carrying the medicine he'd bought for his parents. But just moments later, they became hostages beneath Khitan blades.  

The wanderers gathered around Zhu Yousheng, gritting their teeth as the Khitans made their arrogant demands.
They said the people are innocent. Then they said some sacrifices must be made. And finally they said all of this is for the greater good.  

Hong turned and dropped the mo blade in his hand.  
"To hell with it," he thought. "To hell with your greater good. I don't care anymore."

一年过去了……三年过去了……御风安心做起了世间最最娇气的小猫。
en:
Stormlord is a famously picky little cat. 
She only eats the heads of fish, can't sleep if there's any light, and when playing, only lets people pet half her belly. 
But she wasn't always this delicate. 
Back when she was a stray, she drank the dirtiest ditch water, fed on rotten fish bones, and curled up through freezing blizzards. 
Until one day, in a heavy downpour, a hand that smelled faintly of osmanthus plucked her from beneath a wagon wheel. 
The person said that from now on, she can be the most pampered little cat in the world. 
One year passed... three years passed... Stormlord has lived happily as the most pampered little cat in the world.

The Erudition Hall stands in a place of surpassing beauty, with mountains at its feet and the sea at its face. The land embraces both shadow and sunlight. To the left it draws in green peaks layered with verdure, to the right it takes in the vast expanse of the open sea. The hall is built along the momentum of the mountain, its tiered pavilions rising one upon another like a phoenix alighting among the clouds; the sea wind comes from the east, sweeping away the dust and clamor of the world, and fresh air fills one's robes. Though this place was once a desolate valley, today the cultural lineage has taken root and flourished here, and it has become the foremost crown of all academies under heaven.

zh:
张错吾儿，见信如面：

此信见世之时，不知是吾身后何年。契丹兵退否？汝成人否？河伯之名尚在否？此信落笔之时，正是契丹屠京，汴城魂断，河伯缺位，大局无人可掌。吾实难推脱，方代彦霖河伯之位。
敌寇自孟津南渡，将犯博浪沙，官军知晋亡，闭城弃甲，闻风而逃，吾乡父老竟无路可退。前时闻燕南有拒敌之城，守城数月不降，一朝城破，沦刀下冤魂，万里白骨，尽将新鬼换了旧人。
呜呼！自张氏……（模糊不清）今朝满族皆是妇孺老幼，吾虽代河伯之名，却无……（模糊不清）功力微薄，纵有……在手，亦不得驱使龙王万一。此刻间不容发，吾心生一策，虽铤而走险，却急何能择.....张假神河伯之名制众民之怒......
吾此生最不为意者，唯世人言。诈降契丹，人恐身后骂名而不为之，吾为之；假意降虏，人恐遗臭万年而不为之，吾为之；忍耻贪生，人欲为之而意有愧，吾强令众人为之。
自古皆有死，徇义良独稀。众人之唯唯，不如一士之谔谔，以一人千古易名换众生安乐，何其幸也！
然此事关重大，承蒙洛……（模糊不清）方得成功……契丹军中……吾族……此事绝不可为外人知！切记！切记！冯朱二兄弟前去万古一人殿前便已立下血誓，保全……
吾此生所负，唯有阿错，念尔此后遘残，吾虽百身何赎，歉悔之情，万语难陈，奈何敌寇鼓角已鸣，冯朱二人将至，停笔至此......唯愿汝长于河清海晏之世，一生顺遂，喜乐平安。
en:
My dear son,
When you read this, have the Khitan armies retreated? Does the name "River Master" still hold weight? Now, as I write, the Khitan ravage the capital, and chaos reigns. I have no choice but to take up the position of River Master.
The enemy has closed in from the south, threatening Roaring Sands. Our imperial forces have fled, leaving our people trapped with no escape. 
Alas, though I carry River Master's name... (blurred) my power is weak, and I still could not command the Colossus. So I came up with a desperate plan: to pose as River Master and calm the people's wrath. This secret must never be known outside. Feng and Zhu have sworn a blood oath to protect...
Take care.

“以后你俩就是亲姐俩了。”
两个娃子同时抬起头，眼里全是茫然。
他指了指大的：“你是姐姐。”
又指了指小的：“你是妹妹。”
“凭啥她大？”
“因为她比你高半个头。”
“那俺不干！”
“由得你？”
祝丑公眼睛一瞪，凶相毕露。他年轻时脸就不好看，老来多了褶子，更添几分狰狞。
这一瞪，倒教俩娃子齐齐往后缩了缩，像蔫了的小狗。
他放缓声音，似是叹了口气：“你俩没爹没娘，世上就剩自个儿了。往后要活，一个人可活不成。”
他取下一根桃枝，掰成两截，塞进两人手里。
“跪下，对着磕三个头，就是结拜了。以后她护你，你护她，天经地义。”
俩娃子你看看我，我看看你。
大的先跪了，小的犹豫了一下，也跪了。
磕头的时候谁也不说话，磕完头站起来，手里的桃枝谁也没丢。
祝丑公点了点头：“行了，叫爹。”
大的那个嘴快，怯生生地喊了爹。
小的那个咬着嘴唇，瞪了他半天，最后不情不愿地，从牙缝里挤出一声爹。
祝丑公哈哈大笑，笑起来比不笑还难看……
但那是他这辈子第一次觉得，笑这件事，也不赖。
en:
"From now on, you two are sisters."
Both girls looked up at the same time, eyes full of confusion.
He pointed at the older one: "You're the elder sister."
Then pointed at the smaller one: "You're the younger sister."
"Why is she the elder?"
"Because she's half a head taller than you."
"Ain't doing it!"
"Like you get a say?"
Zhu Chougong's eyes flashed, his fierce nature laid bare. His face had never been much to look at even in his youth, and age had only added more wrinkles, lending him an even more menacing look.
That glare alone made both girls shrink back in unison, like a pair of wilted puppies.
He softened his voice, as if sighing: "You two have no father, no mother. In this world, you've only got each other left. To survive from here on, you can't do it alone."
He plucked a peach branch, snapped it in two, and pressed a piece into each of their hands.
"Kneel. Bow three times to each other, and it's settled. You're now sworn sisters. From now on, she protects you, and you protect her. That's just how it should be."
The two girls glanced at each other.
The older one knelt first; the younger hesitated, then knelt as well.
Neither said a word while bowing. When they rose, neither had let go of the peach branch in her hand.
Zhu Chougong nodded. "Good. Now call me Father."
The older one was quick to speak, timidly calling him Father.
The younger one bit her lip, glaring at him for a long while, before finally forcing out a reluctant "Father" through gritted teeth.
Zhu Chougong burst out laughing, and somehow his laugh looked even worse than his usual scowl...
But that was the first time in his life he thought that laughing wasn't so bad after all.

阳光正好，梨花又飘。午后的天光从竹叶罅隙中漏下，洒做碎金。暖洋洋的风像猫狸子，轻轻挠抓搔你的脸。十六岁离家后，你鲜少回到这里。檐下的蛛网结成画，屋子的主人去了天涯。你坐在昔日他坐着的长椅上，想起曾经自己的童言稚语，缓缓入睡。
恍惚间，你睁开眼，竟看到江叔牵着一匹马，向你走来。印象中的江叔背脊永远这般笔直，宽阔的肩膀如山如岗，为你挡下风雨。可如今你却发现他的衣摆有些脏了，脸上似乎也有了微不可察的疲惫。
此刻你有千言万语想说，但还未及开口，他便抬手止住。他似是猜到你所想，只微颔首，开口询问：
即便如此，你也想入江湖？
看着他的眼睛，你脱口而出——
#Y不想。你突然感觉疲惫。若是永远留在这里，追猫逗狗，和大家一起去桃源，是不是就会拥有另一种人生？#E
听见你的回答，江叔点点头。他的眼神并没有什么波动，仿佛你的回答正如他所预料。在他的面前，你可以畅所欲言。因为你知道，不管你的选择是什么，他永远都站在你的身后。曾经，你是他怀中熟睡的婴孩，是他与这个世界的纽系。未来，你会成为他的骄傲，或是牵挂吗。
你起身奔向江叔，想要问问他去了哪里，问问他过得好不好。倏忽间，你的腿抽动了一下，撞在了桌角——疼痛让你睁开了眼。
阳光依然好，梨花还在飘。天光撒做碎金。风里没有故人的消息，但又处处是他，和他们的消息。
en:
The sun shines bright, and pear blossoms drift down once more. Afternoon light filters through the bamboo leaves, scattering like flecks of gold. A warm breeze, soft as a cat's paw, gently teases your cheek. You have seldom returned since leaving home at sixteen. Cobwebs beneath the eaves have woven into intricate paintings, while the master of the house has wandered to the ends of the earth. Sitting on the long bench where he once sat, you recall your childish prattle from long ago and slowly drift off to sleep.
In a daze, you open your eyes, only to see Uncle Jiang leading a horse toward you. In your memory, Uncle Jiang's back is forever straight, his broad shoulders like a sturdy mountain sheltering you from the wind and rain. Yet now, you notice his hem is slightly soiled, and a barely perceptible weariness lingers on his face.
Thousands of words rush to your lips, but before you can even speak, he raises a hand to stop you. As if guessing your thoughts, he gives a slight nod and asks:
"Even so, do you still wish to wander in the jianghu?"

Meeting his gaze, you blurt out...
#YNo. A sudden, bone-deep weariness washes over you. If you stayed here forever, chasing cats, teasing dogs, and retreating to a peach-blossom haven with everyone, would you have lived a different kind of life?#E
Hearing your answer, Uncle Jiang nods. His gaze remains steady, as if your response is exactly as he expected. Before him, you can always speak your mind. For you know that no matter your choice, he will always stand behind you. Once, you were a sleeping infant in his arms, his tether to this world. In the future, will you become his pride, or his lingering worry?
You rise and run toward Uncle Jiang, curious about where he has been and whether he has been well. Suddenly, your leg twitches, striking the corner of the table. The pain jolts your eyes open.
The sun remains bright, and the pear blossoms keep drifting down. The daylight scatters like flecks of gold. The wind carries no news of old friends, yet traces of him, and of them all, can be found everywhere.

zh:
慧这个名字，起得好也不好。
人说“慧极必伤”，他向来嗤之以鼻。
公输之姓，匠族嫡传；弱冠入内门，得列鹏长老门墙——天资、机心、巧手，无一不全，何伤之有？
他当得起慧这一字，何伤之有？

那时山中春深，降龙木新叶初展，轮到他与鹤长老的弟子楚萤巡山护林。
二人看到一棵被雷劈过的降龙树，突然争论起机关术的至境究竟是“巧”还是“拙”。
楚萤说：“这棵枯树，若是让你用来做机关，何巧可为？”
公输慧：“此树已死……无巧可为。”
楚萤便笑着说，“无巧可为？你且看着……”
说着便将这棵死树推倒，埋了起来，“待来年，它附近这几棵，都会长得更好。”
公输慧觉得此人也是个聪明人。

聪明人不应做蠢事。
所以当楚萤说他要随鹤长老出山游历时，他没有挽留。只是说，若三年后他还不回来，这山崖上最大的那棵降龙木，便归他了。
楚萤大笑：“行，要是我没回来，你就把我埋树下！"
公输慧瞥了他一眼，觉得这话实在太蠢。

聪明人做不得蠢事。
当司南剑客的信传来时，公输慧看着树上的刻痕，难得有些犹豫。
可他也知道，这不过是一棵降龙木而已。
何况枯木难春，唯有砍了朽木，新芽才能成长。

聪明人，从不后悔。
en:
"Hui" means wisdom. It is a name that cuts both ways. 

People always say that too much wisdom brings early ruin, but he scoffed at the notion. Born of the Gongshu bloodline, the true heirs to the artisans' craft, he was admitted to the Inner Sect at the age of twenty and taken in by Elder Peng. Talent, intellect, and a masterful touch, he possessed them all. Where was the ruin in that? He was perfectly worthy of the name Hui. What ruin could there be?

Spring was returning to the mountains, and fresh leaves had just begun to unfurl on the trees. It was his turn to patrol the forest with C
They came across a Dragonbane tree scarred by lightning, which sparked a sudden debate on whether the ultimate pinnacle of mechanics lay in Ingenuity or Simplicity.

"This dead trunk," Chu Ying asked, "if it were yours to fashion into a device, where could the Ingenuity be found?"
"The tree is dead," Gongshu Hui replied flatly. "There is no Ingenuity to be found."
Chu Ying laughed. "No Ingenuity? Just watch."
Saying that, he pushed the dead tree over and buried it beneath the soil. "Come next year, the trees nearby will grow all the better for it."

Gongshu Hui thought to himself that this man should be rather wise, and wise men had no business acting foolish. 

So when Chu Ying announced he was leaving the mountains to wander the world with Elder Crane, Hui did not say a word to stop him. He only said that if Chu Ying did not return in three years, the largest Dragonbane tree on the cliff would belong to him.

Chu Ying laughed heartily. "Deal! And if I don't come back, you can bury me right under it!"
Gongshu Hui shot him a glance, thinking the remark was utterly foolish.
A wise man is never foolish.

When the letter from the Lodestar Swordmaster finally arrived, Gongshu Hui stood staring at the notches carved into the tree, feeling a rare moment of hesitation.
Yet he also knew it was nothing more than a Dragonbane tree.
Besides, withered wood knows no second spring. Only by cutting away the decay can the new sprouts find room to grow.

A wise men never regrets.
Xuan Qi Yu
