zh:
【中庸第三十一】

天命之谓性，率性之谓道，修道之谓教。道也者，不可须臾离也，可离非道也。是故君子戒慎乎其所不睹，恐惧乎其所不闻。莫见乎隐，莫显乎微，故君子慎其独也。喜怒哀乐之未发，谓之中；发而皆中节，谓之和；中也者，天下之大本也；和也者，天下之达道也。致中和，天地位焉，万物育焉。
仲尼曰：“君子中庸，小人反中庸，君子之中庸也，君子而时中；小人之中庸也，小人而无忌惮也。”
子曰：“中庸其至矣乎！民鲜能久矣！”
子曰：“道之不行也，我知之矣：知者过之，愚者不及也。道之不明也，我知之矣：贤者过之，不肖者不及也。人莫不饮食也，鲜能知味也。”
子曰：“道其不行矣夫！”
子曰：“舜其大知也与！舜好问而好察迩言，隐恶而扬善，执其两端，用其中于民，其斯以为舜乎！”
子曰：“人皆曰予知，驱而纳诸罟擭陷阱之中，而莫之知辟也。人皆曰予知，择乎中庸，而不能期月守也。”
子曰：“回之为人也，择乎中庸，得一善，则拳拳服膺弗失之矣。”
子曰：“天下国家可均也，爵禄可辞也，白刃可蹈也，中庸不可能也。”
子路问强，子曰：“南方之强与？北方之强与？抑而强与？宽柔以教，不报无道，南方之强也，君子居之。衽金革，死而不厌，北方之强也，而强者居之。故君子和而不流，强哉矫！中立而不倚，强哉矫！国有道，不变塞焉，强哉矫！国无道，至死不变，强哉矫！”
子曰：“素隐行怪，后世有述焉，吾弗为之矣。君子遵道而行，半涂而废，吾弗能已矣。君子依乎中庸，遁世不见知而不悔，唯圣者能之。”
君子之道，费而隐。夫妇之愚，可以与知焉，及其至也，虽圣人亦有所不知焉。夫妇之不肖，可以能行焉；及其至也，虽圣人亦有所不能焉。天地之大也，人犹有所憾。故君子语大，天下莫能载焉；语小，天下莫能破焉。《诗》云：“鸢飞戾天，鱼跃于渊。”言其上下察也。君子之道，造端乎夫妇，及其至也，察乎天地。
子曰：“道不远人，人之为道而远人，不可以为道。《诗》云：‘伐柯，伐柯，其则不远。’执柯以伐柯，睨而视之，犹以为远。故君子以人治人，改而止。忠恕违道不远，施诸己而不愿，亦勿施于人。君子之道四，丘未能一焉，所求乎子，以事父，未能也；所求乎臣，以事君，未能也；所求乎弟，以事兄，未能也；所求乎朋友，先施之，未能也。庸德之行，庸言之谨；有所不足，不敢不勉，有余，不敢尽；言顾行，行顾言，君子胡不慥慥尔！”
君子素其位而行，不愿乎其外。素富贵，行乎富贵；素贫贱，行乎贫贱；素夷狄，行乎夷狄；素患难行乎患难，君子无入而不自得焉。在上位不陵下，在下位不援上，正己而不求于人，则无怨。上不怨天，下不尤人。故君子居易以俟命。小人行险以徼幸。子曰：“射有似乎君子，失诸正鹄，反求诸其身。”
君子之道，辟如行远必自迩，辟如登高必自卑。《诗》曰：“妻子好合，如鼓瑟琴。兄弟既翕，和乐且耽。宜尔室家，乐尔妻帑。”子曰：“父母其顺矣乎！”
子曰：“鬼神之为德，其盛矣乎？视之而弗见，听之而弗闻，体物而不可遗，使天下之人齐明盛服，以承祭祀。洋洋乎如在其上，如在其左右。《诗》曰：‘神之格思，不可度思！矧可射思！’夫微之显，诚之不可掩如此夫。”
子曰：“舜其大孝也与！德为圣人，尊为天子，富有四海之内。宗庙飨之，子孙保之。故大德必得其位，必得其禄。必得其名，必得其寿，故天之生物，必因其材而笃焉。故栽者培之，倾者覆之。《诗》曰：‘嘉乐君子，宪宪令德。宜民宜人，受禄于天，保佑命之，自天申之。’故大德者必受命。”
……
en:
【Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 31】

What Heaven has conferred is called the nature; an accordance with this nature is called the path of duty; the regulation of this path is called instruction. The path of duty cannot be left for an instant. If it could be left, it would not be the path. On this account, the superior man does not wait till he sees things, to be cautious, nor till he hears things, to be apprehensive. There is nothing more visible than what is secret, and nothing more manifest than what is minute. Therefore the superior man is watchful over himself, even when he is alone. When there are no stirrings of pleasure, anger, sorrow, or joy, the mind may be said to be in the state of Equilibrium. When those feelings have been stirred, and they act in their due degree, there ensues what may be called the state of Harmony. This Equilibrium is the great root from which grow all the human actings in the world, and this Harmony is the universal path which they all should pursue. Let the states of equilibrium and harmony exist in perfection, and a happy order will prevail throughout heaven and earth, and all things will be nourished and flourish.
Zhongni said, "The superior man embodies the course of the Mean; the mean man acts contrary to the course of the Mean. The superior man's embodying the course of the Mean is because he is a superior man, and so always maintains the Mean. The mean man's acting contrary to the course of the Mean is because he is a mean man, and has no caution."
The Master said, "Perfect is the virtue which is according to the Mean! Rare have they long been among the people, who could practice it!"
The Master said, "I know how it is that the path of the Mean is not walked in—The knowing go beyond it, and the stupid do not come up to it. I know how it is that the path of the Mean is not understood—The worthy go beyond it, and the unworthy do not come up to it. There is no one but eats and drinks, but they are few who can distinguish flavors."
The Master said, "Alas! How is the path of the Mean untrodden!"
The Master said, "There was Shun: He indeed was greatly wise! Shun liked to ask others, and to study their words, though they might be shallow. He concealed what was bad in them and displayed what was good. He took hold of their two extremes, determined the Mean, and employed it in his government of the people. It was this which made Shun what he was!"
The Master said, "Men all say, 'We are wise'; but being driven forward and taken in a net, a trap, or a pitfall, they know not how to escape. Men all say, 'We are wise'; but happening to choose the course of the Mean, they are not able to keep it for a round month."
The Master said, "This was the manner of Hui:—he made choice of the Mean, and whenever he obtained anything good, he clasped it firmly, as if wearing it on his breast, and did not lose it."
The Master said, "The kingdom, its states, and its families, may be perfectly ruled; dignity and emolument may be declined; naked weapons may be trodden under the feet; but the course of the Mean cannot be attained to."
Zilu asked about strength. The Master said, "Do you mean the strength of the South, the strength of the North, or the strength which you should make your own? To show forbearance and gentleness in teaching others; and not to revenge unreasonable conduct—this is the strength of the South, and the good man makes it his own. To lie under arms; and meet death without regret—this is the strength of the North, and the forceful make it their own. Therefore, the superior man cultivates a friendly harmony, without being weak.—How firm is he in his strength! He stands erect in the middle, without inclining to either side.—How firm is he in his strength! When good government prevails in the state, he does not change from what he was in retirement.—How firm is he in his strength! When bad government prevails, he will maintain his course to death without changing.—How firm is he in his strength!"
The Master said, "To live in obscurity, and yet practice wonders, in order to be mentioned with honor in future generations—this is what I do not do. The good man tries to walk according to the right path, but when he has gone halfway, he abandons it—I cannot give up. The superior man accords with the course of the Mean. Though he may be all unknown, unregarded by the world, he feels no regret.—It is only the sage who is able for this."
The way of the superior man is extensive, and yet secret. Simple folk, even the ignorant, may know something of it; but in its utmost reaches, there is that which even the sage does not know. Simple folk, even the unworthy, may be able to practice it; but in its utmost reaches, there is that which even the sage is not able to practice. Great as heaven and earth are, men still find some things in them with which to be dissatisfied. Thus it is that, when the superior man speaks about great matters, the world is unable to contain them; when he speaks about small matters, the world is unable to divide them. The Book of Poetry says, "The hawk flies up to heaven; the fishes leap in the deep." This expresses how its influence reaches above and below. The way of the superior man may be found, in its simple elements, in the intercourse of common men and women; but in its utmost reaches, it shines brightly through heaven and earth.
The Master said, "The path is not far from man. When men try to pursue a course which is far from the common indications of consciousness, this course cannot be considered the path. The Book of Poetry says, 'In hewing an axe handle, in hewing an axe handle, the pattern is not far off.' We grasp one axe handle to hew the other; and yet, if we look askance from the one to the other, we may consider the pattern as still remote. Therefore the superior man governs men according to their nature, with what is proper to them, and as soon as they change what is wrong, he stops. When one cultivates to the utmost the principles of his nature, and exercises them on the principle of reciprocity, he is not far from the path. What you do not like when done to yourself, do not do to others. In the way of the superior man there are four things, to not one of which have I as yet attained.—To serve my father, as I would require my son to serve me: to this I have not attained; to serve my ruler, as I would require my minister to serve me: to this I have not attained; to serve my elder brother, as I would require my younger brother to serve me: to this I have not attained; to set the example in behaving to a friend, as I would require him to behave to me: to this I have not attained. Earnest in practicing the ordinary virtues, and cautious in speaking about them; if there be something not attained to in his practice, he dare not but exert himself; if there be something redundant in his words, he dare not allow himself to speak it. Thus his words have respect to his actions, and his actions have respect to his words; is it not just an entire sincerity which marks the superior man?"
The superior man does what is proper to the station in which he is, and does not wish to go beyond it. In a position of wealth and honor, he does what is proper to a position of wealth and honor. In a poor and humble position, he does what is proper to a poor and humble position. In a situation of barbarian tribes, he does what is proper to a situation of barbarian tribes. In a position of sorrow and difficulty, he does what is proper to a position of sorrow and difficulty. He can find no situation in which he is not himself. In a high situation, he does not treat with contempt his inferiors. In a low situation, he does not court the favor of his superiors. He rectifies himself, and seeks for nothing from others, so that he has no dissatisfactions. He does not murmur against Heaven, nor grumble against men. Thus it is that the superior man is quiet and calm, waiting for the appointments of Heaven, while the mean man walks in dangerous paths, looking for lucky occurrences. The Master said, "In archery we have something like the way of the superior man. When the archer misses the center of the target, he turns round and seeks for the cause of his failure in himself."
The way of the superior man may be compared to what takes place in traveling, when to go to a distance we must first traverse the space that is near, and in ascending a height, when we must begin from the lower ground. The Book of Poetry says, "Happy union with wife and children, is like the music of lutes and harps. When brothers live in concord and at peace, the harmony is delightful and lasting. Thus may you regulate your family, and enjoy the pleasure of your wife and children." The Master said, "In such a state of things, parents have entire complacence!"
The Master said, "How abundant and glorious are the powers of spiritual beings! We look for them, but do not see them; we listen to, but do not hear them; yet they are inherent in all things, and there is nothing which is without them. They cause all the people in the kingdom to fast and purify themselves, and array themselves in their richest dresses, in order to attend at their sacrifices. Like the overflowing water, they seem to be above our heads, and on our right and left. The Book of Poetry says, 'The approaches of the spirits, you cannot surmise;—and can you treat them with indifference?' Such is the manifestation of what is minute! Such is the impossibility of repressing the outgoings of sincerity!"
The Master said, "How greatly filial was Shun! His virtue was that of a sage; his dignity was the throne; his riches were all within the four seas. He offered his sacrifices in the ancestral temple, and his descendants preserved the sacrifices to himself. Therefore having such great virtue, it could not but be that he should obtain the throne, that he should obtain those riches, that he should obtain his fame, that he should attain to his long life. Thus it is that Heaven, in the production of things, is sure to be bountiful to them, according to their qualities. Hence the tree that is flourishing, it nourishes, while that which is ready to fall, it overthrows. The Book of Poetry says, 'The admirable, amiable prince, displayed conspicuously his excelling virtue, adjusting his people, and adjusting his officers. Therefore he received from Heaven his emoluments, and Heaven protected him, and appointed him, and renewed his prosperity, sending it down upon him from Heaven.' Therefore he who possesses great virtue will certainly receive the appointment of Heaven."

曾在江湖上引起众豪侠争夺的名剑秋水，最后被权势“买”下。
它辗转于各个“官员侠客”之手。说他们是官员，他们却是江湖出身，以侠客自居。说他们是侠客，他们却早生疏了武艺，为权臣卖命，借着秋水之威才能装点门面。

很多年后，一个姑娘认出了它，夺走它。还用它杀掉了它当时的主人。
它在刺破自己主人喉咙的瞬间，想起来自己铸造出的炽热炉火。它终于鸣叫了起来，鸣叫着，鸣叫着下一次的出手。

但它断在了桃林塞的水边。那姑娘折断了它。它不知道为什么，崩裂的剑身划伤了姑娘的手。于是它再次饮到了血。原来血要和泪混杂在一起，才足够炽热。
它被丢在水中，看到了自己的倒影，一把普通的剑。
剑也会老的，它早就老了。

当心啊，江湖人。权力的代价，不知觉就从你身上拿走。
小心啊，年轻人。江湖的顶峰，只能凭自己到达。
en:
The renowned sword Autumn Water, which once sparked fierce battles among Jianghu heroes, was eventually "bought" by power.
It passed through the hands of various "official swordsmen." Called officials, they hailed from the Jianghu and styled themselves as swordsmen; though called swordsmen, their skills had long rusted as they served powerful ministers, relying on Autumn Water's prestige for a facade.

Years later, a girl recognized it and seized it. She even used it to kill its owner at the time.
The moment it pierced its master's throat, it remembered the blazing forge of its creation. It finally rang out, singing, anticipating its next strike.

But it broke by the waters of the Peach Grove Pass. The girl snapped it. It didn't know why, but its shattered blade cut the girl's hand. And so it tasted blood again. It turned out blood had to mix with tears to be hot enough.
Discarded in the water, it saw its own reflection—an ordinary sword.
Swords age too, and it had grown old long ago.

Beware, Wanderers. The price of power is quietly exacted from you.
Watch out, young ones. The pinnacle of the Jianghu can only be reached on your own.

咔嚓原来没有名字。它是被某位世家子买来讨心上人欢喜的，却在送礼路上糟了祸，摔断了后腿。世家子觉得触了霉头，连表面慈悲都懒得装，让家仆把猫丢出去了事。猫生还未起便遭了大落，可怜猫儿的呼救被淹没在落雨的闹市街头。“啧啧，作孽哦！”快撑不住之时，小猫被一双带着草药气味的温暖大手轻轻托了起来。这双手太暖和，小猫闭着眼睛靠了上去，彻底没了知觉。再次醒来的时候，小猫发现自己正躺在一间大大的屋子里，屋内的草药味比之前闻到的还要浓郁。它刚想支起前爪，就被人轻轻扶住了小猫头。小猫虚弱地咪咪两声，就被抓住了命运的后颈皮，又有另一只手抚上它的背。周围似乎不止一个人，说话声此起彼伏。
“给猫正骨？郎主还会这个？”“嘘，仔细看着……”
“咔嚓！”
“哦哟！腿儿动了！”
就是那咔嚓一声以后，小猫世界里的雨停了。它摇摇晃晃坐起来，看向那双手的主人。咪的天，咪遇到神仙了！从此，陈宅里多了一只叫咔嚓的猫，矫健敏捷，时不时就为厨房添一条刚从西湖里捉上来的大鲩鱼，报答神仙家的救命之恩。
en:
Click had no name at first. It had been bought by a young scion of some noble house, meant as a gift to please the girl he fancied. But disaster struck along the way, and its hind leg was broken in a fall. Deeming this an ill omen, the young man did not even trouble to feign mercy, and had his servant simply toss the cat aside and be done with it. Its life as a cat had scarcely begun before misfortune struck it down, and the poor creature's cries for help were drowned out in the rain-soaked bustle of the marketplace street. "Tsk, tsk, what a wicked shame!" Just as it was about to give out entirely, the little cat was gently lifted by a pair of warm hands that carried the scent of herbal medicine. Those hands were so warm that the kitten closed its eyes and leaned into them, losing all sense of the world. When it woke again, the little cat found itself lying in a large room, the scent of medicinal herbs even stronger here than before. Just as it tried to prop itself up on its front paws, someone gently steadied its little head. The kitten let out a weak little meow, and then found the scruff of its neck caught in a firm grip, while another hand pressed against its back. There seemed to be more than one person about, voices rising and falling around it.
"Setting bones for a cat? Does the young master know how to do such a thing?" "Hush, just watch closely..."
"Click!"
"Oh my! The leg's moving!"
It was after that single click that the rain finally stopped in the little cat's world. It sat up unsteadily and looked up at the owner of those hands. Holy Meow, it'd stumbled upon an immortal! From that day on, there was a cat named Click living in the Chen household, swift and nimble on its feet, who from time to time would bring a great, freshly caught carp from West Lake to the kitchen, as thanks for the life-saving kindness of its benefactor's house.

【系辞上】

天尊地卑，乾坤定矣。卑高以陈，贵贱位矣。动静有常，刚柔断矣。方以类聚，物以群分，吉凶生矣。在天成象，在地成形，变化见矣。
是故刚柔相摩，八卦相荡。鼓之以雷霆，润之以风雨；日月运行，一寒一暑。
乾道成男，坤道成女。乾知大始，坤作成物。
乾以易知，坤以简能；易则易知，简则易从；易知则有亲，易从则有功；有亲则可久，有功则可大；可久则贤人之德，可大则贤人之业。易简而天下之理得矣；天下之理得，而成位乎其中矣。

圣人设卦观象，系辞焉而明吉凶，刚柔相推而生变化。是故吉凶者，失得之象也；悔吝者，忧虞之象也。变化者，进退之象也。刚柔者，昼夜之象也。六爻之动，三极之道也。
是故君子所居而安者，《易》之序也。所乐而玩者，爻之辞也。是故君子居则观其象而玩其辞，动则观其变而玩其占。是以“自天祐之，吉无不利”。

彖者，言乎象者也；爻者，言乎变者也。吉凶者，言乎其失得也。悔吝者，言乎其小疵也。无咎者，善补过也。
是故列贵贱者存乎位，齐小大者存乎卦，辩吉凶者存乎辞，忧悔吝者存乎介，震无咎者存乎悔。
是故卦有小大，辞有险易。辞也者，各指其所之。
《易》与天地准，故能弥纶天地之道。仰以观于天文，俯以察于地理，是故知幽明之故。原始反终，故知死生之说。

精气为物，游魂为变，是故知鬼神之情状与天地相似，故不违；知周乎万物，而道济天下，故不过；旁行而不流，乐天知命，故不忧；安土敦乎仁，故能爱。
范围天地之化而不过，曲成万物而不遗，通乎昼夜之道而知，故神无方而《易》无体。
一阴一阳之谓道。继之者善也，成之者性也。仁者见之谓之仁，知者见之谓之知，百姓日用而不知，故君子之道鲜矣。

显诸仁，藏诸用，鼓万物而不与圣人同忧。盛德大业至矣哉！
富有之谓大业，日新之谓盛德。生生之谓易，成象之谓乾，效法之谓坤，极数知来之谓占，通变之谓事，阴阳不测之谓神。
夫《易》，广矣大矣！以言乎远则不御，以言乎迩则静而正，以言乎天地之间则备矣。
夫乾，其静也专，其动也直，是以大生焉。夫坤，其静也翕，其动也辟，是以广生焉。
广大配天地，变通配四时，阴阳之义配日月，易简之善配至德。
子曰：“《易》其至矣乎！夫《易》，圣人所以崇德而广业也。知崇礼卑，崇效天，卑法地。天地设位，而《易》行乎其中矣。成性存存，道义之门。”

……
en:
[The Great Appendix, Part I]

Heaven is lofty and honourable; earth is low. (Their symbols), Qian and Kun, (with their respective meanings), were determined once for all in this. Things low and high appear displayed in a similar relation. The (upper and lower trigrams, and the relative position of individual lines, as) noble and mean, had their places assigned accordingly. Movement and rest are the regular qualities (of their respective subjects). Hence comes the definite distinction (of the several lines) as the strong and the weak. (Affairs) are arranged together according to their tendencies, and things are divided according to their classes. Hence were produced (the interpretations in the Yi, concerning) what is good [or lucky] and evil [or unlucky]. In the heavens there are the (different) figures there completed, and on the earth there are the (different) bodies there formed. (Corresponding to them) were the changes and transformations exhibited (in the Yi).
After this fashion a strong and a weak line were manipulated together (till there were the eight trigrams), and those eight trigrams were added, each to itself and to all the others, (till the sixty-four hexagrams were formed). We have the exciting forces of thunder and lightning; the fertilising influences of wind and rain; and the revolutions of the sun and moon, which give rise to cold and warmth.
The attributes expressed by Qian constitute the male; those expressed by Kun constitute the female. Qian (symbolises Heaven, which) directs the great beginnings of things; Kun (symbolises Earth, which) gives to them their completion.
It is by the ease with which it proceeds that Qian directs (as it does), and by its unhesitating response that Kun exhibits such ability. One who attains to this ease (of Heaven) will be easily understood, and one who attains to this freedom from laborious effort (of the Earth) will be easily followed. One who is easily understood will have adherents, and one who is easily followed will achieve success. One who has adherents can continue long, and one who achieves success can become great. To be able to continue long shows the virtue of the wise and able person; to be able to become great is the heritage one will acquire. With the attainment of such ease and such freedom from laborious effort, the mastery is got of all principles under the sky. With the attainment of that mastery, the sage makes good one's position in the middle (between heaven and earth).

The sages set forth the diagrams, inspected the emblems contained in them, and appended their explanations; in this way the good fortune and bad (indicated by them) were made clear. The strong and the weak (lines) displace each other, and produce the changes and transformations (in the figures). Therefore the good fortune and evil (mentioned in the explanations) are the indications of the right and wrong (in people's conduct of affairs), and the repentance and regret (similarly mentioned) are the indications of their sorrow and anxiety. The changes and transformations (of the lines) are the emblems of the advance and retrogression (of the vital force in nature). Thus what we call the strong and the weak (lines) become the emblems of day and night. The movements which take place in the six places (of the hexagram) show the course of the three extremes (i.e. of the three Powers in their perfect operation).
Therefore what the superior person rests in, in whatever position one is placed, is the order shown in the Yi; and the study which gives one the greatest pleasure is that of the explanations of the several lines. Therefore the superior person, when living quietly, contemplates the emblems and studies the explanations of them; when initiating any movement, one contemplates the changes (that are made in divining), and studies the prognostications from them. Thus is help extended to one from Heaven; there will be good fortune, and advantage in every movement.

The Tuan speak of the emblematic figures (of the complete diagrams). The Yao speak of the changes (taking place in the several lines). The expressions about good fortune or bad are used with reference to (the figures and lines, as) being right or wrong according to the conditions of time and place; those about repentance or regret refer to small faults (in the satisfying those conditions); when it is said 'there will be no error, or no blame,' there is reference to (the subject) repairing an error by what is good.
Therefore the distinction of (the upper and lower trigrams and of the individual lines) as noble and mean is decided by the (relative) position (of the lines); the regulations of small and great are found in the diagrams, and the discriminations of good and bad fortune appear in the (subjoined) explanations. Anxiety against (having occasion for) repentance or regret should be felt at the boundary line (between good and evil). The stirring up the thought of (securing that there shall be) no blame arises from (the feeling of) repentance.
Thus of the diagrams some are small, and some are great; and of the explanations some are startling, and some are unexciting. Every one of those explanations has reference to the tendencies (indicated by the symbols).
The Yi was made on a principle of accordance with heaven and earth, and shows us therefore, without rent or confusion, the course (of things) in heaven and earth. (The sage), in accordance with (the Yi) looking up, contemplates the brilliant phenomena of the heavens, and, looking down, examines the definite arrangements of the earth; thus one knows the causes of darkness (or, what is obscure) and light (or, what is bright). One traces things to their beginning, and follows them to their end; thus one knows what can be said about death and life.

(One perceives how the union of) essence and breath form things, and the (disappearance or) wandering away of the soul produces the change (of their constitution)—thus one knows the characteristics of the anima and animus. There is a similarity between one and heaven and earth, and hence there is no contrariety in one to them. One's knowledge embraces all things, and one's course is (intended to be) helpful to all under the sky—and hence one falls into no error. One acts according to the exigency of circumstances without being carried away by their current; one rejoices in Heaven and knows its ordinations; and hence one has no anxieties. One rests in one's own (present) position, and cherishes (the spirit of) generous benevolence—and hence one can love (without reserve).
(Through the Yi), one comprehends as in a mould or enclosure the transformations of heaven and earth without any error; by an ever-varying adaptation one completes (the nature of) all things without exception; one penetrates to a knowledge of the course of day and night (and all other phenomena); it is thus that one's operation is spirit-like, unconditioned by place, while the changes which one produces are not restricted to any form.
The successive movement of the inactive and active operations constitutes what is called the course (of things). That which ensues as the result (of their movement) is goodness; that which shows it in its completeness is the natures (of people and things). The benevolent see it and call it benevolence. The wise see it and call it wisdom. The common people acting daily according to it yet have no knowledge of it. Thus it is that the course (of things), as seen by the superior person, is seen by few.

It is manifested in the benevolence (of its operations) and (then again) it conceals and stores up its resources. It gives their stimulus to all things, without having the same anxieties that possess the sage. Complete is its abundant virtue and the greatness of its stores!
Its rich possessions is what is intended by the greatness of its stores; the daily renovation which it produces is what is meant by 'the abundance of its virtue.' Production and reproduction is what is called (the process of) change. The formation of the semblances (shadowy forms of things) is what we attribute to Qian; the giving to them their specific forms is what we attribute to Kun. The exhaustive use of the numbers (that turn up in manipulating the stalks), and (thereby) knowing (the character of) coming events, is what we call prognosticating; the comprehension of the changes (indicated leads us to) what we call the business (to be done). That which is unfathomable in (the movement of) the inactive and active operations is (the presence of a) spiritual (power).
Yes, wide is the Yi and great! If we speak of it in its farthest reaching, no limit can be set to it; if we speak of it with reference to what is near at hand, (its lessons are) still and correct; if we speak of it in connexion with all between heaven and earth, it embraces all.
There is Qian. In its (individual) stillness it is self-absorbed; when exerting its motive power it goes straight forward; and thus it is that its productive action is on a grand scale. There is Kun. In its (individual) stillness, it is self-collected and capacious; when exerting its motive power, it develops its resources, and thus its productive action is on a wide scale.
In its breadth and greatness, (the Yi) corresponds to heaven and earth; in its ever-recurring changes, it corresponds to the four seasons; in its mention of the bright or active, and the dark or inactive operation, it corresponds to the sun and moon; and the excellence seen in the ease and ready response (of its various operations) corresponds to the perfect operations (presented to us in the phenomena of nature).
The Master said, "Is not the Yi a perfect book?" It was by the Yi that the sages exalted their virtue, and enlarged their sphere of occupation. Their wisdom was high, and their rules of conduct were solid. That loftiness was after the pattern of heaven; that solidity, after the pattern of earth. Heaven and earth having their positions as assigned to them, the changes (of nature) take place between them. The nature (of people) having been completed, and being continually preserved, it is the gate of all good courses and righteousness.

zh:
长大后，朱凤英还是嫁了人。婆婆是朱娘子的闺中密友，两家住在同一个村里。夫君唐明亦是自己幼年的玩伴。
朱凤英和夫君恩爱非常。唐明性格温和，和朱凤英的利落倒是互补得般配。
朱凤英依然做得一手好面。她蒸的馍馍，卤的肉臊，香气能飘得出整条巷子。
人人都说朱娘子贤惠，厉害。可朱凤英心里觉得，自己还是那个在门槛上啃馍，被嘲笑的女娃。

朱凤英和夫君建了农场，又生了个女儿，起名叫一朵。
也许是因为生在水草丰美的土地里，唐一朵生得天真烂漫，如同盛开的报春花。
因为扎根在自由而温柔的土里，她的花瓣也有了太阳的温度。

朱凤英始终记得娘在门口安慰自己的样子，也记得自己在灶台前揉出顶好的白面时候的成就感。
“一朵，快来，帮阿娘一起揉面。”看着女儿小心翼翼的样子，朱凤英一边手把手教，一边轻轻在女儿耳边嘱咐。
“揉面要用巧劲，要揉透，最后面团滑滑的，不沾手，不沾盆，才是顶好的……”
可唐一朵只揉了两下，便嘟起小嘴。“阿娘，揉面一点都不好玩，一朵不要揉面。”
“那一朵想干嘛呀？”朱凤英愣了愣，下意识问出了当年一样的话。
“一朵以后想放羊，养鸡，想骑大马！……”
“……还要去采蘑菇。哦对！一朵也要开农场，开一个那——么大的农场！”
朱凤英仿佛回到了多年前的那个下午。那时候的母亲看着自己，会不会也是一样的心态呢？欣慰，惊奇，又隐隐带有一些期待。只要她想，那自己又有什么理由去说“不”呢。
“那若是如此……”朱凤英笑着回答，“一朵就是天底下最最厉害的农场主了。”
en:
Fengying grew up and married. Her mother-in-law was Madam Zhu's old childhood friend. The two families had lived in the same village for generations. Her husband, Tang Ming, was someone she'd known since they were little, a playmate who had never quite left her side.
They were deeply in love. Tang Ming was gentle, a perfect match for Fengying's sharp efficiency.
Fengying never lost her gift for making food. The buns she steamed and the meat sauce she simmered sent rich, comforting aromas drifting down the entire lane.
People praised Madam Zhu for raising such a capable, virtuous daughter. Yet in her heart, she was still that little girl on the doorstep, gnawing on a bun while the neighbors laughed.

She and her husband built a small farm with their own hands. In time, they had a daughter and named her Yiduo.
Raised among clear water and rich grass, Yiduo grew bright and carefree, like an early spring flower opening to the light.
Rooted in land that was gentle and free, even her laughter seemed warmed by sunshine.

Fengying never forgot the look her mother once gave her at the doorway, nor the quiet pride she felt the first time she kneaded a dough so smooth it gleamed.
"Yiduo, come help Mama knead the dough," she said now, guiding her daughter's small hands. She spoke softly, almost to herself.
"Don't force it, use skill. Knead it through, until it's smooth, not sticking to your hands or the bowl..."
After just a few presses, Yiduo pouted. "Mama, this isn't fun. I don't want to knead dough."
Fengying froze for a moment, then heard herself ask the very words she once knew so well. "Then what do you want to do?"
Yiduo's answer came tumbling out. "I want to herd sheep and raise chickens! I want to ride a big horse! And pick mushrooms! Oh—and I want my own farm too. A huge one!"
In that moment, Fengying was carried back to a long-ago afternoon. Had her mother looked at her the same way: part relief, part surprise, and something like hope quietly blooming beneath it all? If this was what her daughter wanted, how could she ever say no?
"Well then," Fengying said with a smile, her voice warm and sure, "you'll be the greatest farmer in the whole wide world."

zh:
驿道边常有无人行囊。有书生欲赴长安赶考，忽见道旁老槐下，倚着个褪色的素布行囊，鼓鼓囊囊，却无主人。周围有群狼环伺，却又无一上前。他心善，恐失主来寻，便提在手中，只觉入手微温，似有低泣声。
行囊不重，却如生根般贴着他掌心。入夜投店，解囊欲看，束口绳结竟如活物般自行收紧。灯下细观，布面陈旧，唯有一股铁锈与陈土混合的腥气挥之不去。
梦中书生见一披甲残躯，于尸山血海中踉跄爬行，口中喃喃“归乡”。书生惊醒，掌中行囊滚烫，竟有湿黏液体从布缝渗出，顺着指缝滴落。他惊觉半边身子麻木，对镜一照，左臂已如烟似雾，渐趋透明。
三日后，行囊自行敞开，内里空无一物，唯余浓重血腥与铁锈气。书生踪迹全无，只那褪色素布行囊静静躺在客栈床上，鼓胀如初，束口绳结松散，仿佛刚被什么人亲手解开。门外风声呜咽，似有甲胄铿锵，渐行渐远。
en:
Forgotten bundles were no rare sight along the post roads. A young scholar bound for Chang'an to sit the examinations came upon a faded cloth sack propped against the gnarled roots of an old locust tree by the road. The sack was full and round, but its owner was nowhere to be seen. A pack of wolves stood circled around it, yet not one would go near. The scholar, not wishing the owner to return and find it gone, reached down and picked it up. It was warm to the touch, and from somewhere within came what sounded like quiet, low weeping.
The sack was not heavy, but it clung to his palm as if it had taken root there. That night, when he stopped at an inn and tried to open it, the drawstring cinched itself tight on its own, like a living thing refusing to give. Under the lamp, the cloth looked old and worn, and a stubborn smell of rust and damp earth clung to it that would not leave.
He dreamed of an armored figure, broken and bloodied, crawling across a field of corpses, murmuring without cease: "Home. Let me go home." He woke with a start to find the sack burning hot in his hand. A sticky, dark liquid was seeping through the weave and dripping between his fingers. Half his body had gone numb. When he looked into the mirror, his left arm had grown faint, fading toward nothing.
Three days later, the sack lay open on the bed at the inn, empty of everything but the thick smell of old blood and rust. The scholar was gone, leaving no trace. Only the faded cloth sack remained, still round and full, the drawstring now slack and loose. Outside, the wind moaned low, and beneath it came the distant sound of armor, fading down the road.

zh:
81阶及以上等级的装备在完成定音后即可开放转律和变音。
选择倾向流派后，消耗转律石即可在对应流派的推荐词库中重新随机一条，转律前后的词条种类不会重复，可加入品质保底材料。
每件装备最多转律一个词条，初始词条不能转，达到105阶的装备可以对已转律词条进行再转律，无次数限制有时间间隔，再转律时首次转律覆盖的词条、当前词条、当前装备使用相同转律库转出过的词条均不会再出现。

可同时进行普通和止戈定音，但每次只能生效其中一个，支持免费切换。
选择定音库后，消耗定音石和变音石后即可在对应定音库中重新随机一条。
变音前后的词条种类可能相同，游侠可自行选择是否覆盖旧定音效果，未选择词条会进入历史变音库，可消耗20长鸣玉重新启用。
变音时若随机到与当前定音相同类型的词条，则数值必定提升。

达到100阶的装备变音累积达到一定次数时，可获得一次定音自选机会，每件装备的普通定音和止戈定音分别独立计数。
定音自选无需消耗变音材料，只能自选词条类型，选定后词条数值会按照变音规则随机生成。
转变为承音装备时会重置变音保底计数。
en:
Gear at Tier 81 and above can be retuned and re-attuned after it has been attuned.
Select a preferred Path, consume a Retuning Stone to gain a random new Attribute from that Path's recommended library. The new Attribute will not be the same as the old one. Quality Guaranteed Materials can be added.
One Attribute can be retuned at most per piece of gear. Initial Attributes cannot be retuned. Gear at Tier 105 can further re-tune a retuned Attribute with no limit on attempts, but there is a cooldown between each re-retune. When re-retuning, any Attributes from the same Retuning Library that have been gained from previous retune attempts will not appear again.

Common and Arena Attunement can be performed simultaneously, but only one can be active at a time. Switching between them is free.
After selecting an Attuning Library, consume Attunement Stones and Re-attunement Stones to gain a random new Attribute from the corresponding library.
The new Attribute may be the same. You may choose whether to overwrite the old Attribute. Unselected Attributes are stored in the re-attuning Library and can be re-enabled by spending 20 Echo Jade.
If the same Attribute as the current one gets rolled from re-attuning, the value is guaranteed to increase.

Once Gear at Tier 100 accumulates a certain number of re-attuning attempts, you will have a chance to select an attunement of your choice. Common Attunement and Arena Attunement counts are tracked independently per piece of gear.
The attunement selection does not consume re-attuning materials. The Attribute type can be selected, but the Attribute value will be randomly generated according to rules.
Converting a piece of gear to Relaid Gear will reset the re-attuning count.
Pei Hengmou

zh:
他踉跄着闯入密林水泽，寒潭的凉意才让中烧的怒火慢慢平息。
他这才惊觉，师父的素白头纱竟在缠斗间挂在了自己身上。
是之前被他不小心扯坏，用缝伤口的针法勉强缝好的旧纱，还是孙愿攒了数月银钱送给师父的新纱？
正怔忡间，齐腰深的流水将头纱卷走，瞬间没了踪影。

偏执心起，明知师父不可能再穿戴他染指之物，可他偏想弄清楚。
他纵身扎入寒潭，俯身在水底摸索，指尖触到一抹莹白，可几近窒息也没能将它捞起。
待破水而出，他才发现，那是月亮在水中的倒影。
en:
He stumbled into the dense marshlands, the frigid water finally cooling his raging fury.
Only then did he notice that his Master's pure white veil had snagged on his clothes during their struggle.
Was it the old one he had accidentally torn and clumsily patched up like a stitched wound, or the new one Sun Yuan had spent months saving up to buy for her? As he stood there dazedly, the waist-deep current swept the veil away, swallowing it in an instant.

A sudden obsession took hold of him. He knew his Master would never again wear something he had touched, yet he had to know which veil it was.
Plunging into the freezing pool, he blindly searched the bottom. His fingertips brushed against a pale shimmer, but even as he ran out of breath, he couldn't grasp it. 
Bursting through the surface for air, he finally realized what it was—just the reflection of the moon.

zh: 青州江畔偶现一翁，撑排驭水，棍扫千浪。世人称其“放排翁”，然其真身早已随黄止水之名自沉无处。或言其棍法得自水势，虚招如赝品惑目，实招似暗流崩石；或传其见学子临水，必以棍点地，授以“破阵”之理。然欲探其过往者，唯见江雾迷蒙中，众排掠影，棍风荡云，真伪莫辨，虚实难分。
en:
An old man is sometimes seen along the rivers of Qingzhou, steering his raft across the currents and sweeping aside churning waves with his pole. The world knows him only as the Old Raftsman, for his true name, Huang Zhishui, has long since vanished beneath the river's depths.
Some say his martial arts are drawn from the tides themselves: his feints are fleeting illusions that deceive the eye, while his true strikes carry the crushing force of a hidden undertow. Others say whenever he meets a young martial artist by the water, he taps his pole upon the ground to impart the truth of "Breakthrough."
Yet those who seek his past find only dense river mist, phantom rafts skimming across the water, and the wind of a swirling pole parting the clouds, leaving truth and illusion hopelessly blurred.

贰贰，皮实好动，上蹿下跳，疯疯癫癫。
从小，娘亲便觉得这孩子奇怪。
每每打猎回来，数他喊饿最大声。但给他分了肉，却又不吃。
唤他外出狩猎，每次都倒地装死。但喵们出门后，又冲出来，打猎最积极。
没有人知道他在想什么。
只有贰贰知道，他，想要成为猫中名伶！
那些都他对自己演技的磨炼！
但这些戏，已经演过太多次了……娘亲兄弟们已习惯不再被他迷惑了。
思考着思考着，他走到了戏台之下，看着台上之人，演绎悲欢离合，演绎各样人生。
此刻，他恍然若悟，这就是喵生梦寐以求的舞台吧！
en:
Deuce was wild, energetic, and chaotic. 
Even Mama thought he was odd. 
When they returned from a hunt, he'd always yell the loudest about being hungry. But once the meat was served, he wouldn't eat a bite. 
They'd call him to hunt, and he'd flop over like he was dead. But the moment the others left, he'd spring up and dash off. Hunt more aggressively than anyone. 
No one understood what went on in his little head. 
Only Deuce knew, he wanted to become the greatest feline actor of all time! 
Those were just rehearsals to hone his acting skills. 
But he'd done the same performances so many times, his family no longer fell for it. 
One day, lost in thought, he wandered beneath a stage. He looked up and saw a human performing love, loss, and every twist of life. 
And suddenly, he knew. That was the stage he had dreamed of all along.

唐之骑射，威震四夷，其术非独中土所创，实融四邦遗风而成。昔高祖李渊起兵太原，北邻突厥，窥其骑射之利，遂效其法。《旧唐书》载："渊选善骑射者二千人，使之饮食舍止一如突厥，或与突厥遇，则伺便击之，前后屡捷，突厥颇惮之。"观此可知，唐初骑兵以突厥为镜，取精用宏，化其悍勇为吾用。（一行批注：亦可学之）突厥骑兵，以骑射为爪牙，驰骤如风，阵无常形，遇利则进，知难辄退。唐军得其精髓，兼习中原兵法，遂成骑射合一、进退有度之新术。

（一行批注：待我召来如此人马十万，不消说占山为王，得让那些当官的给我提靴！）

考其器用，唐骑以角弓为尚。《唐六典》有载："角弓以筋角，骑兵用之。"角弓者，以牛筋、牛角为材，短劲而力强，驰马疾射，矢可及远。（一行批注：牛筋、牛角取其韧）步兵则用长弓，体长力缓，利于步战。（一行批注：弓有异制，各有其长）唐人制弓，技艺精妙，筋角胶合，弓力倍增，遂使骑射之威，冠绝当世。

之尚武，以骑射为标。边关将帅，多具胡戎血统，若哥舒翰、契苾何力、黑齿常之者，皆骁勇善战，箭无虚发。此类胡将，自幼习骑射，弓马娴熟，战必克，攻必取。胡风浸染，使唐军兼具胡将之悍、汉家之谋，故能拓疆万里，镇戍四边。
（一行批注：这些人论及弓箭，说不定还不及我。他们也就当个将领罢了。）


弓马射艺，非止武备，实为唐立国脊梁。角弓劲矢，穿云裂石；胡将汉帅，协心戮力。是以高昌、龟兹望风而降，突厥、吐蕃敛迹而遁。观唐之盛世，岂独文治煊赫？弓马射艺之精，边防体系之固，实为鼎祚永固之基也。

（一行批注：什么仁义弓马，我今方知，武学才是根本！若能得到江湖人消息，学得他们的武功心法，哪里还需什么弓箭之术……）
en:
Found in: Room Earth II Left

Tang mounted archery was renowned throughout the surrounding lands. Its techniques did not arise solely in the Central Plains; they were forged from the traditions of surrounding peoples. When Founding Emperor Li Yuan rose to power in Taiyuan, the Turkic tribes lay to his north. Seeing the value of their mounted archery, he adopted their methods. The Old Book of Tang records: "Yuan selected two thousand men skilled in riding and archery, and ordered them to eat, lodge, and live exactly like the Turks. Whenever they met Turkic forces, they watched for an opening and attacked. They won repeated victories, and the Turks came to fear them." Thus, the early Tang cavalry took the Turkic tribes as their model, adopting the best of their methods. (Margin note: Worth learning.) Turkic cavalry wielded mounted archery as their claws and teeth. They rode like the wind, held no fixed formation, advanced when they had the advantage, and withdrew when the tide turned. Tang soldiers grasped this essence and joined it with Central Plains strategy, creating a new art that united riding and archery with measured advance and retreat.

(Margin note: Once I summon a hundred thousand riders like these, never mind ruling one mountain, I'll have those officials pulling on my boots!)

In equipment, Tang riders prized the horn bow. The Six Codes of the Tang records: "The horn bow is made with sinew and horn and is used by cavalry." Made from ox sinew and ox horn, this bow was short, taut, and powerful, allowing riders to shoot while moving at speed and strike distant targets. (Margin note: Ox sinew and horn are used for their resilience.) Infantry used the long bow instead, its long body and gentler draw better suited to fighting on foot. (Margin note: Bows differ in their making; each has its strength.) Tang bowyers perfected the craft, bonding sinew and horn to multiply the bow's force, and the might of their mounted archery stood unrivaled in its age.

Tang martial culture regarded mounted archery as its emblem. Commanders on the frontier often came from steppe lineages. Geshu Han, Qibi Heli, Heichi Changzhi, and others were all fierce warriors whose arrows never missed. Trained in mounted archery from childhood and masters of both horsemanship and the bow, these generals prevailed in battle and took every stronghold. Shaped by steppe traditions, Tang armies joined their ferocity with the strategy of the Han, allowing them to expand their borders by thousands of li and defend every frontier.
(Margin note: When it comes to bows, these men might not even match me. They only became generals, after all.)

The art of bow and horse was more than preparation for war; it was the pillar upon which the Tang realm stood. Stout horn bows and keen arrows pierced clouds and split stone; steppe generals and Han commanders labored with one heart. Gaochang and Kucha submitted at the mere rumor of their approach, while the Turkic tribes and Tubo forces withdrew before them. Was the Tang golden age built on civil governance alone? The mastery of mounted archery and strength of its frontier defenses formed the true foundation of its enduring throne.

(Margin note: Bows and horses? Now I know that martial arts are the true foundation! If I could get word of those Jianghu fighters and learn their secret arts, who would still need the art of archery...)

（三）机巧·扫地鸡奇人

导师评：“如何规划鸡之行动轨迹？”

en:
A selection of mechanical inventions by the autumn intake of new disciples, with commentary from their mentors.

I. Mechanism: The Self-Illuminating Lamp
Highlights: No flame required. Simply expose it to the light of another lantern, and it will glow on its own. Light one, light all!

Mentor: "And if there is no light source nearby?"
Disciple: "It absolutely, positively will not light up."

II. Mechanism: The Eighteen-in-One Jianghu Treasure
Highlights: Eighteen weapons concealed within a single case. Press the release, and a weapon emerges at random, catching the enemy completely off guard!

Mentor: "What exactly do you mean by 'at random'?"
Disciple: "To strike without warning. To appear where the enemy least expects. The mechanism calculates all things; Heaven decides the rest."
Mentor: "Speak plainly."
Disciple: "The enemy doesn't know which weapon comes out. Neither do I."

III. Mechanism: The Sweeping Chicken Contraption
Highlights: A fusion of living creature and mechanism. A small broom-wielding puppet is attached to the back of a free-range chicken. As the chicken roams the yard, it sweeps the ground behind it. Two tasks accomplished at once!
Mentor: "How do you direct the chicken's path?"
Disciple: "Scatter grain."
Mentor: "Then how do you sweep up the grain?"
Disciple: "Already accounted for. The chicken pecks up every last kernel. Nothing left to sweep."

...And so the showcase continued, invention after invention, each more unexpected than the last. One cannot help but marvel at the ingenuity, and occasionally the audacity, on display.

小小八，虽说现在你只会打更，但我对你可是期盼颇高！若有朝一日你能读书识字，我这封书信也就不算白写。

首先……嗯……还是要感谢你这么多年的陪伴！张万师他们不见了之后，我这么一个怪人，又天天想那么多怪事，也就只能和你说说话——虽然你也听不懂。好了，肉麻的话说完，接下来就是对你的鞭策了！

第一，我外出时，帮我守好悬空屋！但是……也不能真的伤到来人，吓唬吓唬他们就行。虽然我的机关调试总出问题，但我每天晚上给你念叨那么多话，总要起点作用？

第二，交给你一个学会说话的任务！他们都说不可能，但我把你当朋友，当然想听到你的想法。放心，我会努力调整你的机关结构，用来发声！

第三，给你种了很多花草，希望你守屋子的时候不会无聊。

第四，也别忘了打更，很多人指着你报时嘞。

小小八：
如果你永远也看不懂这封信，那也没什么不好的，这样世上就只有小八一个怪脑袋了。

如果有一天我做到了，你真的看懂了这封信，请永远记得这最后一条：小八和小小八，是最好的朋友！
en:
Little Xiaoba, even though you're only a bell toller for now, I still have high hopes for you. If the day ever comes when you can read and write, then this letter will not have been written in vain.

First off... well... thank you for keeping me company all these years. Ever since Zhang Wanshi and the others vanished, I've turned into a bit of an odd soul, always drifting off into my own strange thoughts. Talking to you has been my only real comfort, even if you don't understand a single word I say.

But enough of the mushy stuff. Time for some encouragement!

First, when I'm away, watch over Aloft Abode for me. But don't actually hurt anyone who comes by. Just give them a scare. My mechanisms do go wrong all the time, but after hearing me ramble on every night, you must have picked up something by now, right?

Second, I'm giving you a task: learn how to speak. Everyone says it's impossible, but I think of you as a friend, so of course I want to hear what you think. Don't worry. I'll keep working on your inner mechanisms until you can make your own voice.
Third, I've planted lots of flowers and herbs for you, so you won't get bored while guarding the house.

Fourth, don't forget to keep the night watch. Plenty of people count on you to tell the time.

Little Xiaoba, if you never do learn to read this letter, that may not be such a bad thing. That way, there will only ever be one odd little head like Xiaoba in this world.
But if one day I really do manage it, and you can understand this letter at last, then please remember this one final thing: Xiaoba and Little Xiaoba are best friends.

zh:
游侠，见字如面。
前些时日，老朽随府尹大人巡查蒙学，见学堂里的娃娃们一个个正襟危坐，埋首书卷，连我等走近了都未曾察觉。
老朽心下好奇，是何等妙文，能让这些上蹿下跳的娃娃们如此专心？一问才知，他们手中所读，竟是你前些时日所赠。
老朽又问，这些书好在何处？娃娃们七嘴八舌，老朽这才知道，原来你竟为每个孩子都择了不同的书，实在是费心了。而听闻老朽与你相熟，他们都央着我，定要代他们向你道声谢。
只是，真要问他们想说什么，这群小家伙却面露羞赧，讷讷而止了。最后，老朽想了个法子，让他们把想说的话都诉诸笔端，一并封在信里了。至于写了什么，老朽绝未偷看！
对了，娃娃们还托我转交几幅画作，说是读了书卷后的有感而发。他们都说，游侠你是他们见过最有眼光的人，定能欣赏他们的大作。
哈哈，看来往后若再有与孩子们打交道的差事，找游侠准是没错了。

en:
Dear Wanderer,

The other day, I accompanied the Prefect on an inspection of the village school. The children sat straight at their desks, noses buried in scrolls, so absorbed they didn't even notice us draw near.
Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

zh:
论剑为1v1竞技玩法，采用特殊的段位规则与战斗规则。

段位规则：
玩家在到达【无我】段位后，将不再降级，原论剑止戈积分失效，玩家新获得初始1000无我积分，后续胜负将只影响该积分。无我段位的玩家参与匹配时，优先匹配积分相近的玩家。每期论剑重置时，无我段位的玩家会根据无我积分情况获得额外的侠名奖励，该奖励通过邮件发放。

战斗规则：
箭矢使用上限为20支；玩家造成的治疗效果降低90%；对目标的气血护盾造成的伤害提升100%

玩家的技能大多都可以以卸势应对，破防奇术不仅不会被卸势，在命中处于防御或在释放卸势技能的目标时，反而有更好的效果，但其可以被任意技能打断。论剑中释放卸势会消耗耐力，而处决命中时会回复耐力。

玩家的各类技能（包括奇术和蓄力技）能够打断轻重击，而反过来则不行。解控技能清风霁月可在受击或控制状态下使用，活用可以有效扭转劣势。

移动端与PC端为独立的匹配池。组队参与玩法时，匹配逻辑遵循以下规则：系统将检测队伍内所有成员的设备类型。一旦检测到存在PC端设备，该队伍会被纳入PC端匹配队列。若玩家在移动端匹配成功后出现跨平台顶号等异常行为，则该玩家后续匹配被归入PC端队列。

在限定时间内，率先击败对方的一方获胜，若倒计时结束未分胜负，按以下优先级依次判定:
1.总伤害量更高一方获胜;
2.若伤害量相同，则总治疗量更高一方获胜。
en:
1v1 Arena is a competitive mode with unique Rank and Combat rules.

Rank Rules:
Upon reaching "Mythic" Rank, players will no longer drop in rank. Original 1v1 Arena Points become invalid. Players start with 1,000 Mythic Points; future wins/losses only affect these points. Mythic players are matched based on similar points. When the Arena season resets, Mythic players receive extra hero title rewards via mail based on their Mythic Points.

Combat Rules:
Arrow usage capped at 20; Healing effects reduced by 90%; Damage to HP & Shields increased by 100%.

Most player skills can be countered with Deflection. Defense-breaking Mystic Skills cannot be deflected and are more effective against targets who are defending or deflecting, but they can be interrupted by any skill. Deflecting consumes Endurance, while landing an Execution restores Endurance.

Player skills (including Mystic and Charged) can interrupt Light/Heavy Attacks, but not vice versa. Use Break Control Skills like Serene Breeze to escape control effects and turn the tide.

Mobile and PC players queue separately. In team queue, if any member is using a PC, the entire team enters the PC matchmaking pool. Players showing abnormal cross-platform behavior (e.g., account takeover) on mobile will be moved to the PC queue.

Win by eliminating all opponents. If time expires, victory is decided by:
1. Total Damage;
2. Total Healing.

zh: 日影观测是古代天文观测的重要内容。以太阳初升，和太阳落山时，木杆日影与圆周的交点作连线，即定东西方向。再以此线做垂线，即得南北。而一年之中，随着太阳直射点的变化，正午时的日影长短也会变化。古人以此确定季节变化，订立历法。
en:
The shadow of a standing pole served as an ancient compass and clock. By marking where its tip fell at sunrise and sunset, a line could be drawn to fix east and west, and a perpendicular line would give north and south.
As the seasons changed, the noon shadow lengthened and shortened. Ancient observers used these changes to track the seasons and set calendars.

zh:
钱多多这个名字，是他自己取的。他说，人这辈子，什么都可以少，就是钱不能少。
军中人人笑他，说他是燕北盟第一铁公鸡，怕死鬼。
可他只咧嘴一笑，继续把他的算盘敲得劈里啪啦。
他算了一辈子的账，但最重的那笔是和王清将军的。
那年虏人屠村，为了活命，他硬生生在废井里捱了五日。
饿得不行了，他就啃草根，喝泥水，吃蛆虫。
透过井盖缝隙，他看着火光、听着惨叫，闻着血腥味和焦糊味，学会了从风声里分辨马蹄的远近，从空气的震动里感知是否有人靠近。
滴答，滴答......就这么在腐臭与绝望中蜷缩了五日。
直到井口的光猛地砸下，直到——将军来了。
钱多多没哭，却在心里默默打开了账本，郑重记下：王清，欠命一条。
当他嗅到将军身边那股熟悉的“危险气息”时，这个全军最怕死的人，第一次没有躲。
他仔细地写下那封藏着他所有秘密和温柔的信，然后一如当年在废井里那样安静地，走向了那场为将军而设的死局。
他要去救将军的命。用当年将军从井里捞出来的那条命，去换。
这笔账，他算了半辈子。今天，终于要平了。
en:
He named himself Qian Duoduo, "plenty of coin," saying that a man may go without many things in life, but never without money.
The whole army mocked him for it, calling him the Northern Vow's foremost miser and coward. He only grinned and went back to the busy clatter of his abacus.
He kept accounts his whole life, but the heaviest was the one between him and General Wang Qing.
The year the invaders put his village to the sword, he clawed out five days in an abandoned well to stay alive. When hunger gnawed too deep, he chewed grass roots, drank muddy water, ate maggots. Through the crack beneath the well's lid, he watched the glow of flames, heard the screaming, breathed in blood and burnt flesh, and learned to judge how near the hoofbeats were from the sound on the wind, to sense whether someone drew close from the tremor in the air.
Drip, drip... So he curled there five days, amid the rot and the despair.
Until the light came crashing down through the mouth of the well. Until the general came.
Qian Duoduo did not weep. But quietly, in his heart, he opened a ledger, and set down one solemn line: Wang Qing, one life owed.
So when he caught that familiar scent of danger about the general, the most cowardly man in the whole army, for the first time, did not run.
He wrote out, with great care, the letter that held all his secrets and all his tenderness. Then, as quietly as he had once endured that ruined well, he walked toward the death trap laid for the general.
He would go to save the general's life. With the very life the general once hauled up out of that well, he would settle it.
This debt he had carried for half a lifetime. Today, at last, it would balance.

zh:
何事晚来还欲饮，隔墙闻卖蛤蜊声。

蛤蜊，壳卵呈圆形、三角形或长椭圆形，大曰二三寸。蛤蜊极富鲜味，是古人颇为喜爱的一种食物。晋代葛洪《抱朴子》中提及，蛤蜊各煮炙，凡人所能啖，况君子与士乎？《南史·王融传》记载：不知许事，且食蛤蜊。此外，蛤蜊在唐宋诗词中也经常出现，皮日休曾有“何事晚来还欲饮，隔墙闻卖蛤蜊声”之句，足见其普遍。
en:
Why do I still long to drink as evening falls? Beyond the wall, I hear someone calling out clams for sale. 

Clams come in rounded, triangular, or elongated oval shapes, some reaching two or three cun in size. Rich in umami flavor, they were a beloved delicacy in ancient times. Ge Hong of the Jin Dynasty wrote in Alchemical Codex: "Clams may be boiled or roasted—if common folk can enjoy them, how much more the gentlemen and scholars?" The History of the Southern Dynasties - Tales of Wang Rong records: "No matter the trouble—let us eat clams." Clams frequently appear in Tang and Song poetry as well, the poet Pi Rixiu once wrote, "What stirs my thirst so late at night? A clam-seller's call beyond the wall." Showing just how common it was

zh:
初，吾欲得百年前长生仙人之术，使举世皆无病痛，亦能解医者世代牺牲之苦。
柳青衣获长生时，吾以为此道已成，不料此女每醒辄入水寻短见，欲返寻常人身，常吟此间古墓碑文“生如岁华，一世一荣”。
吾所造长生者，躯体长生而七情仍存，吾之力终不达人心，可叹！
en:
At first, I intended to master the ancient art of immortality passed down from a century ago, hoping to free all people from the grasp of sickness and to end the relentless toil and sacrifice borne by generations of healers.
When Liu Qingyi finally attained eternal life, I believed my quest was complete. Yet, to my dismay, each time she awoke, she plunged into the water, seeking death and yearning to reclaim a simple, mortal existence. She often whispered the words carved upon the ancient tomb's stone: 
"Life, like flowers, fades and grows, 
One bloom alone a lifetime knows." 
Though I fashioned immortals whose bodies would never decay, their hearts remain tethered to mundane desires. In the end, my power cannot touch or alter the human spirit. It's truly a sorrow beyond words!

zh:
《还陕述怀》

“慨然抚长剑，济世岂邀名。
星旂纷电举，日羽肃天行。
遍野屯万骑，临原驻五营。
登山麾武节，背水纵神兵。
在昔戎戈动，今来宇宙平。”

铁画银钩的笔迹，抄录着前朝太宗的诗句。
昨日之战血流漂橹，换来今日天下安乐和平。
谁人之手，写谁人之心。
en:
Reflections on Returning to Shaanxi

"Stroking my blade with a heavy sigh,
I seek no glory in mending a fractured world.
Star-wrought banners raised like flashing thunder,
Sunlit feathers marching in solemn grace beneath the firmament.
Ten thousand riders, garrisoned across the sprawling wilds,
Five vanguards, stationed upon the desolate plains.
Scaling the crags to brandish the martial tallies,
Backs against the crushing tide, unleashing a divine host.
Halberds clashed in a bygone age,
Ushering an era of unyielding peace."

These bold and forceful brushstrokes transcribe a poem by Emperor Taizong of the previous dynasty.
Rivers of blood, shed in the merciless slaughters of yesterday, have bought the fragile tranquility of today.
Whose hand forged these characters, and whose soul bleeds through the ink.

zh:
【大射仪第七】

大射之仪。君有命戒射，宰戒百官有事于射者。射人戒诸公、卿、大夫射，司士戒士射与赞者。
前射三日，宰夫戒宰及司马、射人宿视涤。司马命量人量侯道与所设乏以貍步，大侯九十，参七十，干五十，设乏各去其侯西十、北十。遂命量人、巾车张三侯。大侯之崇，见鹄于参；参见鹄于干，干不及地，不系左下纲。设乏西十、北十，凡乏用革。
乐人宿县于阼阶东，笙磬西面，其南笙钟，其南鑮，皆南陈。建鼓在阼阶西，南鼓，应鼙在其东，南鼓。西阶之西，颂磬东面，其南钟，其南鑮，皆南陈。一建鼓在其南，东鼓，朔鼙在其北。一建鼓在西阶之东，南面。簜在建鼓之间，鼗倚于颂磬西紘。
厥明，司宫尊于东楹之西，两方壶，膳尊两甒在南。有丰。幂用锡若絺，缀诸箭。盖幂加勺，又反之。皆玄尊。酒在北。尊士旅食于西鑮之南，北面，两圜壶。又尊于大侯之乏东北，两壶献酒。设洗于阼阶东南，罍水在东，篚在洗西，南陈。设膳篚在其北，西面。又设洗于获者之尊西北，水在洗北。篚在南，东陈。小臣设公席于阼阶上，西乡。司宫设宾席于户西，南面，有加席。卿席宾东，东上。小卿宾西，东上。大夫继而东上，若有东面者，则北上。席工于西阶之东，东上。诸公阼阶西，北面，东上。官馔。羹定。
射人告具于公，公升，即位于席，西乡。小臣师纳诸公、卿、大夫，诸公、卿、大夫皆入门右，北面东上。士西方，东面北上。大史在干侯之东北，北面东上。士旅食者在士南，北面东上。小臣师从者在东堂下，南面西上。公降，立于阼阶之东南，南乡。小臣师诏揖诸公、卿大夫，诸公、卿大夫西面北上。揖大夫，大夫皆少进。大射正摈。摈者请宾，公曰：“命某为宾。”摈者命宾，宾少进，礼辞。反命，又命之。宾再拜稽首，受命。摈者反命。宾出，立于门外，北面。公揖卿、大夫，升就席。小臣自阼阶下北面，请执幂者与羞膳者。乃命执幂者。执幂者升自西阶，立于尊南，北面东上。膳宰请羞于诸公卿者。摈者纳宾，宾及庭，公降一等揖宾，宾辟，公升，即席。

en:
【The Seventh Ceremony of the Grand Archery】

The ritual of the Grand Archery. When the ruler issues a command to proclaim the archery event, the Prime Minister admonishes all the officials involved in the archery. The Archery Officer admonishes the dukes, ministers, and great officers to shoot, and the Marshal of the Gentlemen admonishes the gentlemen and assistants to shoot.
Three days before the archery, the Steward of the Household admonishes the Prime Minister, the Minister of War, and the Archery Officer to inspect the preparations overnight. The Minister of War orders the Surveyor to measure the distance of the targets and the placement of the screens using the Stride of a fox. The Grand Target is ninety Strides away, the Secondary Target seventy, and the Lesser Target fifty. Screens are placed ten Strides west and ten Strides north of each target. He then orders the Surveyor and the Master of the Carriages to set up the three targets. The height of the Grand Target is such that the center of the Secondary Target is visible above it; the center of the Lesser Target is visible above the Secondary Target. The Lesser Target does not touch the ground and its lower left cord is not tied. Screens are placed ten Strides west and ten Strides north, all made of leather.
The musicians hang their instruments overnight on the east side of the Eastern Steps. The Sheng chimes face west, with Sheng bells to their south, and large bells further south, all arranged facing south. A standing drum is placed west of the Eastern Steps, facing south, with a response drum to its east, also facing south. West of the Western Steps, the Ode chimes face east, with bells to their south and large bells further south, all arranged facing south. A standing drum is placed south of these, facing east, with a leading drum to its north. Another standing drum is placed east of the Western Steps, facing south. The flutes are placed between the standing drums, and the small drum leans against the western cord of the Ode chimes.
The next day at dawn, the Palace Steward sets up the wine vessels west of the eastern pillar: two square pots, and two jars of the ruler's fine wine to the south. These are placed on stands. The covers are made of tin or fine linen, attached to the poles. The covers are lifted to add ladles, then replaced. All are dark wine vessels. The wine is placed to the north. Vessels for the officers' common fare are set south of the western large bells, facing north, with two round pots. Another vessel is placed northeast of the screen of the Grand Target, with two pots of offering wine. The washing basin is set southeast of the Eastern Steps, with the water jar to its east and the basket west of the basin, arranged facing south. The ruler's basket is placed north of this, facing west. Another washing basin is set northwest of the wine vessels for the one who announces the hits, with water north of the basin. The basket is to the south, arranged facing east. The Junior Servant sets the ruler's mat on the Eastern Steps, facing west. The Palace Steward sets the guest's mat west of the door, facing south, with an additional mat. The ministers' mats are east of the guest, arranged from the east. The lesser ministers are west of the guest, arranged from the east. The great officers follow, also from the east; if any face east, they are arranged from the north. The musicians' mat is set east of the Western Steps, arranged from the east. The dukes are west of the Eastern Steps, facing north, arranged from the east. The officials prepare the food. The meat is cooked and ready.
The Archery Officer reports to the ruler that all is prepared. The ruler ascends and takes his seat on the mat, facing west. The Junior Servant leads in the dukes, ministers, and great officers, who all enter through the right side of the gate, facing north, arranged from the east. The gentlemen are on the west, facing east, arranged from the north. The Grand Recorder stands northeast of the Lesser Target, facing north, arranged from the east. The officers' common fare is south of the gentlemen, facing north, arranged from the east. The Junior Servant's attendants stand below the Eastern Hall, facing south, arranged from the west. The ruler descends and stands southeast of the Eastern Steps, facing south. The Junior Servant instructs the dukes, ministers, and great officers to bow; they face west, arranged from the north. He instructs the great officers to bow, and they all take a slight step forward. The Grand Archery Officer acts as the usher. The usher requests the guest, and the ruler says: "Appoint so-and-so as guest." The usher instructs the guest, who steps forward slightly and declines with courtesy. The usher reports back, and the ruler insists again. The guest bows twice with his head to the ground and accepts the command. The usher reports back. The guest exits and stands outside the gate, facing north. The ruler bows to the ministers and great officers, then ascends to his seat. The Junior Servant, from below the Eastern Steps facing north, requests the one to hold the cover and the one to present the food. He then appoints the one to hold the cover. The cover-holder ascends from the Western Steps and stands south of the wine vessels, facing north, arranged from the east. The Steward of the Kitchen requests to present food to the dukes and ministers. The usher leads in the guest. When the guest reaches the courtyard, the ruler descends one step to bow to the guest. The guest withdraws. The ruler ascends and takes his seat.

睡道人身世神秘，世人只知他自终南山来。其人整日骑一头青驴，昏昏沉沉仿若沉睡，但其实心如明镜。他擅使卜筮之术，曾推算得契丹入侵清河之事。故而乃指引汇聚八俊，使清河免遭覆巢之祸。后来，太平初定，睡道人骑驴飘然而去。

有人说，曾在清河的驴肉火烧摊见过睡道人，那时他声称要解天下驴之困局。又有人说，那清河巨树上困睡的老道便是。但切莫好奇，须知惊扰熟睡之人，必受那起床之气！
en:
The Sleeping Daoist's origins are shrouded in mystery, people only know he came from Zhongnan Mountains.
He rides a green donkey and drifts through the day in a sleepy haze, though his mind is sharp as crystal. He is a master of divination, once foretold the Khitan invasion of Qinghe, and thus gathered the Eight Heroes of Qinghe to save the land from annihilation. When peace returned, he rode his donkey and vanished into the wind. 

Some say they spotted him at a donkey meat stall in Qinghe, claiming to be the liberator of all donkeys. Others insist the old man napping on top of the giant tree is none other than he. But heed this warning: disturbing a man from his slumber is to risk the wrath of one freshly awakened!

叠加流派增益，使自身思路点上限及回复速度提高，从而获取出卡优势。

前期释放大量【絮絮叨叨】卡，主动对撞对方卡牌，从而积攒废话卡防线。

en:
Path of Provocation:
Against low or mid-attack Gab Cards: Use [The Hidden Channel] to flank and gain attack advantage.
Against high-attack Gab Cards: Flank 3 times to reduce their Presence and instantly destroy the card.

Path of Bluster:
Inspiration Points recover slowly early on. Use [Final Push] to gain extra points and play more Gab Cards.
Avoid clashes. Use low-point Gab Cards to quickly attack Inner Bastions and build [Cheer] stacks.

Path of Rebuttal:
Use high-attack Gab Cards to actively clash with the opponent's cards.
Stack buffs to increase Inspiration Point limit and Recovery for better card flow.

Path of Filibuster:
Play many [Chatterbox] cards early on to clash with the opponent's cards and build up a Fluff Card defense.
Watch for when the opponent's weakest remaining Inner Bastion falls below your Fluff Card pile's total attack.

zh:
【公孙丑章句下】

孟子曰：天时不如地利，地利不如人和。三里之城，七里之郭，环而攻之而不胜。夫环而攻之，必有得天时者矣，然而不胜者，是天时不如地利也。城非不高也，池非不深也，兵革非不坚利也，米粟非不多也，委而去之，是地利不如人和也。故曰：域民不以封疆之界，固国不以山溪之险，威天下不以兵革之利。得道者多助，失道者寡助。寡助之至，亲戚畔之；多助之至，天下顺之。以天下之所顺，攻亲戚之所畔，故君子有不战，战必胜矣。
孟子将朝王，王使人来曰：寡人如就见者也，有寒疾，不可以风。朝将视朝，不识可使寡人得见乎？
对曰：不幸而有疾，不能造朝，
明日，出吊于东郭氏，公孙丑曰：昔者辞以病，今日吊，或者不可乎？
曰：昔者疾，今日愈，如之何不吊？王使人问疾，医来。
孟仲子对曰：昔者有王命，有采薪之忧，不能造朝。今病小愈，趋造于朝，我不识能至否乎？
使数人要于路，曰：请必无归而造于朝。
不得已而之景丑氏宿焉。
景子曰：内则父子，外则君臣，人之大伦也。父子主恩，君臣主敬。丑见王之敬子也，未见所以敬王也。
曰：恶！是何言也？齐人无以仁义与王言者，岂以仁义为不美也？其心曰是何足与言仁义也云尔，则不敬莫大乎是。我非尧、舜之道，不敢以陈于王前，故齐人莫如我敬王也。
景子曰：否，非此之谓也。礼曰：父召，无诺，君命召，不俟驾，固将朝也。闻王命而遂不果，宜与夫礼若不相似然。
曰：岂谓是与？曾子曰：晋、楚之富，不可及也。彼以其富，我以吾仁；彼以其爵，我以吾义。吾何慊乎哉？夫岂不义，而曾子言之，是或一道也。天下有达尊三：爵一，齿一，德一。朝廷莫如爵，乡党莫如齿，辅世长民莫如德。恶得有其一以慢其二哉？故将大有为之君，必有所不召之臣，欲有谋焉，则就之。其尊德乐道，不如是不足与有为也。故汤之于伊尹，学焉而后臣之，故不劳而王；桓公之于管仲，学焉而后臣之，故不劳而霸。今天下地丑德齐，莫能相尚。无他，好臣其所教，而不好臣其所受教。汤之于伊尹，桓公之于管仲，则不敢召。管仲且犹不可召，而况不为管仲者乎？
陈臻问曰：前日于齐，王餽兼金一百而不受；于宋，餽七十镒而受；于薛，餽五十镒而受。前日之不受是，则今日之受非也；今日之受是，则前日之不受非也。夫子必居一于此矣。
孟子曰：皆是也。当在宋也，予将有远行，行者必以赆，辞曰：餽赆，予何为不受？当在薛也，予有戒心，辞曰：闻戒，故为兵餽之，予何为不受？若于齐，则未有处也。无处而餽之，是货之也。焉有君子而可以货取乎？
孟子之平陆，谓其大夫曰：子之持戟之士，一日而三失伍，则去之否乎？曰：不待三。

en:
【Gongsun Chou, Part B】

Mencius said, "Opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven are not equal to advantages of situation afforded by the Earth, and advantages of situation afforded by the Earth are not equal to the union arising from the accord of Men. There is a city, with an inner wall of three li in circumference, and an outer wall of seven. The enemy surround and attack it, but they are not able to take it. Now, to surround and attack it, there must have been vouchsafed to them by Heaven the opportunity of time, and in such case their not taking it is because opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven are not equal to advantages of situation afforded by the Earth. There is a city, whose walls are distinguished for their height, and whose moats are distinguished for their depth, where the arms of its defenders, offensive and defensive, are distinguished for their strength and sharpness, and the stores of rice and other grain are very large. Yet it is obliged to be given up and abandoned. This is because advantages of situation afforded by the Earth are not equal to the union arising from the accord of Men. In accordance with these principles it is said, 'A people is bounded in, not by the limits of dykes and borders; a kingdom is secured, not by the strengths of mountains and rivers; the empire is overawed, not by the sharpness and strength of arms.' He who finds the proper course has many to assist him. He who loses the proper course has few to assist him. When this, the being assisted by few, reaches its extreme point, his own relations revolt from the prince. When the being assisted by many reaches its highest point, the whole empire becomes obedient to the prince. When one to whom the whole empire is prepared to be obedient, attacks those from whom their own relations revolt, what must be the result? Therefore, the true ruler will prefer not to fight; but if he do fight, he must overcome."
Mencius was about to go to court to see the king, when the king sent a person to him with this message, "I was wishing to come and see you. But I have got a cold, and may not expose myself to the wind. In the morning I will hold my court. I do not know whether you will give me the opportunity of seeing you then."
Mencius replied, "Unfortunately, I am unwell, and not able to go to the court."
Next day, he went out to pay a visit of condolence to some one of the Dongguo family, when Gongsun Chou said to him, "Yesterday, you declined going to the court on the ground of being unwell, and today you are going to pay a visit of condolence. May this not be regarded as improper?"
"Yesterday," said Mencius, "I was unwell; today, I am better. Why should I not pay this visit?"
In the meantime, the king sent a messenger to inquire about his sickness, and also a physician. Meng Zhongzi replied to them, "Yesterday, when the king's order came, he was feeling a little unwell, and could not go to the court. Today he was a little better, and hastened to go to court. I do not know whether he can have reached it by this time or not."
Having said this, he sent several men to look for Mencius on the way, and say to him, "I beg that, before you return home, you will go to the court."
Mencius felt himself compelled to go to Jing Chou's, and there stop the night. Mr. Jing said to him, "In the family, there is the relation of father and son; abroad, there is the relation of prince and minister. These are the two great relations among men. Between father and son the ruling principle is kindness. Between prince and minister the ruling principle is respect. I have seen the respect of the king to you, Sir, but I have not seen in what way you show respect to him."
Mencius replied, "Oh! what words are these? Among the people of Qi there is no one who speaks to the king about benevolence and righteousness. Are they thus silent because they do not think that benevolence and righteousness are admirable? No, but in their hearts they say, 'This man is not fit to be spoken with about benevolence and righteousness.' Thus they manifest a disrespect than which there can be none greater. I do not dare to set forth before the king any but the ways of Yao and Shun. There is therefore no man of Qi who respects the king so much as I do."
Mr. Jing said, "No. That was not what I meant. In the Book of Rites it is said, 'When a father calls, the answer must be without a moment's hesitation. When the prince's order calls, the carriage must not be waited for.' You were certainly going to the court. When you heard the king's order, then you did not carry your purpose out. This does seem as if it were not in accordance with that rule of propriety."
Mencius answered him, "How can you give that meaning to my conduct? The philosopher Zeng said, 'The wealth of Jin and Chu cannot be equalled. Let their rulers have their wealth; I have my benevolence. Let them have their nobility; I have my righteousness. Wherein should I be dissatisfied as inferior to them?' Now shall we say that these sentiments are not right? Seeing that the philosopher Zeng spoke them, there is in them, I apprehend, a real principle. In the empire there are three things universally acknowledged to be honorable. Nobility is one of them; age is one of them; virtue is one of them. In courts, nobility holds the first place of the three; in villages, age holds the first place; and for giving one's self the right to influence others, and governing the people, the two other things are not equal to virtue. How can the possession of only one of these be presumed on to despise one who possesses the other two? Therefore a prince who is to accomplish great deeds will certainly have ministers whom he does not call to go to him. When he wishes to consult with them, he goes to them. The prince who does not honor the virtuous, and delight in their ways of doing, to this extent, is not worth having to do with. Accordingly, there was the behavior of Tang to Yi Yin: he first learned of him, and then employed him as his minister; and so without difficulty he became sovereign. There was the behavior of Duke Huan to Guan Zhong: he first learned of him, and then employed him as his minister; and so without difficulty he became chief of all the princes. Now throughout the empire, the territories of the princes are of equal extent, and in their achievements they are on a level. Not one of them is able to exceed the others. This is from no other reason, but that they love to make ministers of those whom they teach, and do not love to make ministers of those by whom they might be taught. So did Tang behave to Yi Yin, and the duke Huan to Guan Zhong, that they would not venture to call them to go to them. If Guan Zhong might not be called to him by his prince, how much less may he be called, who would not play the part of Guan Zhong!"
Chen Zhen asked Mencius, saying, "Formerly, when you were in Qi, the king sent you a present of 2,000 taels of fine silver, and you refused to accept it. When you were in Song, they sent you 1,680 taels, which you accepted; and when you were in Xue, they sent you 1,200 taels, which you likewise accepted. If your declining to accept the gift in the first case was right, your accepting them in the latter cases was wrong. If your accepting them in the latter cases was right, your declining to do so in the first case was wrong. You must accept, Master, one of these alternatives."
Mencius said, "I did right in all the cases. When I was in Song, I was about to take a long journey. Travelers must be provided with what is necessary for their expenses. The prince's message was, 'A present against traveling expenses.' Why should I have declined the gift? When I was in Xue, I was apprehensive for my safety, and taking measures for my protection. The message was, 'I have heard that you are taking measures to protect yourself, and send this to help you in procuring arms.' Why should I have declined the gift? But when I was in Qi, I had no occasion for money. To send a man a gift when he has no occasion for it, is to bribe him. How is it possible that a superior man should be taken with a bribe?"
Mencius having gone to Pinglu, addressed the governor of it, saying, "If one of your spearmen should lose his place in the ranks three times in one day, would you, Sir, put him to death or not?" "I would not wait for three times to do so," was the reply.

en: The Inkbound Order never sought the center of power; it stood at the edge and watched. When swords were drawn and banners fell, its scholars served as witnesses. Disciples who had barely earned their robes bundled scrolls into sleeves, loaded fragile volumes onto handcarts, and carried a civilization's memory across broken roads. 天上桃源、救世神女……真耶幻耶……是耶非耶……

……


第五十三封家书

诸人不信神女不信吾言然桃源即此间玉卿在兹阿月在兹阿春在兹其声真切吾必使众人信之……

……

第六十二封家书

玉卿，神女已示吾新途。

en:
The First Family Letter

Yuqing, my dearest wife, have you seen Ayue and Achun? Have you found our parents?

Since you departed, I have missed you with every breath. Yet each time I lift my brush, your face appears before me, and those of Ayue and Achun beside you. Ink and tears run together on the page, and the words will not come.

...

The Seventh Family Letter

Last night I was swept back to those days of war, the roads lined with the dying and the starved.

#YSuddenly, peach blossoms drifted down from the clouds. The sky darkened as though veiled by some vast shadow, yet it guided the suffering toward a way out. You once smiled and called it the Haven in the heavens. I laughed at you then, and called it a foolish dream.#E

But now, far more souls are drowning in despair than in floodwaters.

And so I tell people your story of the Haven, hoping it will give the weary something to hold on to, and spare them from being consumed by the wretchedness before them.

...

The Thirty-sixth Family Letter

#YToday, Master came to say farewell. He is leaving with a woman of the jianghu named Halcyon, to seek a way to save the world.#E

The refugees here are only just gathering, and the shelters barely stand. I cannot bring myself to stop him, nor can I follow.

The Haven in the heavens, the Goddess who saves... is it real or a dream... is it right or wrong...

...

The Fifty-third Family Letter

many will not believe in the Goddess will not believe my words but the Haven is here Yuqing is here Ayue is here Achun is here I hear their voices clear and true I will make them all believe...

...

The Sixty-second Family Letter

Yuqing, the Goddess has shown me a new path.

I shall follow the Goddess's decree and seek another place to rebuild the Haven. I will restore what we once had, and our family will be whole once more.
Xiao Yiyi

有诗仙抬头见月，月辉皎洁、硕大空悬，触之可及。落笔名篇《静夜思》，千古传诵。其后盛唐倾覆、栋折榱崩，有人曾于月盈之夜，听闻月中有声声吟诵《静夜思》句。其声之哀，哀不可闻；其声之恸，今人同感。

人言此为哀唐之声，流离失所之人，闻之抬首，可见诗仙所见之月，可听盛唐之声。不知此言真耶？幻耶？亦或，失乡人梦呓耶？
en:
A poetic immortal looked up to see the moon, bright, huge, hanging in the sky as if within reach. He picked up his brush and wrote the masterpiece In the Quiet of Night, which has been passed down through the ages. Later, the glorious Tang Dynasty fell, its pillars collapsing. On nights when the moon is full, some have heard the lines of In the Quiet of Night recited from the moon. Its sorrow is unbearable, its grief resonates even with people today. 

People say this is the cry of the fallen Tang. Displaced souls, upon hearing it, look up to see the same moon the poetic immortal saw and hear the echoes of the glorious Tang. No one knows if this is true, an illusion, or just the delirium of the homeless.

zh: 脾与胃合俱象土，外荣肌肉，腐熟水谷。风寒暑湿袭于外，则留连肌腠，传于脾胃。食饮不节害于内，则肠胃乃伤，不化糟粕。皆能为病，所得之源不一，故立名多端。且久风入中则为飧泄，湿胜则为濡写，寒中则为洞泄，暑胜则为毒痢。而又或冷、或热、或赤、或白、或色杂、或肠垢、或滞下、或休息、或疳、或蛊之类，种种不同。悉由将摄失宜，饮食不慎，致肠胃不调、邪气交攻。
en: The spleen and stomach, both associated with the Earth element, govern the nourishment of the flesh and the digestion of food and drink. When wind, cold, summer heat, or dampness attack from outside, they linger in the flesh and skin, eventually entering the spleen and stomach. When dietary excess or imbalance harms from within, the intestines and stomach lose function and cannot properly separate waste. As illness arises from many sources, so too are its names manifold. Persistent wind may cause chronic diarrhea. Excess dampness leads to sluggish, heavy stools. Cold invasion causes watery diarrhea. Excess heat results in toxic dysentery. It may be cold, hot, red, white, mixed-colored, intestinal residue, retentive, intermittent, or linked to worms, parasites, and other conditions, each with distinct patterns. All stem from poor regulation of the body and careless eating, leading to internal imbalance and a clash of healthy and pathogenic Qi.

青溪弟子$N亲启：
你猜昨夜我去翻方子的时候发现了什么？你的晋升安排！我问了一圈儿怎么落这儿了，都说不知道，后来看见姜掌院在那儿煞有介事的安排晋升，我大着胆子上去问，才发现他一直说胡话呢！一诊脉，言语错乱·四重！
后来才知道，前几日他不知从哪儿得了个据说是麻沸散的方子，用了使人无知无觉，恍若醉死。本想研究一下药性。结果自己中了招。
放心吧，姜掌院已经醒了，正黑着脸后悔呢。这次晋升结果一定给你弄对！哈哈，我跟他说了，多给你点补偿。#Y长鸣玉#E和#Y江湖声望#E都有。
好啦，莫让这事儿误了悬壶济世的正事。但若心里还堵得慌，尽管来后山寻我——姜掌院把他的顾渚紫笋当做诊金给了我，等你回来，咱们且喝且聊。
en:
To Lone Cloud Disciple: 
Guess what I found while looking for prescriptions last night? Your promotion arrangement! I asked around, no one knew why it was left there. Then I saw Master Jiang arranging promotions with great gravity, but when I boldly asked him, I realized he was spouting nonsense! I checked his pulse, only to find him with Speech Disorder, Stage IV! 
Turns out, he got a recipe for Anesthesia Powder recently. Used it to render one unconscious, like being dead drunk. He wanted to study the effects but ended up knocking himself out. 
Don't worry, Master Jiang is awake now, looking grim with regret. We'll get your promotion right this time! Haha, I told him to give you extra compensation. There's #YEcho Jade#E and #YJianghu Reputation#E in it for you. 
Alright, don't let this delay your Healer's Calling. But if you still feel stifled, come find me at the back mountain—Master Jiang gave me his Purple Bamboo Tea as a consultation fee. When you return, we'll drink and chat.

zh:
猫是不会冬眠的，但报春觉得自己是一只特别的猫。
等到冬天快要来临，报春就会像大熊一样，四处寻找可以搭窝的东西。
衔几个果子，推一些麦穗，再向人类喵喵叫，在他们的屋檐下找到暖烘烘的稻草窝。
渴了，报春吃一些果子；饿了，报春啃几颗穗子。馋了，报春向人类喵喵叫，就有小鱼干送到稻草窝里来。
报春的每一个冬天都这么懒洋洋地度过。
等到第一支报春蕊冲破了寒冬的凛冽，香气就会第一时间传到报春的鼻子里。
喵喵！喵喵！报春发出响亮的声音，人们呵呵地笑起来。
春天到啦。
en:
Cats don't hibernate. But Spring Herald, well, Spring Herald thought she was special.
As winter's chill approached, she'd gather treasures: a few fruits, some stray wheat stalks, and with a well-placed "meow" by the humans' door, a warm bed of straw would appear.
Thirsty? She had her fruits. Hungry? She had her grain. Feeling peckish? A "meow" or two would summon a dried fish right to her doorstep. She'd laze away the cold months in perfect comfort.
Then, one day, the first brave flower would pierce the frost, its scent a tiny trumpet call.
"Meow! Meow!" Spring Herald would announce, and the humans would chuckle. Spring had arrived.

zh:
背尸的老人从李会五尸身的舌头下，找到了这枚钥匙。
为了保住钥匙不被杜重威的人发现，李会五死死含住钥匙，不曾哭喊半分。
审讯的人用鞭子，将他抽打出千万条血痕。
他咬着牙，脑海里全是想着他的女儿。也唯有女儿，能让他将痛苦短暂忘记。
他多想在死前见她一次，唤她一次。
只消舌尖向上，轻轻抬起。
他就能呼出那个朝思暮想的名字——
可是，他不可以。
en:
The old corpse bearer found this key beneath Li Huiwu's tongue.
To keep it from being discovered by Du Chongwei's men, Li Huiwu held it fast in his mouth and never let out so much as a cry.
Those who questioned him lashed him with whips, leaving his body covered in bloody welts.
He clenched his teeth, and all that filled his mind was his daughter. Only thoughts of her could make him forget the pain, if only for a moment.
How dearly he wished to see her once before he died, to call her name just once.
All he had to do was lift the tip of his tongue, ever so slightly.
Then he could have breathed out that long-yearned-for name.
But he could not.
