zh:
高悬九霄的节度使府张灯结彩，此刻正举行一场盛大的庆功宴。小张将军远征归来，大张将军即将归唐。此番宴请宾客，既是慰问军心，也是为凉州父老吃下一颗定心丸。然而宾朋满座，未见二位将军。你来到佛手郎的书房，看到两位将军坐在案前似乎再商议什么。正当你犹豫是不是打扰他们，佛手郎看到你进来，丢下笔，热切揽过你的肩膀邀你入座。大张将军也颔首致意。此番相聚，你胸中有千言万语，却不知从何说起。此刻，你只想和他们一道……
⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛
听闻你的建议，佛手郎开怀一笑，大张将军也欣然允诺。
en:
The Governor's Residence blazes with lantern light and festal colors, where a magnificent victory banquet is currently underway. General Zhang Huaishen has returned from his campaign, and General Zhang Yichao is about to return to the Tang court. The feast is meant not only to honor the army, but also to reassure the people of Liangzhou and set their hearts at ease. And yet, though the hall is crowded with guests, the two generals themselves are nowhere to be seen. You find your way to the Buddha Hand's study, where the two of them sit facing one another at the desk, seemingly deep in discussion. You are still hesitating over whether to disturb them when the Buddha Hand looks up, drops his brush, and, with easy warmth, slips an arm around your shoulders, urging you to join them. General Zhang Yichao also inclines his head in greeting.
In this gathering, you have thousands of words in your heart, yet no idea where to begin. At this moment, you simply want to...

Hearing your suggestion, the Buddha's Hand laughs heartily, and General Zhang Yichao readily agrees.

夫清浊剖判，上下攸分，三才肇基，五行落，万物淳朴，无得而称。燧人氏出，观（天极）以定方名，始有火化。伏羲氏作，因之而（画十八卦）、立庖厨，滋味既兴，瘵萌起。大圣神农氏悯黎元之多疾，（遂破百邪）以救疗之，犹未尽善。黄帝受命，创制九针，与（剑士裴公、兰公之伦），备论经脉，旁通问难，详究义理，以为经论，故后世可得根据而畅焉。（冬春之际，锐意凌然），六国之时，则有扁鹊，汉有仓公，仲景，魏有华佗，并皆探赜索隐，穷幽洞微，用药不过二三，灸炷不逾七八，而疾无不愈者。晋宋以来，虽复名医间出，然治十不能愈五六，良由今人嗜欲太甚，（立心不坚），淫放纵逸，有阙摄养所致耳。余缅寻圣人设教，欲使家家自学，人人自晓。君亲有疾不能疗（破）之者，非忠孝也。末俗小人，多行诡诈，倚傍圣教而为欺，遂令朝野士庶咸耻医术之名。多教子弟诵短文，枸小策，以求出身之道。医治之术，阙而弗论，吁可怪也。嗟乎！深乖圣贤之本意。
en:
Rain Blurs the Distant Peaks.
When the pure and turbid first parted, when heaven and earth found their places, the Three Powers were established, the Five Elements settled. All things were simple then, beyond naming. Then came Suiren, who studied the celestial pole to mark the directions and first brought fire to mankind. Fuxi followed, drawing the Eighteen Trigrams and establishing the kitchen, with cooked food came flavor, and with flavor, disease. The Divine Farmer, pitying the people's suffering, shattered a hundred evils to heal them, yet his methods remained imperfect. The Yellow Emperor, receiving heaven's mandate, created the nine needles. With swordsmen like Pei Gong and Lan Gong, he mapped the meridians, debated their pathways, and compiled the classics so future generations might follow. In the harsh transition between winter and spring, during the Warring States came Bian Que; in the Han Dynasty, Lord Cang and Zhongjing; in Wei, Hua Tuo, each delving into mysteries, mastering the subtle arts, curing diseases with but two or three herbs or seven or eight moxa cones. Yet from the Jin and Song dynasties onward, though famous physicians occasionally emerged, fewer than half of ten patients recovered. The fault lies with modern men, and their desires too great, their resolve too weak, indulgent and unrestrained, neglecting self-care. The sages taught so that every household might learn, every person understand. To fail in healing one's lord or parent is to fail in loyalty and filial piety. But now, petty men practice deceit under the guise of sacred teachings, making nobles and commoners alike despise the medical arts. They teach children to memorize trivial essays and petty stratagems, seeking only advancement. The art of healing goes neglected. How baffling! How far we've strayed from the sages' intent.

zh: 执于出世，执于入世，都是离了道……圣人处无为之事，行不言之教。万物作焉而不辞，生而不有，为而不恃，功成而弗居。夫唯弗居，是以不去。
en: To be fixed upon withdrawing from the world, or fixed upon engaging with it — both are to stray from the Dao. The Sage acts without contriving and teaches without words. He lets things arise and take their course; he creates, but does not possess; acts, but takes no credit; achieves, but does not dwell on the achievement. Because he does not take credit, it is never taken from him.

zh:
游侠青鉴：
自游侠告知兄长消息后，不熄心境开阔，渐生云游四方之志。此番原欲乘渡船北行，不料途中失道，几经周折，竟于雾散时得遇奇山——此地人唤“不见山”。
此山绝壁千仞如削，其间栈道悬空高架，每走一步，都须得留心脚底……途径一名叫”天陉“之地时，不熄偶遇石刻艺人摩崖。他技艺十分精湛，只是所雕内容，却叫人摸不着头脑。譬如什么“这么近，那么美，周末到河北”“找婆娘”，再譬如“加强无名”“优化爆率” 之类……也不知受何人之委托，竟被堂而皇之地刻于崖壁之上。

见此巍然石屏，不熄忽而想起游侠常念的寒掌柜、江大侠等人——若将思念刻于崖上，或可被有缘瞥见，可转念一想，不见山外人罕至，恐难传音信。想来那些刻字之人，本意亦非广讯，不过是借这云崖铁石，寄一缕无主之思罢了。
山中虽险，却藏一奇景：蒲公英花开如雪海，絮舞似云潮。倒是一处不错的游赏之地。游侠若是得空，不妨来此一聚。

烈不熄 盼复
于不见山天陉
en:
To the Wanderer:
Since you shared the news about my brother, my mind has cleared, and I have gradually developed a desire to wander the world. I originally planned to take a ferry north, but I lost my way. After many twists and turns, I stumbled upon a wondrous mountain when the mist cleared. The locals call it "Hidden Mountain."
The mountain features sheer cliffs towering thousands of feet, with suspended plank roads. You must watch every step... While passing a place called "Heaven's Threshold," I encountered a stone carver named Mo Ya. His skills are exquisite, but the contents of his carvings are baffling. For example, phrases like "So close yet so beautiful, let's spend our weekend in Hebei," "Looking for a wife," "Buff Nameless," and "Improve drop rates"... I don't know who commissioned these, but they are grandly carved right onto the cliff face.

Seeing this majestic stone screen, I suddenly thought of the people you often mention, like Shopkeeper Han and Hero Jiang. If longing could be carved into the cliff, perhaps it might be seen by fate. But then I realized outsiders rarely visit Hidden Mountain, so it would be hard to pass on any messages. I suppose the original intent of those carvers wasn't to broadcast news, but merely to entrust a wisp of untethered longing to these clouds and iron-like stones.
Though the mountain is treacherous, it hides a wondrous sight: dandelions blooming like a sea of snow, their seeds dancing like a tide of clouds. It is quite a nice place to visit. If the Wanderer has time, perhaps we could meet here.

Awaiting your reply, Lie Buxi
At Heaven's Threshold, Hidden Mountain
Calamities in the Mountains
Observe the Jadecrest Runner

zh:
山外来的游侠：
都说跟着妙妙喵的寻龙尺走，就能找着真正的宝贝。可别说这寻龙尺的动静了，那妙妙喵也总是来无影去无踪，我足足翘了半个月的课，这才寻到了它的踪迹。可我们几个同门跟着它爬了半天的山，宝藏到没找着，只见着了熟睡的游侠。
难不成那宝贝就在游侠身上？还是说……游侠就是妙妙喵要找的宝贝？
游侠迟迟不醒，妙妙喵也迟迟不离。原本打算去妙妙庙参拜的同道们，渐渐都寻到这儿来，奉上书卷，祈求学业顺遂，考校通过。时间长了，连山里的猴子也仿着弟子们，将野果衔来此地。难道它们也有课业之忧？还是说，它们也在替墨门弟子祈愿？
不知是妙妙喵显灵，还是猴儿们诚心，抑或是游侠所处果真为智慧流转之地，来此参拜过的弟子，考校果然有所进益！同道们便凑了些通宝，给妙妙喵备了点小鱼干，给猴子们带了碧水云涛的桃子，也给游侠附了份谢礼。
山物简陋，不成敬意，与游侠这番机缘，墨门弟子定当时常感念！
en:
Dear Wanderer,
They say Meow Meow's Dragonfinder will lead you to the real treasure. Yet the Dragonfinder remains silent, and Meow Meow is like a ghost without a trace. I skipped class for half a month before I finally found its trail. A few of us from the sect followed it up the mountain for ages, but instead of treasure, all we found was you, fast asleep.
Could the treasure be on you? Or perhaps... Could you be the treasure Meow Meow was looking for?
As you remained in your deep slumber, Meow Meow wouldn't leave. Soon, disciples bound for Meow Meow Temple found their way here instead, offering scrolls and praying for smooth studies and successful exams. After a while, even the mountain monkeys started following suit, carrying wild fruit over in their mouths. Do monkeys worry about homework too? Or were they praying on behalf of us Mohist disciples?
Whether it was Meow Meow's grace, the monkeys' sincerity, or the fact that your resting place is a confluence of wisdom, those who came to pay their respects have indeed seen their marks flourish! Thus, we chipped in some Coins to get dried fish for Meow Meow, peaches from Jadestream Valley for the monkeys, and a small thank-you gift for you as well.

It's not much, just a few humble mountain offerings, but we Mohist disciples will always be grateful for this strange little stroke of fate that brought us to you!

zh:
匡安世是什么时候能独挡一面的，恐怕连他自己也不清楚。
也许，是在天工阁当职的时候。
当有人来寻那浩如烟海的门内资料，他总是下意识地喊——
鸿师兄，来看看这本书在哪？
可过了好久都无人应答，他这才反应过来，鸿已游学北上，未曾归还。
他只好自己到书架上一本一本翻阅，半个时辰后，才得以捧着书和一身灰尘出来。可眼前一片空荡荡，赶着上课的同道，早就没了踪影。

也有可能，是在驭岭堂看诊的时候。
堂上就诊的人排成条条长龙，各式的机关问题，看得他眼花缭乱。
他想，要是途师兄也在就好了，再冷门的机枢图谱，对途师兄来说，都不过是开胃小菜。
可当他下意识往身后看，才想起途师兄也已归乡，又只得自个儿好好对着图谱，挨个解决麻烦。

如此以上的情形，在鸿师兄与途师兄离去的头一年里，反复上演。
或许后头的日子里也有，只是……他慢慢忘了那个总是要求助的自己。
二人从他的世界褪去，那个曾被保护得很好的小师弟，终究得自个儿走上舞台。
二人离去后的第十四年，不见山有授新名为鹄者，
黄鹄一举，于飞千里。
此为匡安世的授名。
en:
Even Kuang Anshi himself may not know when he truly learned to stand on his own.

Perhaps it was during his time at the Divinecraft Pavilion. Whenever someone came looking for a volume amid the sect's vast sea of records, he would instinctively call out, "Senior Brother Brant, come see where this book is, will you?" Only after a long silence would he remember that Brant had gone north on his travels and had yet to return. So he could only search shelf by shelf on his own. By the time he emerged, book in hand and covered in dust, half an hour had passed, and the fellow disciples who had been hurrying off to class were long gone.

Or perhaps it was at Yuling Hall, while seeing patients. The line stretched on and on, and all manner of mechanism-related ailments left him dizzy with confusion. He would think that if only Senior Brother Tu were here, even the most obscure mechanism charts would be nothing more than light work to him. But every time he glanced back out of habit, he would remember that Tu, too, had already returned home. And so he could only bend over the diagrams himself and work through each problem one by one.

Scenes like these played out again and again in the first year after Senior Brother Brant and Senior Brother Tu left. Perhaps they continued in the years that followed. It was only that, little by little, he forgot the self who had always been asking others for help.

As the two of them gradually faded from his world, the junior brother who had once been so well protected finally had to step onto the stage himself.

In the fourteenth year after their departure, a new name was bestowed in Hidden Mountain: Swan.
Like a swan taking flight, soaring a thousand miles.
This was the name granted to Kuang Anshi.

路遥，河东人氏。尝从军征伐，郓州之役、太原之围、阳城之战，皆在行间，临危未尝遁走。受侠士感召，率粮秣赴中渡桥。
康成林，代州人氏，初隶晋军步卒。会契丹寇边，惧而亡归。既至，见乡邑皆为虏所焚掠，其妻为护乡人而亡。悲愤盈胸，遂重执兵戈，复返中渡桥。
任尔白，籍贯不详，以剑艺傍身。闻燕北盟号令，北上滹沱。因见粮运孤危，遂仗剑护送，粮车赖以全。
金巧，清河人氏。兄尝贾于河东，开运二年，音问遂绝。闻乡人云见其兄于滹沱，乃束装北上，奔战场而来。
许一雁，开封人氏。其母习青溪术方，悬壶市井。雁幼承家学，颇通岐黄。既长，闻北边战伤病苦，乃循母志，奔赴滹沱。
en:
The grain wagons trundle north, taking in fellow travelers. Under the moonlight, the grains seem to whisper the stories of these nameless souls:
Lu Yao of Hedong. He served in the army through Yunzhou, Taiyuan, and Yangcheng, never fleeing in the face of danger. Inspired by a wanderer's righteous spirit, he now leads this convoy to Zhongdu Bridge.
Kang Chenglin of Daizhou, once a foot soldier. When the Khitans raided the border, he fled in fear, only to find his village burned and his wife slain defending the townsfolk. Consumed by grief and fury, he took up arms again and headed for Zhongdu Bridge.
Ren Erbai, origins unknown, living by his blade. Answering the Northern Vow's call, he headed north to the Hutuo. Seeing the grain convoy vulnerable, he drew his sword to guard it, ensuring its safe passage.
Jin Qiao of Qinghe. Her brother went to trade in Hedong years ago, but all news ceased. Hearing he was spotted near the Hutuo, she packed her bags and headed straight for the battlefield.
Xu Yiyan of Kaifeng. Her mother practiced the art of the Silver Needle among the common folk. Learning the craft young, Xu resolved to follow her mother's path and journeyed to the Hutuo to tend the wounded.

zh:
《玉篇》有云：“骅骝，骏马。”赤色骏马，即为骅。骅骝本为名马，周穆王八骏之一，后代指同色马匹，故西南矮脚中以纯赤色骏马为贵。
《华阳国志·南中志》记载：“长老传言，滇池有神马，或交焉，即生骏驹，俗称称之曰‘滇池驹’，日行五百里。”唐宋时期，《蛮书》又云：“马出越赕山东面一带……尾高，尤善驰骤，日行数百里。……腾冲及申赕亦出马，次赕，滇池尤佳。”《新唐书·南诏传》亦载：“越赕之西有荐草，产善马，世称‘越赕骏’。始生若羔，岁中，细莎縻之，饮以米渖，七年可御，日驰数百里。”滇马即为矮脚马，因产于滇池，故名“西南矮脚”。
西南矮脚体格极小，四肢较细，颈短头直，眼大额广，蹄小而质坚，以耐力见长，乘、挽、驮均可，为西南最常见的马种。
en:
The Jade Chapters dictionary states: "Hualiu is a superior steed." A pure red steed of this kind is a Hua. The original Hualiu was one of the legendary Eight Steeds of King Mu of Zhou, and its name later came to describe all fine horses of this pure red color, which are considered the most prized among the Southwestern Ponies.
Legends from the Huayang Chorography tell of a divine steed that once rose from Dianchi Lake. Its offspring, known as "Dianchi Foals," were said to travel five hundred li a day. Later, during the Tang and Song dynasties, texts like the Book of the Man and the New Book of Tang praised the swift, high-tailed horses bred on the lush grasslands of the region, famed as "Yuetan Steeds." These Dian Horses, named for their origin near Dianchi Lake, are also known as Southwestern Ponies.
Small in stature, they have fine limbs, a short neck, a broad forehead, and firm, compact hooves. Prized for their endurance, they are suited for riding, pulling, and carrying loads, making them the most common breed in the southwest.

【士虞礼第十四】

士虞礼。特豕馈食，侧亨于庙门外之右，东面。鱼腊爨亚之，北上。饎爨在东壁，西面。设洗于西阶西南，水在洗西，篚在东。尊于室中北墉下，当户，两甒醴、酒，酒在东。无禁，幂用絺布，加勺，南枋。素几，苇席，在西序下。苴刌茅，长五寸，束之，实于篚，馔于西坫上。馔两豆菹、醢于西楹之东，醢在西，一鉶亚之。从献豆两亚之，四笾亚之，北上。馔黍稷二敦于阶间，西上，藉用苇席。匜水错于槃中，南流，在西阶之南，箪巾在其东。陈三鼎于门外之右，北面，北上，设扃鼏。匕俎在西塾之西。羞燔俎在内西塾上，南顺。
主人及兄弟如葬服，宾执事者如吊服，皆即位于门外，如朝夕临位。妇人及内兄弟服、即位于堂，亦如之。祝免，澡葛絰带，布席于室中，东面，右几，降，出，及宗人即位于门西，东面南上。宗人告有司具，遂请拜宾。如临，入门哭，妇人哭。主人即位于堂，众主人及兄弟、宾即位于西方，如反哭位。祝入门，左，北面。宗人西阶前北面。
祝盥，升，取苴降，洗之，升，入设于几东席上，东缩，降，洗觯，升，止哭。主人倚杖，入。祝从，在左，西面。赞荐菹醢，醢在北。佐食及执事盥，出举，长在左。鼎入，设于西阶前，东面北上。匕俎从设。左人抽扃、鼏、匕，佐食及右人载。卒，朼者逆退复位。俎入，设于豆东，鱼亚之，腊特。赞设二敦于俎南，黍，其东稷。设一鉶于豆南。佐食出，立于户西。赞者彻鼎。祝酌醴，命佐食启会。佐食许诺，启会，却于敦南，复位。祝奠觯于鉶南。复位。主人再拜稽首。祝飨，命佐食祭。佐食许诺，钩袒，取黍稷，祭于苴三，取肤祭，祭如初。祝取奠觯，祭，亦如之；不尽，益，反奠之。主人再拜稽首。祝祝卒，主人拜如初，哭，出复位。
祝迎尸，一人衰絰，奉篚，哭从尸。尸入门，丈夫踊，妇人踊。淳尸盥，宗人授巾。尸及阶，祝延尸。尸升，宗人诏踊如初。尸入户，踊如初，哭止。妇人入于房。主人及祝拜妥尸。尸拜，遂坐。
……
en:
【The Fourteenth Book of Ceremonies: The Mourning Rites for an Officer】

The mourning rites for an officer. A single pig is offered as food, and it is boiled on the side outside the right of the temple gate, facing east. The fish and dried meat cauldrons follow in order, arranged from the north. The rice-cooking stove is against the east wall, facing west. A basin is set southwest of the western steps, with water west of the basin and a basket east of it. The wine vessels are placed in the chamber beneath the north wall, opposite the door, with two jars of sweet wine and wine, the wine on the east. No stand is used, and the cover is made of fine linen cloth, with a ladle placed on top, its handle pointing south. A plain table and a reed mat are set beneath the western eaves. Chopped thatch grass, five inches long, is bundled and placed in a basket, set on the western stand. Two dishes of pickled vegetables and meat sauce are arranged east of the western pillar, with the meat sauce on the west, and a single tripod vessel following. Two additional dishes for accompanying offerings follow, and four baskets of dried fruits follow, arranged from the north. Two round vessels of millet and glutinous millet are set between the steps, with the western one higher, placed on a reed mat. A ewer with water is placed in a basin, with its spout facing south, south of the western steps, and a basket with a towel is east of it. Three tripods are set outside the right of the gate, facing north, arranged from the north, with their crossbars and covers set in place. The ladles and cutting boards are placed west of the western study. The roasted meat offering board is set on the inner western study, aligned southward.
The host and his brothers wear mourning clothes as at the burial, while the guests and attendants wear mourning garments as at condolence visits, and all take their positions outside the gate, as at the morning and evening mourning stations. The women and the host's female relatives, in mourning attire, take their positions in the hall, likewise. The invocator, with a hempen band and girdle, spreads a mat in the chamber, facing east, with the table on the right, then descends, goes out, and with the clan officer takes a position west of the gate, facing east, with the northernmost as the highest. The clan officer announces that the attendants are ready, and then requests to welcome the guests. As at a condolence visit, upon entering the gate, there is weeping, and the women weep. The host takes his position in the hall, while the other principals, brothers, and guests take positions in the western area, as at the return weeping station. The invocator enters the gate, goes to the left, and faces north. The clan officer stands before the western steps, facing north.
The invocator washes his hands, ascends, takes the thatch bundle, descends, washes it, ascends again, enters, and places it on the mat east of the table, aligned eastward, then descends, washes a goblet, ascends, and the weeping ceases. The host leans on his staff and enters. The invocator follows, standing on the left, facing west. The assistant presents the pickled vegetables and meat sauce, with the meat sauce on the north. The food server and attendants wash their hands, go out, and lift the cauldrons, with the eldest on the left. The tripods are brought in and set before the western steps, facing east, arranged from the north. The ladles and cutting boards follow and are set in place. The person on the left removes the crossbars, covers, and ladles, while the food server and the person on the right load the offerings. When finished, the ladle bearers withdraw in reverse order and return to their positions. The cutting boards are brought in and set east of the dishes, with the fish following, and the dried meat placed separately. The assistant sets two round vessels south of the cutting boards, with millet, and glutinous millet to its east. A single tripod vessel is set south of the dishes. The food server goes out and stands west of the door. The attendants remove the tripods. The invocator pours sweet wine and instructs the food server to open the covers. The food server agrees, opens the covers, and places them back south of the round vessels, then returns to his position. The invocator places the goblet south of the tripod vessel and returns to his position. The host bows twice, touching his head to the ground. The invocator offers the blessing and instructs the food server to make the offering. The food server agrees, rolls up his sleeves, takes millet and glutinous millet, and offers them on the thatch three times, then takes the skin and offers it, doing as before. The invocator takes the placed goblet, makes an offering, and does likewise; if not exhausted, he adds more and returns it to its place. The host bows twice, touching his head to the ground. When the invocator finishes the prayer, the host bows as before, weeps, and goes out to return to his position.
The invocator welcomes the impersonator, and one person in mourning attire, holding a basket, weeps and follows the impersonator. When the impersonator enters the gate, the men leap, and the women leap. The impersonator washes his hands, and the clan officer hands him a towel. When the impersonator reaches the steps, the invocator leads him up. When the impersonator ascends, the clan officer announces the leaping as before. When the impersonator enters the door, there is leaping as before, and the weeping ceases. The women enter the chamber. The host and the invocator bow to settle the impersonator. The impersonator bows and then sits.
……

zh:
小米打小就不听话，别人说东，他就非要往西。
他姑总说，都怪这娃生在芒种，带了一身的刺儿芒。
小米就呛回去，“那你找我爹娘去，还给我起了这么个名，那谷子哪能没有芒！”
他姑一听小米提他爹娘就不说话了。只连声说，说不过他，要等他再大些，就送去碧水云涛开蒙，让那儿的鸦先生，好好管教。
小米不知道他姑为什么每次一提他爹娘就不说话了，他没见过爹娘，也不知道爹娘有啥子用。他只知道他姑是不想养他了，想送他走。
“我才不去。什么鸭先生，鸡先生，自己名字这么难听，我不跟他学。”
“哈哈哈，说得好。”
“你，你是谁，我怎么没见过你？你别过来啊——我的搏楞鼓可厉害了。”
那人站在门口的老槐树下，瘦长瘦长，很高一条。
小米握着搏楞鼓，悄悄往后退了几步。
“别怕，”那人说，“是你姑说机关牛又不动了，我便过来看看。看来之前的机关牛，也都是你拆的？”
“我……才不是我！而且我都装回去了。”小米松了口气。
“你装得很好，”这人见小米不害怕了，才走了进来。他蹲下身，刚好平视小米，“就是有几处装反了。”
“你说反了就反了，你又不是墨家巨子！”
那人闻言笑了好几声，才继续说，“我是不是墨家巨子不打紧。可你装错的棘轮上其实刻了正反二字。你若是习了字，便不会装错了。”
小米眼睛又滴溜一转，他可不傻：“那我只学那两个字就够了，习字读书，哪有骑着机关牛漫山跑有意思？”
“嗯，有几分道理，那若是能骑着机关牛读书习字，你可愿来碧水云涛？”
“你，你就是鸦先生？那这搏楞鼓……是你做的啊……”
“是我做的，而且不只有搏楞鼓，还有机关牛、机关木鸢、机关小马……我都会做。”
“那……那我要跟你学！”
………………
春去秋来，又是一年芒种。
小米拿着搏楞鼓，骑上了机关牛。他听到了，种子在碧水云涛。他得回去，保护先生的种子。要是过了芒种，就错过今年播种的时候了。
en:
Mi had been stubborn since the day he could walk. Tell him to go east, and he would head west just to spite you. 

His aunt always grumbled that it was because he was born during Grain in Ear. She said he was born full of prickles, just like the wild crops that sprout this time of year. 
Mi would shoot right back at her. "Then blame my parents for naming me Mi! Mi means grain, and grain is supposed to have prickles!"

The moment he brought up his parents, his aunt would fall silent. She would only mutter under her breath that she could not argue with him, and that once he was a little older, she would send him to Jadestream Valley. She hoped Grandmaster Raven over there could knock some sense into him. 

Mi did not understand why his parents were a forbidden topic. He had never met them and did not see what use they were anyway. He only knew his aunt wanted to get rid of him and ship him off. 

"I am not going! Master Raven? Sounds like some old crow. With a bird name like that, I am not learning a thing from him!"
"Ha. Well said."
"Who are you? I have never seen you before. Do not come any closer! My rattle-drum is no joke!"

A man stood beneath the old locust tree by the gate. He was long, lean, and tall as a beanpole. 
Mi clutched his drum and edged back a few steps. 

"Steady now," the man said. "Your aunt mentioned the mechanical ox had stalled again, so I came to take a look. I assume you are the one who took it apart?"
"It was not me! And I put it all back together anyway." Mi breathed a sigh of relief. 
"You did a clean job of it." Seeing the boy's guard drop, the man stepped inside. He crouched down to meet Mi's eyes. "Except for a few gears you installed backward."
"They are not backward! Who do you think you are, some Mohist Grandmaster?"

The man laughed out loud before replying. "It does not matter if I am a Grandmaster. But those ratchets you fumbled with have 'Forward' and 'Reverse' carved right into the metal. If you had learned to read, you would not have botched the job."

Mi rolled his eyes, knowing he was not stupid. "Then I will just learn those two words! What is the point of books? I would rather spend my days riding that ox across the hills."
"A fair point. But what if you could ride that ox while you learn? Would you come to Jadestream Valley then?"
"You... You are Master Raven? Then this rattle-drum... You made it?"
"I did. And not just drums. Mechanical oxen, wooden eagles, clockwork ponies... I build them all."
"Then... I want to learn from you!"

...

Seasons drifted by, and Grain in Ear returned once more. 

Mi clutched his rattle-drum and mounted the mechanical ox. He had heard the news. The seeds were at Jadestream Valley. He had to go back. He had to protect his master's seeds. 

If Grain in Ear passed, the time for planting would be lost for good.

古代历法往往以物候来表示节令，蛙类的鸣噪与否也是其一。礼记月令就记载了孟夏之月，蛙的鸣叫便是其到来的重要特征。同样，天气的预示，对于蛙类来说也十分强烈，“雨过不知龙去处，一池草色万蛙鸣”，可见古人对蛙类与气象的联系，已知晓得颇为清晰。
en:
At dusk, the frogs croak in evening's noisy chorus, This year the rice fields brim with a full autumn harvest. 

In ancient times, people observed nature's rhythms to track the seasons. The Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances notes that in the first month of summer, the frogs begin to sing—a sign of seasonal change. Frogs were also keen forecasters of weather. As the old poem says:
"After the rain, the dragon is gone without a trace. But a pond thick with grass echoes with ten thousand frogs." To the ancients, a chorus of frogs was both a song of life and a sign of things to come.

zh:
“成何体统呀！成何体统！”
在墨城，有这么一位长老，你甚至无需记得他的传承授名——他的别号实在太多。
说一句“提桶兄”，你在指代谁大家便欣然领会。由此而始，诸如“大力士”、“九桶王”、“再来一桶”类的称号如雨后春笋而生，颇有三生万物的繁盛气象。
对此，鵙长老的反应自然只有一个：“成何体统呀成何体统！竟不知长幼尊卑！”
但当其他长老为其出头，勒令门中弟子不得为长老胡取外号时，他又轻叹一句“成何体统呀成何体统。以威权迫后辈，谈何兼爱？”
长老们哭笑不得，后来反为此事，与鵙长老一同向门中弟子道了歉。
鵙长老守体统是颇坚决的，坚决在不因人而异：
有一次课上，鵙长老恰读到一篇文章，看完之后便皱了眉头。
“胡编乱造，异想天开！如此空想的文章，怎还归属在了上等集录？成何体统！”
一看署名，作者竟恰是当年的自己。
“就算是当年的我，这篇文章，它也是狗屁不通……课上竟说此等污言秽语，我这是成何体统！呸呸！”
纵是自己，也批评无误。
鵙长老的体统，有时又有变化余地，可因时而异：
鵙长老年轻时，墨山道与文津馆交好，互相之间颇多学问探讨。他大为恼怒，连说了五个“成何体统”：
墨家非儒，文津馆则以儒说行事，那套假称仁义，实求功名的学说，还是少听为妙！
及至后来，墨山道封山愈严，与文津馆甚少往来，门中弟子阅儒家典籍渐少，曾与文津馆弟子有诸多论辩的鵙长老又暗自念叨了十次“成何体统”：
墨学自非儒中来，若全然不问不知儒说，怎能理解墨门之精要？
前后“体统”浑然相反，但实则亦有不变之处。那便是，“体统”须是当下见识中，认定的最好。
至年纪大了些，任了长老之位，管了年轻弟子们的诸多杂事，“体统”被冲撞得愈发频繁。
于城中冒冒失失，胡乱冲撞，成何体统！
见了先生，却不问礼，成何体统！
男女有别，拉拉扯扯，成何体统！
……
杂事多多，便有多多的“成何体统”，又不只停于“成何体统”。
冒失的弟子，便压压他的性子；恐惧先生不敢问礼的，便长其信心；男女弟子间有了情义，便教导其如何真正爱人。
鵙长老守着自己的“体统”，说出一句句“成何体统”的同时，也没忘了试着去了解着别的“体统”。
大家立于光阴长河各处，立于茫茫俗世各处，“体统”便难免有变化，有不同。
但不多不少，人人都需有一个“体统”。
世上也总要有一些，一路坚持着自己“体统”的人。
en:
"Beyond the pale! Truly beyond the pale!"

There is an elder in Mohist City whose official title and lineage hardly anyone bothers to remember, simply because he has far too many nicknames. Just mention "Brother Pail," and everyone immediately knows who you mean, a cheeky phonetic play on his favorite catchphrase. From there, titles like "Mr. Strongman" (for carrying all those pails), "King of Nine Pails," and "One More Pail" sprang up like mushrooms after rain, multiplying with endless creativity.

Elder Shrike's reaction to all this is always the same: "Beyond the pale! Truly beyond the pale! Have you all forgotten your respect for your elders?"
Yet, when other elders tried to step in and ordered the disciples to stop giving him nicknames, he simply sighed. "Using authority to pressure the younger generation... Is this the 'Universal Love' we preach? Absolutely beyond the pale!" 
The other elders didn't know whether to laugh or cry, and eventually ended up apologizing to the disciples alongside him.

Elder Shrike's dedication to decorum is absolute, and he applies it to everyone equally.
Once during a lesson, he frowned deeply after reading an essay. "Total fabrication! Utter nonsense! How did such an absurd piece of writing make it into the Master Collection? Beyond the pale!"
Upon checking the author's name, he realized it was his own work from years ago.
"Even if I wrote it back then, it's still complete garbage," he declared without missing a beat. "For me to spew such nonsense in a classroom... is completely beyond the pale! Pah!" 
He never spared himself from his own harsh criticism.

However, his strict sense of decorum occasionally leaves room for flexibility, shifting with the times.
In his youth, Mohist Hill was on excellent terms with the Inkbound Order, and they often engaged in scholarly debates. He would grow furious, stringing together five "beyond the pales" in a row: 
"Mohism is the opposite of Confucianism! The Inkbound Order operates on Confucian ideals. They preach benevolence but are really just chasing fame. It's best we ignore their nonsense!"
Later on, as Mohist Hill became increasingly isolated and had little contact with the Inkbound Order, the disciples read far fewer Confucian texts. Elder Shrike, who had once debated extensively with the Order's students, muttered "beyond the pale" a dozen times to himself: 

"Mohism was born from the critique of Confucianism. If they know absolutely nothing about it, how can they grasp the true essence of the Mohist way?"
His standards of propriety had completely reversed, yet at its core, one thing remained unchanged. To him, "decorum" always meant holding fast to the highest ideals one's current wisdom could comprehend.
As he grew older, officially took on the mantle of an elder, and managed the daily affairs of the young disciples, his sense of decorum was challenged more and more often.

"Running around the city so recklessly, absolutely beyond the pale!"
"Passing a teacher without a proper greeting, beyond the pale!"
"Boys and girls teasing and grabbing at each other in public, beyond the pale!"
With so many trivial matters came countless cries of "beyond the pale," but he never stopped at just scolding them.

For the reckless disciples, he tempered their impatience. For those too timid to greet their teachers, he helped build their confidence. And when true affection blossomed between disciples, he taught them how to genuinely care for one another.
While guarding his own sense of propriety and constantly exclaiming "Beyond the pale," Elder Shrike never forgot to try and understand the decorum of others.

We all stand at different points in the great river of time, scattered across this vast world. It is only natural that our standards of propriety change and differ.
But everyone needs a sense of decorum, no more and no less. And the world will always need those who hold steadfast to their own.
Paw-some Friend

偶尔他会停下，闻一闻路边的柱子。
偶尔他会摔倒，但又马上爬起，支着四肢在那爬行。
醉鬼与狗，你想，原来，也没什么区别。
en:
After finishing his rambling words, the Master First Cave wobbles to his feet and staggers toward the Nether Crossing. 
Watching his unsteady retreat, you can't tell if he's truly awake or still lost in a haze. 
At times, he pauses to sniff the posts lining the path. 
At others, he stumbles and falls but scrambles back up on all fours. 
Drunkard or dog—they aren't so different after all.

zh:
“好孩子，是你。你且往那边摸摸，可有一个朱红的小瓶？”
“没有灯火，我……我瞧不见……”
“摸一摸便是。两个瓶子，都取来给我。”
“老贼婆之前还骂人‘贱婢’呢，这会儿使唤上人了。姑娘，莫要信她，把东西给我！
“啊呀！”
“怎么了？”
“我、我绊倒了，瓶子都碎了……”
“哪个碎了？红的，还是黑的？”
“老贼婆，这黑灯瞎火的，便是你我也分不清，她能看出什么？”
“药丸，洒了……”
“给我拿来！”
“给我！”
“老贼婆急了？想必你这两瓶，一瓶是解药，另一瓶尽是害人的毒药。这下好了，混在一处，分不清了。”
“哈哈——咱俩都要被这蠢女人害死了！”
“我有个办法，只是，只是……”
“有屁快放。”
“啰嗦什么，快说！”
“只是，要老天爷看着办……”
“我摸到了两颗药，喂你们一人一颗，好不好？我什么武功也不会，谁也不敢得罪，就当老天爷替你们选了，怪不着我……”
“……”
“……好，好呀。死到临头，还能赌这一局——痛快！痛快！”
“我先！”
en:
"Oh, it's you, child. Feel around over there. There should be a small red vial."
"It's too dark. I... I can't see anything..."
"You don't need to see. Use your hands. There are two vials. Bring me both."
"She was calling you a filthy whore a moment ago, and now she's ordering you around. Don't trust her. Give the vials to me!"
"Ahh!"
"What's wrong?"
"I tripped... The bottles broke..."
"Can you find the pills from the red one?"
"It's pitch-black, old hag. Even we can't tell what's what. How could she?"
"They spilled everywhere..."
"Give them here!"
"Give them to me!"
"Nervous now? One vial must have held the antidote, and the other poison. Too bad they're all mixed together."
"Hah! Looks like this idiot's killed us both!"
"I-I might have an idea, but..."
"Quit rambling and say it!"
"Out with it."
"Only... Heaven will have to decide..."
"I found two pills. What if I give you one each? I can't fight, and I don't want to wrong either of you. We'll let Heaven choose. Neither of you can blame me for the outcome."
"..."
"Fine by me. One last gamble before I die? Nothing better!"
"Me first!"

一只信雀自月下飞来，兜兜转转落在褚清泉的手边。他拆开信反复读了几遍，其中最后的一句——“此乃大义之举，为天下计，为万民愿，望君莫辞。”在他心中回荡许久。虽然他早知道自己会为大义献身，但他没想过要与香寻走到如今这般地步。想到此处，褚清泉起身回屋，在信纸上写下，“大丈夫为天下献身，义不容辞，然吾心中有愧。洛神一事，褚某当再做打算。望君静候。”

凡天下事，终难两全。但至少，他不想骗她。
en:
A message sparrow flew in beneath the moonlight, circling once, then twice, before it landed beside Chu Qingquan's hand. He opened the letter and read it over and over, but it was the final line that echoed in his mind:

"This is an act of great righteousness, for the realm, for the people. I pray you do not refuse."

He had always known that one day he would offer his life for the greater good. What he hadn't expected was to come this far with Xiangxun. The thought stirred him. He rose and returned to his room. On a fresh sheet of paper, he wrote:

"A true man gives himself for the world. It is his duty and honor. Yet I carry shame in my heart. As for the matter of the Water Lady, I must reconsider. I ask you to wait." 

In this world, nothing is ever perfectly resolved. But at the very least, he didn't want to lie to her.

好的大夫，不会听病人的话，即使是比自己大很多武功也更高强的病人。

兰澳是幸运的，她遇上了拥有菩萨心肠和医术天赋的小盘。
兰澳也是不幸的，当时距离小盘能被称为水月先生的日子，还有数十年之久。

最终，兰澳成了小盘救人无数的一生中，第一个没救下来的病人。

多年之后，执掌青溪的水月先生，无数次想告诉自己的弟子，关于兰澳的故事。但她每次欲言又止。
好的大夫，不会听病人的话。但她是兰澳“捡来的女儿”，是她的“小丫鬟”、“小哑巴”。
en:
A herb sachet made by Xiaopan for Lan Ao to alleviate the symptoms of her Sleeping Puppet poison.

Lan Ao stubbornly insisted Xiaopan omit any sedatives, as pain kept her awake. However, Xiaopan remained silent, simply stuffing the sachet with an unrecognizable blend of medicinal powders according to her own prescription.
A good doctor ignores a patient's demands, even if the patient is much older and a far superior martial artist.

Lan Ao was fortunate to meet Xiaopan, who possessed both a Bodhisattva's heart and a genius for medicine.
Yet, Lan Ao was also unfortunate—it would be decades before Xiaopan earned the title of Master Moonstream.

Ultimately, Lan Ao became the very first patient Xiaopan failed to save in a lifetime of rescuing countless others.

Years later, Master Moonstream, being the head of Silver Needle, wanted countless times to tell her disciples Lan Ao's story. Yet, every time, words failed her.
A good doctor never listens to a patient. But she was Lan Ao's "found daughter," her "little maid," her "little mute."

zh:
风静，叶落。蓦地林鸟惊飞。
她站在树梢最高处将呼哨穿林过的山匪们尽收眼底，剑动，风未止，人已归天。
妇孺们怯怯从运货箱里爬出，自以为隐秘地观察这个与山匪没有太多不同的黑衣女人，犹犹豫豫，又终于畏惧她身上浓重的血腥，无声一躬身就离去。
软弱的步伐踏得又重又慢。她俯身从尸体上捡取财货，忽然有一声稚嫩的叫喊和风一起钻进她的帷帽垂帘。
“多谢你啊大侠！”

大侠。她像甩掉剑上血痕一样，把这两个字从自己身上甩掉。
世道太烂，随便一个人过路，随手杀一个人就是恶贼，就能莫名其妙救下两个人，就能被喊一声大侠。这名号比野草疯长得还快，价贱得很。
至少要到人人都有口饭吃，幼童至少能活到十岁，山里除了野兽没有山匪的时候，要还有人管她叫大侠，这名头才配让她担着。

那样的时候，就叫作太平。
有人这么告诉过她，又承诺过她。如今，他却成了不在山野的贼匪。
山野的贼匪她要杀，不在山野的贼匪她也要杀。

林鸟落回又振飞。
她从深林中飞出，寻往下一个杀人之地。
en:
The wind stills, and leaves fall. Suddenly, forest birds take flight in alarm.
She stands atop the highest bough, taking in the sight of the bandits whistling through the woods. Her sword flashes; before the wind settles, the men have met their end.
Women and children crawl out from the cargo crates, stealing glances at the black-clad woman, who seemed little different from the bandits. They hesitate, shrink back at the smell of blood, bow without a word, and slip away with heavy, timid steps.
She bends down to loot valuables from the corpses, when suddenly a tender shout slips through the veil of her bamboo hat along with the wind.
"Thank you, hero!"

Hero. She shakes the title off herself just as she flicks the blood off her sword.
The world is rotten. In times like these, any random passerby can kill someone and be called a bandit; save two lives, and people will slap the title "hero" on you as if it were nothing. The title spreads faster than wild grass, cheap and worthless.
That title will only mean anything when everyone has food to eat, children can live past ten, and the hills are free of bandits.

Such a time is called peace.
Someone had once told her so and promised her as much. Now, however, he has become a bandit himself, one who does not hide in the mountains.
Bandits in the mountains, she will kill. Bandits not in the mountains, she will kill just the same.

The birds settle in the woods, only to take flight again.
She leaps forth from the deep woods, flying toward the next place where blood must be shed.
(alert) "Friend," you say? Guards, watch this one!

zh:
荧渊对无相皇来说，是起点，也是归宿。
他在幼年之时，随父母入渊，后来父母病亡，他便一直由那个柳枝般的女子抚养。
后来，那个女子也死了。她死时，荧渊的花像下雪一样飘了很久很久，那个白发的男人在落花之中，默然而立。
那是他第一次和白发男人说话。
那个男人以无缺无相为意，赐给他名字，无相皇从此便为他卖命。
因为一头野兽若是被起了名字，便从此拥有主人。

无相皇跟随主人离开荧渊之后，从无败绩。只有一次，输给了一个抱孩子的男人。
主人的表情还是淡淡的，但他分明从中看出了失望。
不，吾主，不要对我失望……我还是你说的无缺无相，我还是武者之皇。
于是他自愿入渊为那女子守墓，发誓不斩落一千个人头不出渊。
十多年过去，他只差最后一个，便可以再度向主人证明。
证明他无相皇，配得上所赐之名，不曾叫人失望。
可为什么……
无相皇重重倒在地上，看向面容不清的那人。他努力伸出手去，想触碰那个永远遥远而模糊的影子，却最终还是沉入黑暗。
en:
Gleaming Abyss to the Void King marks both a start and an end.
As a child, he entered the Gleaming Abyss with his parents. But when they passed away, a slender woman, as graceful as a willow branch raised him.
Yet, in the end, that woman too was taken from him. When she died, the flowers of Gleaming Abyss fell like snow, drifting endlessly through the air. Amidst the sea of petals, the white-haired man stood, silent and still.
It was then that he spoke to the man for the first time.
The man, embodying the very essence of Formless Reign, gave him a name. From that moment on, The Void King has become his.
For once a beast is named, it belongs to its master.

Ever since the Void King followed his master out of the Gleaming Abyss, defeat has never again been his companion. There was only one exception: a single loss to a man carrying a child.
His master's face remained impassive, but the disappointment in his eyes was undeniable. 
No, my lord, please don't be disappointed in me... I am still the Void King Reign you want. I am still the Emperor of Warriors.
Since then, he has been back in the Pond, vowing to guard the tomb of that woman, swearing never to leave until he claims a thousand heads.
More than a decade passes. He is just one head away, one step from fulfilling his vow and proving himself worthy to his master once more.
He has to prove that the Void King deserves the name bestowed upon him. That he has not failed his master.
But why...
The Void King collapses heavily, staring at the indistinct figure before him. He reaches out, desperate to touch that far-off shadow, but in the end, he is consumed by darkness.

感谢游侠对《燕云十六声》的理解与支持，如果您有其他疑问和需求，也可以点击前往来获得帮助，或拨打燕云专用客服电话95163988。祝游侠快意江湖，万事胜意。
en:
After the version 1.7 update, Sixteen Lanes observed and fixed the following issues:
[1] Fixed an issue where the "Camel" at Camel Station could be harvested repeatedly to quickly gain large amounts of "Camel Milk."
[2] Fixed an issue in some modes where "Goldcrest Runners" could be repeatedly refreshed to quickly gain large amounts of "Golden Vessel Fragments" and "Prismatic Essences." There is a cap on these items now; the fix does not affect the daily acquisition limit.
Additionally, Sixteen Lanes noted that the acquisition of "Camel Milk" needed optimization and made the following changes:
[1] Utuk enemies will drop "Camel Milk" upon death.
[2] "Camel Milk" can now be obtained in the Hexi Co-op World, with a refresh time of 5 minutes.
[3] The number of "Camels" available for harvesting "Camel Milk" will be increased in the future.
We deeply apologize for the inconvenience caused by the anomaly and offer this #4d734dsmall gift#E as a token of our regret. The quantity of compensated "Camel Milk" is based on the#H total obtained#E before the fix, ensuring fairness for all Wanderers.
Thank you for your understanding and support of Where Winds Meet. If you have further questions or concerns, you may click to visit [Link] for assistance, or call our dedicated service line at 95163988. May your journey through the jianghu be filled with joy, and may all things go better than you wish.

en:
To Master Lu Li 

The jade case has been received, with unexpected craftsmanship. The seams are flawless, not a drop leaks through. Few in the world possess such skill, and you, Master Lu, are foremost among them. Neither you nor the jade should be blamed for the Liangzhou incident—it was Bochen who betrayed my men. Seeing this jade case, I know you have rallied. We should drink together at Jade Pond. Best to forget old wounds, but if you cannot, remembering is fine too. Their blades can sever limbs, but not the backbone. This case aids me greatly. I, Zhang Yichao, will remember your kindness. 

Enclosed is an item I recovered from Bochen. Though discarded by the blind-hearted, a flaw does not diminish its radiance. Returning it to its rightful owner, hoping it brings you peace. 

Written by Zhang Yichao

那小家伙也不说话，只点了点头，想说什么却憋红了脸。

一戴便是很多年。
en:
Chen Tu first met Chen Shezhi as he was getting ready to officially accept apprentices from the village.
As tradition required, the villagers seeking his approval offered gifts of dried meat before Chen Tu.
Suddenly, a dusty little figure desperately squeezed through the crowd.
A small, pitted stone bangle was held up before Chen Tu.
Though rough and uneven, carving a solid stone bangle without breaking it was incredibly difficult for a child.
"Little one, did you make this stone bangle?"
The child did not speak, only nodding, his face flushed red from trying to utter a word.
The villagers advised, "Master Chen Tu, that boy stutters! How can a stutterer learn a fine craft?"
Chen Tu merely smiled, accepted the stone bangle, and slipped it onto his wrist.
He wore it for many years to come.

zh:
【宪问第十四】

宪问耻。子曰：“邦有道，谷，邦无道，谷，耻也。”
“克、伐、怨、欲不行焉，可以为仁矣？”子曰：“可以为难矣，仁则吾不知也。”
子曰：“士而怀居，不足以为士矣。”
子曰：“邦有道，危言危行；邦无道，危行言逊。”
子曰：“有德者必有言，有言者不必有德。仁者必有勇，勇者不必有仁。”
南宫适问于孔子曰：“羿善射，傲荡舟，俱不得其死然。禹、稷躬稼，而有天下。”夫子不答。南宫适出，子曰：“君子哉若人！尚德哉若人！”
子曰：“君子而不仁者有矣夫，未有小人而仁者也。”
子曰：“爱之，能勿劳乎？忠焉，能勿诲乎？”
子曰：“为命，卑谌草创之，世叔讨论之，行人子羽修饰，东里子产润色之。”
或问子产。子曰：“惠人也。”问子西，曰：“彼哉！彼哉！”问管仲，曰：“人也，夺伯氏骈邑三百，饭蔬食，没齿无怨言。”
子曰：“贫而无怨难，富而无骄易。”
子曰：“孟公绰为赵魏老则优，不可以为藤薛大夫也。”
子路问成人。曰：“若臧武仲之智，公绰之不欲，卞庄子之勇，冉求之艺，文之以礼乐，亦可以为成人矣。”曰：“今之成人者何必然？见利思义，见危授命，久要不忘平生之言，亦可以为成人矣。”
子问公叔文子于公明贾曰：“信乎，夫子不言、不笑、不取乎？”公明贾对曰：“以告者过也。夫子时然后言，人不厌其言也。乐然后笑，人不厌其笑也。义然后取，人不厌其取也。”子曰：“其然，岂其然乎？”
子曰：“臧武仲以防求为后于鲁，虽曰不要君，吾不信也。”
子曰：“晋文公谲而不正，齐桓公正而不谲。”

en:
【Book XIV: Xian Wen】

Xian asked about shame. The Master said, "When the state is well-governed, to take office and draw salary is honorable. When the state is ill-governed, to take office and draw salary is shameful."
"If one refrains from ambition, boasting, resentment, and greed, can he be considered benevolent?" The Master said, "That can be considered difficult, but whether it is benevolence, I do not know."
The Master said, "A scholar who is attached to comfort is not worthy of being called a scholar."
The Master said, "When the state is well-governed, speak boldly and act boldly. When the state is ill-governed, act boldly but speak cautiously."
The Master said, "A virtuous person will have good words, but one with good words may not be virtuous. A benevolent person will be courageous, but a courageous person may not be benevolent."
Nangong Kuo asked Confucius, "Yi was skilled in archery, and Ao was skilled in sailing, yet both died unnatural deaths. Yu and Ji personally tilled the land and gained the world." The Master did not answer. After Nangong Kuo left, the Master said, "What a gentleman! What a virtuous man!"
The Master said, "There are gentlemen who are not benevolent, but there are no petty men who are benevolent."
The Master said, "If you love someone, can you avoid laboring for them? If you are loyal to someone, can you avoid instructing them?"
The Master said, "In drafting decrees, Pi Chen drafted them, Shishu discussed them, the diplomat Ziyu polished them, and Dongli Zichan refined them."
Someone asked about Zichan. The Master said, "He was a kind man." Asked about Zixi, he said, "That one! That one!" Asked about Guan Zhong, he said, "He was a man. He took three hundred households from Bo Shi's Pianyi, yet Bo Shi ate coarse food and harbored no resentment till his death."
The Master said, "It is difficult to be poor without resentment, but easy to be rich without arrogance."
The Master said, "Meng Gongchuo would excel as an elder in Zhao or Wei, but he would not be suitable as a minister in Teng or Xue."
Zilu asked about the complete person. The Master said, "With the wisdom of Zang Wuzhong, the lack of desire of Gongchuo, the courage of Bian Zhuangzi, and the talents of Ran Qiu, adorned with ritual and music, one could be considered a complete person." He added, "But what about the complete person of today? One who thinks of righteousness when seeing profit, risks his life in danger, and never forgets his lifelong promises—such a person can also be considered complete."
The Master asked Gongming Jia about Gongshu Wenzi, "Is it true that your master does not speak, laugh, or take?" Gongming Jia replied, "Those who told you this exaggerated. My master speaks when it is timely, so people do not tire of his words. He laughs when he is joyful, so people do not tire of his laughter. He takes when it is righteous, so people do not tire of his taking." The Master said, "Is that so? Could it really be so?"
The Master said, "Zang Wuzhong used Fang to secure a successor in Lu. Even if it is said he did not coerce his lord, I do not believe it."
The Master said, "Duke Wen of Jin was crafty but not upright; Duke Huan of Qi was upright but not crafty."

zh: 《仪礼》成于先秦，乃周代贵族礼仪规范之汇编。原名《礼》，亦称《礼经》《士礼》，汉代尊为五经之一。全书共十七篇，分冠礼、昏礼、丧服、士丧礼、既夕礼、士虞礼、特牲馈食礼、少牢馈食礼、有司彻、乡饮酒礼、乡射礼、燕礼、大射仪、聘礼、公食大夫礼、觐礼、丧服传诸目，所涉冠婚丧祭、射御朝聘之仪节程式，兼及器物陈设、服制等差，多记进退揖让之细节。汉初高堂生传十七篇，为今文经；鲁恭王坏孔子宅得古文《礼》五十六篇，其十七篇与今文同，余皆逸。汉郑玄合并今古文，作《仪礼注》，遂为传世定本。唐贾公彦据郑注作《仪礼疏》，纳入官学，列于三礼。
en: The Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial was compiled before the Qin dynasty, and is an assemblage of the ritual codes and ceremonial norms of the Zhou nobility. Originally titled the Book of Rites, and also known as the Canon of Rites and the Rites of the Gentleman-Officers, it was revered in the Han dynasty as one of the Five Classics. The full work comprises seventeen chapters, divided into the following sections: the Capping Rite, the Marriage Rite, Mourning Garments, the Mourning Rite of the Gentlemen-Officer, the Eve-of-Burial Rite, the Post-Burial Offering Rite, the Special Sacrifice Feast Rite, the Lesser Sacrifice Feast Rite, the Steward's Withdrawal, the Village Wine Drinking Rite, the Village Archery Rite, the Banquet Rite, the Grand Archery Ceremony, the Reception Rite, the Duke's Feast for Nobles, the Audience Rite, and the Transmission of Mourning Garments. Its subjects encompass the ceremonial forms and procedural steps of capping, marriage, mourning, sacrifice, archery, defense, court audience, and diplomatic reception, extending also to the arrangement of vessels and implements and the gradations of dress, with much detail recorded on the proper deportment of advance, withdrawal, salutation, and deference. In the early Han, Gaotang Sheng transmitted seventeen chapters as the New Text recension. When King Gong of Lu demolished the residence of Confucius, fifty-six chapters of an Old Text Book of Rites were discovered, seventeen of which accorded with the New Text, while the rest were all lost. The Han scholar Zheng Xuan combined the New and Old Text recensions and composed the Annotations on the Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial, which became the established text transmitted to posterity. In the Tang, Jia Gongyan composed a subcommentary based on Zheng Xuan's annotations, and the work was incorporated into the official academies and listed among the Three Rites.

太始四年正月
……昔吾游历八荒，实见奇草异木，然致长生者，终究不过行尸也。吾归而不敢以实告，恐帝愈求。乃诈称一无所获，藏所集奇珍于泰山之阴。
吾常思：帝之所以为帝，不在其寿，而在竹帛之名。使后世知汉有盛世，则帝不死矣。
然吾平生以滑稽进，未敢直言。今将死，乃凿墓设覆，置酒以待。帝他日封禅泰山，必发吾墓，见此覆碗。覆中无物，唯谜而已。谜底，即吾欲言而不能言者。
唯愿帝亲启之，如对饮然。若帝不罪吾欺，则九泉之下，犹当奉觞……
en:
First month, fourth year of Taishi.
...In truth, when I roamed the realm, I indeed beheld rare herbs and wondrous trees. Yet those who attained longevity through them were nothing more than walking corpses. Upon my return, I dared not speak the truth, fearing Your Majesty would pursue them with even greater fervor. Thus, I falsely claimed to have found nothing, concealing the rarities I gathered on the northern slopes of Mount Tai.
I have often reflected: what makes a sovereign great is not the length of his life, but his legacy inscribed upon the annals of history. If future generations remember the Han Dynasty at its zenith, then Your Majesty lives forever.
Yet throughout my life, I found favor only as a jester, never daring to speak plainly. Now, on the brink of death, I have carved this tomb, laid out an overturned bowl, and set wine to wait. When Your Majesty performs the Fengshan sacrifices at Mount Tai in the days to come, you will surely unearth my tomb and find this bowl. Beneath it lies nothing but a riddle, the answer to which holds the very words I longed to speak in life.
My only wish is that Your Majesty lifts it in person, as though we were sharing a cup. Should Your Majesty forgive my deceit, then even in the Underworld, I shall raise a cup to you once more...

zh:
朱鱼从不信神。
目睹博浪沙张氏以投龙简祈雨，以“河伯”自居愚弄百姓后，朱鱼对神的厌恶达到了极致。世上诸神，不过魍魉。
可世间人信。
朱鱼望着傩面前虔诚下跪哭求的百姓，默默熄了手中的火折子。
“有时候，人总得相信一些东西。”朱鱼这才发现，她背后站着的张家长子，或者说……第六十七代“河伯”。
“相信，是世上最好的良药，女侠，你信不信？”张公子问。
“信。可我的‘信’，不是信天，信地，信神佛，是信自己。”
“好一个‘信自己’。”张家公子抛出的投龙简，落在了朱鱼的掌心。
“如果有一天，你成了‘河伯’，我希望，你还记得今日的话。”
“不信神佛，只信自己。”
en:
Zhu Yu never believed in gods.
After witnessing the Zhang clan of Roaring Sands deceive the people with Dragon's Rite Scroll offerings and rain rituals—claiming to be the River Master—her disdain for deities reached its peak. To her, all so-called gods were just trickery.
But people believed.
As she watched the villagers kneel and weep before a Nuo Dance Mask, Zhu Yu silently snuffed out her foldable fire.
"Sometimes, people need something to believe in." Only then did she notice the Zhang clan's eldest son behind her—or rather... the 67th 'River Master.'
"Belief is the best medicine in this world. Do you believe, swordswoman?" he asked.
"I do. But my belief isn't in heaven, earth, or gods. I believe in myself."
"What a fine answer," he said, tossing a Dragon's Rite Scroll that landed in her palm.
"If one day, you become the River Master, I hope you'll remember this moment."
"No gods, no Buddha—only myself."

zh:
它还记得最早的时候，那些高高大大的人管这个院子叫“宣武军节度使治所”；也还记得那个喂它剩饭的小卒，笑起来有颗虎牙。

后来，院墙推了又砌，高楼塌了又起。金阙依旧在，几度夕阳红。穿黄袍的人从它眼前经过了一个又一个，姓朱的、姓李的、姓郭的……他们都说自己是这里的主人，可明明一个个都来来去去，行色匆匆。
只有它一直都在。

它守着这金殿，身子也随着漫长岁月，一点点圆润庞大起来。
偶尔微阖双目小憩时，脸上忽觉一阵酥痒。那一瞬，它恍惚以为是那个小卒又来挠它的下巴，喊它：“小猫，开饭了！”

睁开眼，原来只是花又落了，擦过胡须。

——意兴阑珊，正想重新闭上眼，忽闻一声清脆的呼哨。
花影摇曳间，一张年轻的面庞在树下、在簇拥的群猫间流连。忽然，少年人的视线穿透了层层枝叶，直直撞进树梢之间——正对它的眼睛。

太久没有人这样看着它了。
目光里没有宫人的惶恐，没有权贵的算计，只有清澈的好奇，如秋月，如春风。
记忆深处那张露着虎牙的笑脸在眼前一闪而过。
它抖了抖耳尖，没有像往常那样隐入风里，而是站起身，弓着背大大方方伸了个懒腰……
就像一只寻常的猫那样。

能陪它玩的朋友终于来了。它想。
en:
It still remembers the earliest days, when those towering humans called this courtyard the "Xuanwu Army Governor's Command." It remembers, too, the grunt who fed it scraps, a boy with a canine tooth that peeked out when he smiled.

Later, walls were leveled and relaid; towers crumbled and rose anew. The imperial pavilions endure as ever, through countless crimson sunsets. Figures in imperial yellow passed before its eyes in endless succession: Zhus, Lis, Guos... Each claimed mastery over this realm, yet each was but a fleeting traveler, hurrying toward their end.
Only it remained, ever-present.

It kept watch over the golden halls, its form growing stout and grand as the long years rounded its edges.
Sometimes, dozing with half-lidded eyes, it would feel a sudden, soft itch upon its face. For a fleeting moment, it would fancy the grunt had returned to scratch its chin, calling: "Little cat, time for your meal!"

Upon opening its eyes, it saw nothing but a falling blossom, grazing its whiskers.

With interest fading, it prepared to drift back into sleep until a crisp, clear whistle rang out.
Amidst the swaying shadows of flowers, a youthful face lingered beneath the trees, surrounded by a feline throng. Suddenly, the youth's gaze pierced the dense foliage and crashed into its own amidst the branches.

It had been an eternity since anyone had looked at it so.
In that look, there was no servant's dread, no noble's scheme; only a clarity of curiosity, pure as the autumn moon, gentle as the spring breeze.
A flash of memory: that smiling face with the canine tooth flickered past.
It flicked the tips of its ears. Instead of vanishing into the wind as was its wont, it rose, arched its back, and gave a grand, unhurried stretch, just like any ordinary cat.

"A companion to pass the time has finally arrived," it thought.

zh:
“妮儿，没事吧？”
在暗无天日的匪寨地窖里，京娘听到的第一句话是带有中原口音的问候，看到的第一样东西是一根平平无奇的棍子。她顺着棍子看过去，见到一个满脸大胡子的男人。
京娘眼神一凛，裙裳下藏的刀陡然出鞘猛攻。男人举棍格挡，颇为惊讶，“原是玩扮猪吃老虎的。”
“你看到了，我不必你救。所以也不欠你恩情。”京娘丢下一句话，收回刀转身就走。
身后传来：“兵器一寸短一寸险，先入险境再翻身是取巧，这种示人以弱的招数不是长久的道理。”

刀逼近脖颈的时候，京娘恨恨想，确实不够长久。但这已经是她最能杀人的方式。早知道就把那人的棍子抢了。
想棍子棍子到。京娘第二次见到这根平平无奇的棍子，是在满地尸体的山林里，一棍就扫开了难缠的匪头，再一棍，钝器居然生生杵进了匪头的胸口。
京娘咋舌，果然应该抢这人的棍子。
可惜抢不过。她便谢他道：“我要学你的棍子。”
“俺这棍法太刚硬，不适合妮儿学。俺教你剑。”
“剑够强吗？”
“凭你的心性，肯定能练到够强。”
“那我学。”

在千里长途中，京娘学到一套剑式，得到一柄好剑。后来每一次出剑，她都记得这一路的恩义。
一如她也记得他违背的承诺。
en:
"You alright, girl?"
In the lightless cellar under a bandit stronghold, the first thing Jingniang heard was a greeting in a Central Plains accent. The first thing she saw was an ordinary wooden staff. Following it up, she found a bearded man.
Jingniang's gaze sharpened. The blade hidden beneath her skirts flashed out and struck.
He snapped the staff up to block, surprise crossing his face. "So you play weak, then strike hard."
"You saw it," Jingniang said. "I didn't need saving. I owe you nothing."
She sheathed her blade and turned to leave.
Behind her, he said, "A weapon is more dangerous the shorter it is. Throwing yourself into danger and flipping the fight may be clever, but pretending to be weak isn't something you can live on."
Later, with a knife at her throat, Jingniang thought bitterly that he was right. It wouldn't last. But it was still the deadliest way she knew.
She should've taken his staff.
As if summoned by the thought, she saw that same plain staff again in a forest strewn with bodies. One swing swept aside the troublesome bandit chief. The next drove the blunt end straight into his chest.
Jingniang clicked her tongue. She really should have taken that staff.
Too bad she couldn't.
So she thanked him and said, "Teach me the staff."
"My staff work is too hard for you," he said. "I'll teach you the sword."
"Will it be strong enough?"
"With your nature, you'll make it strong enough."
"Then I'll learn."
Over the long road that followed, Jingniang learned a sword form and came to own a fine blade. And every time she drew it after that, she remembered the kindness she was shown along the way.
Just as she remembered the promise he broke.

zh:
【宫室·一】

【草庐】

缑山西峰草堂作
岑参
结庐对中岳，青翠常在门。
遂耽水木兴，尽作渔樵言。

日色隐空谷，蝉声喧暮村。
曩闻道士语，偶见清净源。
隐几阅吹叶，乘秋眺归根。
独游念求仲，开径招王孙。
片雨下南涧，孤峰出东原。
栖迟虑益澹，脱略道弥敦。

草阁
杜甫
草阁临无地，柴扉永不关。
鱼龙回夜水，星月动秋山。
久露清初湿，高云薄未还。
泛舟惭小妇，飘泊损红颜。

茅屋为秋风所破歌
杜甫
八月秋高风怒号，卷我屋上三重茅。
茅飞渡江洒江郊，高者挂罥长林梢，下者飘转沉塘坳。
南村群童欺我老无力，忍能对面为盗贼。
公然抱茅入竹去，唇焦口燥呼不得，归来倚杖自叹息。
俄顷风定云墨色，秋天漠漠向昏黑。
布衾多年冷似铁，娇儿恶卧踏里裂。
床头屋漏无干处，雨脚如麻未断绝。
自经丧乱少睡眠，长夜沾湿何由彻！
安得广厦千万间，大庇天下寒士俱欢颜，风雨不动安如山。
呜呼！何时眼前突兀见此屋，吾庐独破受冻死亦足！

【宫殿】

和贾舍人早朝大明宫之作

en:
【Palaces and Dwellings · Part One】

【Thatched Hut】

"Composed at the Thatched Hall on the Western Peak of Mount Gou"
By Cen Shen
My hut faces the central peak, its evergreen gate a constant sight.
Enraptured by the streams and woods, I speak only of fishing and woodcutting's delight.
Lately, I've neglected verses and prose, seeking only to ease my soul's plight.
The sun hides in the empty valley, cicadas clamor as dusk veils the village light.
Once I heard a Taoist's words, glimpsed a source of purity, clear and bright.
Leaning on my desk, I watch leaves blown, gazing at autumn's return from a height.
Roaming alone, I think of seeking companions, clearing paths to welcome noble friends in flight.
A shower falls on the southern stream, a lone peak rises from the eastern plain's site.
Dwelling in seclusion, worries grow faint; shedding constraints, the Way feels more right.
Wild mist gently brushes my pillow at dawn, distant sails enter my view from afar, a tranquil sight.
Where is Shang Ping now? With whom can I share this thought, this insight?
I stand still until clouds disperse, under the pale moon, the garden opens bright.

"Thatched Pavilion"
By Du Fu
The thatched pavilion overlooks the void, its wooden gate never closed tight.
Fish and dragons churn the night waters, stars and moon stir the autumn mountain's height.
Long dew has moistened the fresh dawn, high clouds linger thin, not taking flight.
Boating shames this humble wife, adrift, her rosy cheeks worn by plight.

"Song of My Thatched Roof Torn by Autumn Winds"
By Du Fu
In the eighth month, autumn winds howl in rage,
Tearing three layers of thatch from my cottage stage.
The thatch flies across the river, scattering on the shore,
Some caught high on tall treetops forevermore,
Some drifting down to sink in ponds, a soggy, silent score.
Village boys from the south mock my aged, feeble might,
Daring to be thieves before my very sight.
Boldly they grab the thatch and vanish into bamboo groves,
My lips parched, voice hoarse, no call their mischief moves,
Returning, leaning on my cane, a sigh my spirit proves.
Soon the wind stills, clouds turn ink-black in hue,
The autumn sky stretches vast, dusk's darkness coming true.
My cotton quilt, years old, is cold as iron to the touch,
My restless child kicks in sleep, tearing the lining much.
By the bed, the roof leaks, no dry spot can be found,
Raindrops fall like hemp strands, soaking all the ground.
Since chaos came, sleep has been rare and slight,
How can I endure the long, damp, endless night?
If only I had a thousand spacious rooms, grand and bright,
Sheltering all the world's poor scholars from their plight,
Joyful faces, safe from wind and rain, steadfast as a mountain's height.
Alas! When will such houses rise before my eyes?
If my hut alone is ruined, I'd freeze to death without sighs!

【Palace】

"In Response to Secretary Jia's 'Early Audience at the Daming Palace'"
By Wang Wei
The crimson-turbaned cock-man announces dawn's first light,
Attendants present the emperor's robe, kingfisher-clouds bright.
The nine-layered palace gates swing open wide,
Envoys from myriad lands bow before the imperial crown's pride.
Sunlight touches immortal-palm screens, setting them in motion,
Incense smoke clings to the dragon-embroidered gown, a fragrant ocean.
After court, the five-colored edict must be penned with care,
Jade pendants tinkle as he returns to Phoenix Pool, his lair.

"Palace Pleasures: Eight Poems, No. 3"
By Li Bai
Loquats grow as trees from Qin, grapes emerge from Han's domain,
Fireworks suit the setting sun, strings and pipes drunk on spring's refrain.
Flutes play like dragons chanting over water, clear and deep,
Panpipes sound as phoenixes descend from skies asleep.
The sovereign finds abundant joy in many a thing,
Sharing it with all the world, making the whole realm sing.

"Autumn Meditations: Eight Poems, No. 5"
By Du Fu
The Penglai Palace faces the Southern Mountain, grand and high,
Its dew-receiving stem of gold pierces the starry sky.
Westward, one sees the Jasper Pool where the Queen Mother might descend,
Eastward, purple aura fills the Hangu Pass, an auspicious trend.
Clouds part like pheasant-tail fans, palace screens drawn with grace,
The sun circles dragon scales, revealing the sage emperor's face.
Once I lay by the river, startled by the year's late phase,
How often at the blue-locked gate did I mark the morning's maze?

"The High Palace at Mount Li"
By Bai Juyi
High on Mount Li stands a palace, proud and tall,
With vermilion towers and purple halls, three or four layers in all.
Slowly, slowly comes the spring day, warm and long,
Jade pools heat, hot springs overflow in a soothing song.
Softly, softly blows the autumn wind, a gentle sigh,
Mountain cicadas chirp, palace trees blush red against the sky.
The imperial banners have not come for many a year,
Moss clothes the walls, pines sprout on tiles, decay drawing near.

"The Palace of Wu"
By Li Shangyin
The dragon balustrade sinks in silence, water halls clear and still,
Forbidden gates deeply shut, cutting off human voices at will.
The King of Wu's feast ends, the whole palace drunk with cheer,
At dusk, flowers float out on the water, leaving the city's sphere.

zh:
胡辣汤
胡辣汤是中原早餐摊上当之无愧的王者。正宗的胡辣汤汤底由牛肉汤或羊肉汤制成，闻起来有浓厚的肉汤香味，碗内添加有肉块，面筋、腐皮等辅料。但即便是中原人常吃的典型美食，不同地方也有不同的做法。宫人中有人说自己从小喝的是黄色的胡辣汤，较为粘稠，以辣为主。也有人说自己平日里喝的是黑色的胡辣汤，汤体较稀，以麻为主。但无论何种胡辣汤，都好喝，很好喝，多喝，爱喝。
en:
1. Hulatang (Spicy Pepper Soup)

Hulatang is the undisputed king of breakfast stalls in the Central Plains. A proper bowl starts with beef or mutton broth, fragrant with rich stock, then comes with pieces of meat, wheat gluten, tofu skin, and other add-ins.

Even so, it varies from place to place. Some say the hulatang they grew up with was yellow and thick, with the spice taking center stage. Others swear by a darker, thinner version that leans more numbing than hot.

Either way, it's delicious. The kind you end up craving again.

【明堂位第十四】

昔者：周公朝诸侯于明堂之位，天子负斧依，南乡而立；三公中阶之前，北面东上；诸侯之位，阼阶之东，西面北上；诸侯之国，西阶之西，东面北上；诸子之国，门东，北面东上；诸男之国，门西，北面东上；九夷之国，东门之外，西面北上；八蛮之国，南门之外，北面东上；六戎之国，西门之外，东面南上；五狄之国，北门之外，南面东上；九采之国，应门之外，北面东上。四塞，世告至。此周公明堂之位也。
明堂也者，明诸侯之尊卑也。昔殷纣乱天下，脯鬼侯以飨诸侯，是以周公相武王以伐纣。武王崩，成王幼弱，周公践天子之位以治天下，六年，朝诸侯于明堂，制礼作乐，颁度量，而天下大服。七年，致政于成王。成王以周公为有勋劳于天下，是以封周公于曲阜，地方七百里，革车千乘，命鲁公世世祀周公以天子之礼乐。是以鲁君孟春乘大路，载弧韣，旗十有二旒，日月之章，祀帝于郊，配以后稷，天子之礼也。
季夏六月，以禘礼祀周公于大庙，牲用白牡，尊用牺象山罍，郁尊用黄目。灌用玉瓒大圭，荐用玉豆雕篹，爵用玉盏仍雕，加以璧散、璧角，俎用梡嶡；升歌清庙，下管象，朱干玉戚，冕而舞大武；皮弁素积，禓而舞大夏。昧，东夷之乐也；任，南蛮之乐也。纳夷蛮之乐于大庙，言广鲁于天下也。

en:
【The Positions in the Bright Hall, Part XIV】

In ancient times, when the Duke of Zhou received the feudal lords at the Bright Hall, the Son of Heaven stood with his back to the axe-embroidered screen, facing south. The Three Dukes stood before the central steps, facing north, with the highest on the east. The feudal lords took their positions east of the eastern steps, facing west, with the highest on the north. The lords of the states stood west of the western steps, facing east, with the highest on the north. The sons of the lords stood east of the gate, facing north, with the highest on the east. The lords of the minor states stood west of the gate, facing north, with the highest on the east. The nine Yi tribes stood outside the East Gate, facing west, with the highest on the north. The eight Man tribes stood outside the South Gate, facing north, with the highest on the east. The six Rong tribes stood outside the West Gate, facing east, with the highest on the south. The five Di tribes stood outside the North Gate, facing south, with the highest on the east. The nine Cai tribes stood outside the Ying Gate, facing north, with the highest on the east. The four frontier regions reported their arrivals at each generation. Such were the positions of the Duke of Zhou at the Bright Hall.
The Bright Hall was meant to distinguish the noble and humble ranks of the feudal lords. In former times, King Zhou of Yin threw the realm into chaos, making dried meat of the Marquis of Gui to feast the lords. Thus, the Duke of Zhou assisted King Wu in overthrowing Zhou. When King Wu passed away and King Cheng was young and weak, the Duke of Zhou ascended to the position of the Son of Heaven to govern the realm. After six years, he received the lords at the Bright Hall, established rites and music, issued standards of measures, and the whole realm was greatly subdued. In the seventh year, he returned the government to King Cheng. King Cheng, recognizing the Duke of Zhou's great merit and labor for the realm, enfeoffed him at Qufu, with a territory of seven hundred li square, a thousand war chariots, and commanded that the Duke of Lu should forever sacrifice to the Duke of Zhou with the rites and music of the Son of Heaven. Therefore, in the first month of spring, the ruler of Lu rode in the grand carriage, bearing the bow case, with a banner of twelve streamers adorned with the sun and moon, and sacrificed to God in the suburb, with Hou Ji as his companion—rites of the Son of Heaven.
In the sixth month of summer, they performed the Di sacrifice to the Duke of Zhou in the Grand Temple, using a white bull as the victim, vessels of the Xiong, Xiang, and Shan Lei types, and a yellow jar for the fragrant wine. For the libation, they used a jade gui with a great jade tablet; for offerings, jade dishes and carved baskets; for the goblets, jade cups with further carving, supplemented by jade bi and jade jue; for the stands, the Kun and Jue types. They sang the Qing Miao in the hall, and below played the Xiang with pipes. With shields of red lacquer and axes of jade, wearing crowns, they performed the Da Wu dance. With skin caps and plain white skirts, baring their arms, they performed the Da Xia dance. Mei was the music of the Eastern Yi; Ren was the music of the Southern Man. Bringing the music of the Yi and Man into the Grand Temple signified the extension of Lu's glory throughout the realm.

zh: 《莱丽与麦吉侬》的故事起源于7世纪中亚民间传说，讲述一对心心相印的纯情恋人，因双方家庭阻挠、世事不从，双双殉情。“麦吉侬”在阿拉伯语、维吾尔语中的含义为“疯子”、“痴人”，即“情痴”，故事中原名盖斯的青年因痴情而死，葬于大漠，被称为“莱丽的痴情人”，人们也不再用他的名字，直接称呼他“麦吉侬”。以这一故事为蓝本，不同语言、不同体裁的创作相继问世，目前已有50多个版本。
en: The story of Layla and Majnun originated in 7th-century Central Asian folklore, telling of a pair of pure-hearted lovers deeply devoted to each other, who, due to family opposition and worldly obstacles, both die for love. "Majnun" means "madman," "infatuated person," which is "love-crazed," in Arabic and Uyghur. In the story, a youth originally named Qais dies of lovesickness and is buried in the desert, called "Layla's infatuated one." People no longer use his name, directly calling him "Majnun." Based on this story, creations in different languages and genres have appeared successively, with over 50 versions to date.

Long before the morning rooster crows, while stars still scatter across the dark sky, the river is already aglow. Countless lanterns drift like fireflies upon the water as fishermen row in from their night moorings, their boats heavy with catches that still carry the raw, crisp scent of the lake. On the shore, merchants stand waiting, lanterns held high in the darkness. Before the boats even touch the docks, voices ring out across the water. The frantic, overlapping shouts of offers and counteroffers create a wild symphony, a chaotic energy that eclipses even the busiest midday bazaar. I have woken early to witness this spectacle, captivated by the magical interplay of lantern light and shimmering scales dancing on the dark ripples.

zh:
孟宽的酒囊从前总挂在腰侧，瘪了又满，满了又瘪。
曾经他以为，只有灌下烈酒时，耳边才稍得清净——否则，战鼓声、马蹄声、还有那些渐渐微弱下去的呼唤声、尖利的哀嚎声……便会如潮水般将他淹没。
可世间再好的酒也止不住那般喧嚣的声音。谁说人死了就是一走了之？只要他还活着，那些人也能活着。他带着他们的名，一块儿活。
直到最后一滴酒也没了。
他将空囊举至耳边，听风穿过囊口的呜咽，像极了当年号角。
随之响起的，还有那些从他喉间爬出来的名字，那些死去战友们的名字。
他望着远处的烽火，静立良久，将空囊系回了腰间。
是该回去了。
别辜负了他们的名字。
他驾马向北，旧名随蹄尘渐醒。
en:
Meng Kuan's wine pouch used to hang at his waist, sometimes empty, sometimes full.
He once thought that only by gulping down strong brew could his ears find peace; otherwise, the drums, the hooves, the fading calls, and the piercing screams would drown him like a tide.
But no wine in the world could stop such noise. Who says death is a final departure? As long as he lived, they lived too. He carried their names, living for them all.
Until the very last drop was gone.
He held the empty pouch to his ear, listening to the wind wail through the opening, just like the horns of old.
Following that sound were the names crawling from his throat: the names of his fallen brothers.
He gazed at the distant beacon fires, standing still for a long time, then tied the empty pouch back to his waist.
It was time to go back.
Don't let their names down.
He rode north, his old name waking with the dust of his horse's hooves.

en:
Long has the Way been absent from the world. Heaven shall make the Master its Clarion Chime.
The Clarion Chime is the Inkbound Order's instrument of warning to the world. The tower housing it stands atop the Goldentone Ridge, open on all four sides. The body of the bell is cast in bronze, while the tongue is fashioned from hard wood. The wood tongue serves as a symbol: though knowledge may be preserved in metal, its transmission relies upon suppleness and yielding. The bronze body serves as another: that the Way of Righteousness endures through all calamity, unbroken. In ordinary days, the bell rests in silence. Only when the Rite of the Sages is observed does it ring out like a thunderclap.

zh:
能改变一个人生命走向的句子并不多，而陈慎在短短的半炷香里听到了三句。
第三句是——他每次想起这句话时都会顿住。它像热泉一样从心底涌出，砰咚，砰咚的，一股股被泵向血管能抵达的最远的一片疆域：指尖、耳膜，或是眼底——第三句是，天呐，他真的不想把这句话说出来。小孩子把吃不完的糖葫芦藏在枕头下面又被大人好笑地摇着头翻出来时，总是要难为情的，或许是因为自己做了错事把枕头和褥子搞得脏兮兮变成一个无法承担和隐藏的烂摊子，或许是因为把几颗瘪掉发霉的糖山楂紧紧地攥在手里显得太饥饿太丢脸太不体面。所以他把这句话藏起来偷偷掖进一层一层的心事下面，只在四下无人的时候小心翼翼地翻出来，在心里小声说给自己听：

“以后师父每天都给你点。”

说这句话的时候，陈子奚的食指上还沾着印泥。

参加陈氏考校的这一路上，小孩小心翼翼地护着这个小点儿，但还是轻易地被汗、手掌，巾帕或风沙抹了去。发现小红点儿没了的时候小孩的模样仿佛天塌了。不过在陈子奚把他叫到身边来，亲手给他再次点上开智朱砂后，小孩又换了一种眼神看着他。
陈子奚端详着自己的大作，左看右看都十分满意。要是冷眼来看，这算不上世上最好的小红点儿——它有点大了，不够圆，边缘还有一点毛糙和晕开。要是陈子奚下手再重一点，简直就是在小孩脑门儿上按了个指头印。不过这是陈子奚第一次作为长辈给小孩点朱砂，点成这样他已经很得意了。虽然他不知道这个习俗是怎么来的，但既然孩子看上去这么想要，那就点一个。
他刚收的徒弟还啪嗒啪嗒眨着眼看他，紧紧地抿起嘴角。

一个小红点儿。一件这么轻易的事怎么能让世上的另一个生命如此欢喜……世上的小孩都这般么？还是只有这孩子是这样？

“……还会掉的。”小孩捂着头捂了一会儿，又故作成熟地把手挪开，“……师父不用麻烦了。很容易掉的。”虽这么说着，小孩的手却还放在头旁边，依依不舍地护着。

在陈慎的记忆里，有一只温暖的手伸了过来，像送出一件礼物。

“掉了就再点。以后师父每天都给你点。”

于是小孩的心“忽”得踩空了一下。他这时才对“师父”有了实感。“陈子奚”会漫不经心地顺手给孤零零的小孩一件礼物，但“师父”……“师父”每天都会给他的徒弟带，带很多很多件。徒弟可以被师父点一颗小红点，哪怕不小心弄花了，只要一天里不要弄花太多次；哪怕已经点过三百六十五次，只要在长大前及时主动叫停；哪怕大人很忙，只要他有点眼色，找到大人闲下来的间隙……只要不超过“懂事”的限度，小孩可以向“家中长辈”近乎无赖地索求。

“师父”，和他下定决心参与这场争夺时想要的一样好。

但陈子奚做师父是另一回事了。

他曾在一天里弄花过五次脸，如今也早已过了三千六百五十天，而玉山君在杀人的间隙还会隔着血雨问他，脸花成这样，一会儿要重新点个小红点了。
en:
Few things anyone says can change the course of a life. Chen Shen heard three such things in the time it took half a stick of incense to burn.
The third was... He always stopped here. Just remembering it sent warmth rising from deep in his chest. Thump, thump. Each heartbeat carried it a little farther, all the way to his fingertips, the pulse in his ears, the backs of his eyes. The third was... Heaven help him, he really didn't want to say it aloud. A child who hides unfinished candied hawthorns under a pillow always feels ashamed when an adult finds them and shakes their head in amusement. Perhaps it's the sticky mess left on the bedding, too much to put right and impossible to hide. Or perhaps it's the indignity of clutching a few shriveled, moldy sweets so tightly, as if he were still starving. So he hid those words beneath layers of private thoughts. Only when he was alone did he carefully take them out and whisper them to himself:

"I'll put a fresh red dot on your forehead every day."

Chen Zixi still had red ink on his fingertip when he said it.

Throughout the Chen family's examinations, the boy had tried so hard to protect that little dot. But sweat, a stray hand, a cloth, or windblown grit could wipe it away in an instant. When he realized it was gone, he looked as though his whole world had fallen apart. Then Chen Zixi called him over and reapplied the vermilion mark, a blessing meant to awaken a child's wisdom. The boy looked at him differently after that.
Chen Zixi inspected his handiwork from every angle and found it most satisfactory. An impartial observer might have disagreed. The dot was a little too big, not quite round, and blurred at the edges. Had he pressed any harder, it would have been a fingerprint stamped on the boy's forehead. Still, this was his first time bestowing the mark as an elder, and he was rather proud of himself. He had no idea where the custom came from. But the boy clearly wanted it, so why not?
His new disciple kept blinking up at him, lips pressed tightly together.

One little red dot. How could something so simple make another person so happy? Were all children like this? Or just this one?

"...It'll only rub off again." The boy cupped his forehead for a while, then tried to look grown-up and lowered his hand. "...You don't have to bother, Master. It comes off so easily." Even so, his hand lingered beside his head, still trying to protect the mark.

In Chen Shen's memory, a warm hand reached toward him, as though offering a gift.

"Then I'll put it back. I'll put a fresh red dot on your forehead every day."

The boy's heart gave a sudden lurch, as if he had missed a step. Only then did he begin to understand what it meant to have a master. Chen Zixi might casually give a lonely child a gift. But his master... His master would bring him gifts every day. So many gifts. A disciple could ask his master to renew the little red dot, even if he had smudged it by accident, provided it didn't happen too many times in one day. Even if his master had already done it three hundred and sixty-five times, provided he knew to stop asking before he grew too old. Even if his master was busy, provided he had the sense to wait for a quiet moment... As long as a child knew not to go too far, there was nothing wrong with pestering the grown-ups at home for what they wanted.

Having a master was every bit as wonderful as he had hoped when he decided to compete for that place.

But Chen Zixi had his own way of being a master.

There had been a day when Chen Shen smudged his face five times. More than three thousand six hundred and fifty days had now passed. And still, between killing blows, Mister Jade Hill would call to him through the spray of blood: "Look at that face. We'll have to put your little red dot back on when we're done."
