zh:
《千帆一舟》

夜深了，天工阁内仍灯火通明。
”邹师兄，还不走啊，早点休息啊。" 路过的师弟关切道。
“邹师兄还在改论文呢，别打扰他了。“一旁的另一人低声劝阻。
"邹师兄，我先走了，钥匙给你放老位置了，记得关门。” 
邹师兄笑笑，温声应下。
邹师兄不是墨门的大师兄，甚至连内门弟子都不是，他只是一个普通的外门弟子。但提起邹师兄，上到长老，下到阿旺，无人不夸周师兄的好。
无他，只因他待人至诚。无论什么事，只要找邹师兄帮忙，他都尽心尽力，从不推诿。
然而这样的人，却有个记了他十七年的 “仇人”。
说仇人也不全对，杨千言从不主动提邹易州。他们俩只是默契地避开所有相见的场合。
故而无人知晓，莘野坊不务正业卖话本子的杨千言，与外门弟子中最受人欢迎的邹师兄，曾是知交挚友。

十七年前，碧水云涛的桃花林还没像如今这般繁盛。
春三月，桃枝斜斜探向水面，嫩红的花苞缀在枝头，像绿绸上的胭脂碎。
十六岁的邹易州背着半旧的书箧，鞋尖沾着晨露打湿的青草，正往林深处走，忽听得一阵吟诵声从高处飘来，清朗朗的：“东风吹醒桃花雨，明月照彻碧水波。”
他脚步顿了顿，循着声音抬头看过去，见个瘦高的少年坐在桃树上，青布衫洗得发了白，袖口磨出了毛边，手里攥着卷泛黄的诗稿。少年听见脚步声抬头，见了他，只扬了扬手里的稿子，笑着问：“你也喜欢诗？”
邹易州原本想拱手作揖，“在下邹易州……”
不成想他这一弯腰，书箧里探出头了只小山猪。那小山猪眨了眨眼睛，三俩下拱出了书箧，跳了下来，一溜烟跑走了。
“哈哈哈哈——” 书上的少年连声大笑，“竟有人书箧里不装书，装的是只山猪！妙人，真是妙人！”
笑完，他轻巧跳了下来，也拱手回礼，见指尖还沾着墨渍，便随手蹭在长衫下摆上。“在下杨千言。刚凑了两句闲诗，让邹兄和猪兄……噗嗤，都见笑了。”
邹易州望着跑远的小山猪，又看了看笑得直不起腰的杨千言，忙解释道：“原本是我怕它闯祸，才暂时放进书箧里……” 话没说完，倒被自己逗乐了 —— 好好的书箧成了 “猪窝”，确实荒唐。
杨千言笑够了，拍了拍他的肩，眼里满是兴味：“管它装书还是装猪，能把山猪藏进书箧的，邹兄是头一个。” 他晃了晃手里的诗稿，“刚念的两句还没写完，邹兄看着也懂诗，帮我推敲推敲？”
墨门封山千载，人人皆崇尚机巧，诗词歌赋反倒少有人读。因而两人一见如故。
邹易州说，他于机巧一事无甚天赋，却爱写些话本传奇，精怪志异。怕被夫子发现，便在写话本时改了个笔名。结果还是被发现了，说是不务正业。杨千言说，正巧，我也是个机巧白丁，连夫子都不肯收我。只会写些酸诗。这样，以后邹兄尽可以拿我的名字去写话本，我不怕。我还能给你写诗，写批语。
日头偏西时，邹易州见小山猪还未回来，有些着急。
杨千言拉着他往林外走：“别急，我刚才瞧见它往南边去了，那地方有嫩草，准在那儿。”
果然，两人在田边的土坡上找到了猪兄 —— 它正蜷在暖阳里打盹，嘴角还沾着草屑。邹易州上前轻轻抱起它，小山猪哼唧了两声，竟往他怀里蹭了蹭。杨千言站在一旁看着，忽然笑道：“邹兄，这传奇志异的故事，我看第一篇就得是这山猪。”
说完两人哈哈大笑。

自那以后，桃林便成了两人常来之处。
他们说等开山以后，要游遍河山，像当年的李杜，元白，一人写一人和。
他们还约定，以后要一起在山外开个书社。
“听说开封城最热闹，咱们到时候就把书社开在最热闹的街口，门口种上两株从山里带出去的桃树！” 杨千言在誊抄最新的话本。他俩的书已经在山中风靡开了。
邹易州笑着点头，指尖在纸上写下 “千金不易” 四个字，“那书社的牌匾，就挂这四个字。”
杨千言的千，邹易州的易。
千帆一舟，千金不易。
那时的他们还年少，以为这样的日子还有很多，以为碧水云涛的桃花明年还会再开，以为两人会一起把故事写尽，以为那只小山猪会长着大山猪的样子。
那是十七年前的春三月。
后来，有人从天工阁角落里寻到几本破旧不堪的话本子，题诗之人是杨千言。有几页，还夹着几根猪鬃毛。
有弟子拿着书去问这书是谁的，“邹师兄，这杨千言是何人啊……你见过吗？”
“见过的，很久以前。”
en:
Together in One Boat 

The night had deepened, yet Divinecraft Pavilion remained brightly lit. 
"Senior Brother Zou, still here? You should get some rest," a passing junior called out with concern. 
"He's still revising his paper—let's not disturb him," another whispered softly. 
"Senior Brother Zou, I'm heading off. I left the key where I always do. Don't forget to lock up." 
Zou smiled warmly in reply. 
Zou isn't the head disciple of the Mohist Hill. In fact, he's not even a core disciple, just an ordinary outer one. Still, whenever his name comes up, everyone from the elders to Buster speaks highly of him. 
The reason was simple: he treated everyone with sincere kindness. No matter the request, if anyone sought his help, Zou gave his all—never hesitant, never turning anyone away. 
But even a man like him had someone he'd been estranged from for seventeen years. 
Though calling it hatred was too strong—Yang never spoke of Zou, and the two quietly avoided each other whenever chance might bring them face to face. 
What no one knew was that Yang, the carefree storyteller, and Zou, the most admired senior among outer disciples, had once been inseparable friends. 

Seventeen years ago, the peach grove by the sparkling waters of Jadestream Valley had yet to bloom into the lush sea of blossoms it is now. 
In early spring, peach branches stretched gently over the water, their delicate pink buds like scattered rouge on vibrant green silk. 
Sixteen-year-old Zou walked deeper into the forest, a worn book satchel slung over his shoulder, his shoes damp from the morning dew kissing the grass beneath his feet. Suddenly, a clear, melodious voice drifted down from above:
"The east wind wakes the peach blossom rain,
The bright moon lights the jade-green waves." 
He paused, lifted his gaze, and spotted a slender youth perched among the branches of a peach tree. His faded blue shirt was worn thin and frayed at the cuffs, and he clutched a yellowed scroll of poetry. Catching sight of Zou, the boy smiled and raised the scroll. "You like poetry too?" 
Zou bowed politely, about to introduce himself. "I am Zou Yizhou…" 
But as he bent forward, a tiny wild boar poked its snout from the satchel. Blinking its bright eyes, the little creature clumsily scrambled free and darted off into the woods. 
The boy burst into laughter. "Hahaha! Who hides a wild piglet inside their book satchel instead of books? Truly one of a kind!" 
His laughter ringing through the grove, the boy gracefully leapt down, returning Zou's bow with a playful grin. Noticing ink stains on his fingertips, he casually wiped them on the hem of his robe. "I'm Yang Qianyan. Just tossing together a few stray lines of poetry. Looks like I've made fools of both you and your piglet friend." 
Zou watched the boar disappear into the underbrush, then glanced back at Yang, who was still chuckling. He hurried to explain, "I only tucked it in the satchel to keep it from running wild..." He couldn't help but laugh too—the idea of a book satchel turned pigsty was absurdly charming. 
When the laughter settled, Yang clapped him on the shoulder with genuine warmth. "Whether it's books or boars, you're the first I've known to carry a wild pig in a satchel." He waved the scroll playfully. "Those lines I just read aren't finished yet. You seem to have an ear for poetry—care to help me refine them?" 
For a thousand years, the Mohist Hill disciples prized mechanical ingenuity above all else—poetry, prose, and song had fallen into neglect. Because of this, the two young men connected instantly, as if old friends reunited. 
Zou confessed he lacked any real talent for mechanics but found joy in writing tales of legends, strange creatures, and the supernatural. To keep this secret from their master, he adopted a pen name. Still, he was caught and scolded for neglecting his proper duties. Yang laughed and said, "Funny enough, I'm a complete novice when it comes to mechanics, and even the master wouldn't take me in. All I do is write bitter little poems. If you want, you can use my name for your stories—I don't mind. I can even craft poems and notes to accompany them." 
As the sun dipped westward, Zou grew anxious—the little wild boar had yet to return. 
Yang took his hand and led him toward the forest's edge. "Don't worry—I saw it wander south earlier. There's fresh grass there; it's probably resting nearby." 
Sure enough, they found the boar curled in a patch of warm sunlight on a hillside by the fields, dozing with bits of grass stuck at its mouth. Zou gently lifted the creature, which softly snuffled and nestled against his chest. Watching this, Yang smiled and said, "Zou, I believe your first tale of legends should be about this wild boar." 
They laughed together, their joy echoing through the grove. 

From that day on, the peach grove became their treasured refuge. 
They dreamed of the day the mountain would reopen, when they could journey across the land like the great poets of old—one writing verses, the other composing replies. 
And they vowed to open a bookstore beyond the mountain, a place where their stories and poems could live and breathe, together. 
"I've heard Kaifeng City is the liveliest place around," Yang said as he copied out the latest manuscript. "When the time comes, let's open our bookstore right at the busiest street corner—and plant two peach trees at the doorway, ones we bring all the way from the mountains." Their stories had already become wildly popular deep within the mountains. 
Zou smiled and nodded, then penned four characters on the paper: Qian Jin Bu Yi—"Priceless and Rare." "That will be the sign above our shop." 
The "Qian" from Yang, the "Yi" from Zou. 
Together in one boat, priceless and rare. 
They were young then, believing such days would stretch on forever—that the peach blossoms by the crystal-clear Jadestream Valley would bloom again next spring—that they would share countless stories side by side—that the little wild boar would one day grow into a mighty beast. 
That was the spring seventeen years ago. 
Later, a few weathered, fragile scripts were found tucked away in a forgotten corner of Divinecraft Pavilion. The poems inside bore the name Yang Qianyan, and pressed between the pages were a few strands of boar's bristles. 
One disciple held the books and asked, "Senior Brother Zou, who exactly is this Yang Qianyan? Have you met him?" 
"I have. Long ago."

zh:
年轻人：
       好久不见，最近过得还好吗？
       托你的福，摊子的生意很好。你阿婶她很久没有这么高兴了，每天笑盈盈地和来往客人唠家常，开心的时候还会借着琵琶摊小娘子的曲子跳上几步！不忙的时候，老张和老幺还张罗着去和赛神队的几个小伙子比赛，哈哈。
      天水集的大伙儿都会提起你，说你行侠仗义，我们听着都很开心，也惦记着你。你阿婶怕你在外面吃不饱穿不暖，时常念叨你呢。有时间就来摊子坐坐啊。
      对了，开烫菜摊子赚了些钱，我们想着也帮衬帮衬别人，就做了些饭菜送给了几个老伙计。怕他们觉得不好意思，我们几个就说，是你要给他们送的。他们还奇怪，说怎么会有没见过的好心人惦记他们呢。老张说这孩子就是这样的，是个热心肠的大侠！他们不太好意思，就给你写了字条，你一起看看吧。
      好了，不说了，待会要来客人了，就到这儿吧。
      希望你一个人在外吃饱穿暖，平平安安。

en:
Young Hero: 
Long time no see. How have you been? 
Thanks to you, the stall is doing great. Your Auntie hasn't been this happy in ages—she smiles, chatting with customers all day, and even dances a few steps when the Pipa lady plays! When it's slow, Old Zhang and Old Yao even try to race the lads from the deity competition team, haha. 
Everyone at Skybrim Market speaks of your chivalry. We are happy to hear it and miss you often. Your Auntie worries you aren't eating well or staying warm. She talks about you all the time. Come visit the stall when you can. 
Oh, we made some money from the scalding vegetable stall, so we thought we'd help others out. We sent some food to a few old partners. We were afraid they'd feel embarrassed, so we said it was from you. They were surprised a kind hero remembered them! Old Zhang said, "That child is just warm-hearted like that!" They were shy, so they wrote you notes. Take a look. 
Okay, customers are coming. I'll stop here. 
Stay warm, fed, and safe out there.

To the south, however, stand Rainfall Pavilion and Treasure Hall. Crowded, profit-driven, and teeming with ambition. Countless swordsman set off from here, never to return from the Fogwood Treasure Hunt.

zh:
若问墨城谁的课上的最好？每个弟子心中都有自己的答案。可若要说谁能把墨经讲的最有趣，十个弟子里，便有八个会提名鸥大匠。

鸥大匠讲解的墨经，不仅引经据典，深入浅出，而且还总是以食喻事，令人胃口大开。从墨子当年四处奔走路上食饮，到各国君王为墨子一行所设之宴，鸥大匠都一一例举考据。用他的话说，墨子弟子十五，再传者众，他们写下“我有天志”这四个字时，吃的究竟是山肴野簌，还是肥鱼大肉，这当然是关乎墨门之本的大问题。

况且这古往今来的机巧图纸大同小异，难翻新意。这些食方就不同了，食材之丰富，组合之多样，口味之繁杂，比大多数俗世机巧，更合墨道变化由心之法。课业之余，他总爱秉持着墨家试验之道，去追溯那些失传的方子。试食材，试火候，试调味……

弟子们也没有闲着，每隔三个时辰，就轮流去向鸥大匠讨教问题。倒不是因为他们多勤学好问，实在是鸥大匠的这美食研究的失败率感人，若无人过问，指不定他又要晕倒在一堆诡异的食材中，说些什么胡话了。

窗外云翳渐散，山鸡晨啼，几个弟子雷打不动地在院子里背诵着“兼相爱，交相利”，谈论墨城最新的机巧，又或因开山封山这样的话题从早辩到晚。
鸥大匠把墨经这本食方交给了弟子们，由着他们往里面加入闻鸡起舞的辛酸，劳作实践的艰苦，投入几分交锋辩驳的辣味，再来一点同道而行的甜。还有人更愿意往里面倒入大把大把的盐巴，或者掺入游历各地的江水……

“拿起刨子，或者汤勺，最重要的是，要做出一锅属于自己的菜。”鸥大匠给弟子们留下这句话后，又钻进了自己的小屋子里，留下众弟子和一锅微妙的菜肴面面相觑。

每当此时，一些年纪稍大的弟子忍不住怀想当年还没有走上“歧途”的鸥大匠。你说，好端端一位稳健博学的大匠，究竟为何抛弃钻研半生的机巧之论，沉迷于在各种食谱古方之中？
这是诸弟子们至今未解的谜团。
en:
Ask around Mohist City whose classes are the best, and every disciple will give you a different answer. But ask who makes the Mohist Canons the most entertaining, and eight out of ten will name Grand Artisan Gull.

When Grand Artisan Gull lectures on the Canons, he quotes widely, explains things clearly, and somehow always manages to bring food into it. By the end of class, everyone is hungry. From what Mozi and his followers ate on the road to the banquets rulers prepared for them, he can cite and cross-reference it all. As he likes to put it, Mozi had fifteen disciples, and later generations followed in great numbers, so what exactly they were eating when they wrote "I Have Heaven's Will" is obviously a matter of great importance to Mohism itself.

Besides, old mechanism blueprints are all more or less the same, and there is only so much novelty to be found in them. Recipes are another matter. The range of ingredients, the endless combinations, the sheer variety of flavors all suit the Mohist way of change and adaptation far better than most ordinary mechanisms ever could. So outside of class, he is forever applying the Mohist spirit of experimentation to tracking down lost recipes, testing ingredients, testing heat, testing seasoning...

The disciples have not been idle either. Every six hours, someone takes a turn going to ask Grand Artisan Gull a question. Not because they are especially diligent, but because his food experiments fail at an alarming rate. If no one checks on him, there is no telling when he might faint in the middle of a pile of strange ingredients and start muttering nonsense again.

Outside, the clouds are beginning to clear, mountain pheasants are calling in the morning, and a few disciples are, as always, out in the courtyard reciting "Universal Love, Mutual Benefit." They talk about the latest mechanisms in Mohist City, or spend the whole day arguing over matters like opening the mountain or sealing it off again.

Grand Artisan Gull has handed this cookbook of the Mohist Canons over to his disciples and let them season it for themselves, with the hardship of rising at dawn, the toil of labor and practice, the sharpness of debate, and a little sweetness from walking the same path together. Some would rather pour in handful after handful of salt, while others might mix in the river waters of all the places they have traveled...

"Whether you pick up a plane or a ladle, what matters most is making a dish of your own."

Having left them with that, Grand Artisan Gull ducks back into his little room, leaving the disciples staring at one another, and at the pot of rather questionable food before them.

At times like this, some of the older disciples cannot help but think back to the days before Grand Artisan Gull wandered so far down this particular path. How did such a steady, learned master, after spending half his life studying mechanisms, end up so obsessed with old recipes instead?

To this day, none of the disciples has solved that mystery.

高悬九霄的节度使府张灯结彩，此刻正举行一场盛大的庆功宴。小张将军远征归来，大张将军即将归唐。此番宴请宾客，既是慰问军心，也是为凉州父老吃下一颗定心丸。然而宾朋满座，未见二位将军。你来到佛手郎的书房，看到两位将军坐在案前似乎再商议什么。正当你犹豫是不是打扰他们，佛手郎看到你进来，丢下笔，热切揽过你的肩膀邀你入座。大张将军也颔首致意。此番相聚，你胸中有千言万语，却不知从何说起。此刻，你只想和他们一道……
#Y【共饮一杯满江红。】纵有千万言，不如一杯饮。你知晓史书记载的终局，但你无法改变这既定的因果。此刻，你只想与二位将军共醉一场，记住此刻。#E
听闻你的建议，佛手郎开怀一笑，大张将军也欣然允诺。
en:
The Governor's Residence blazes with lantern light and festal colors, where a magnificent victory banquet is currently underway. General Zhang Huaishen has returned from his campaign, and General Zhang Yichao is about to return to the Tang court. The feast is meant not only to honor the army, but also to reassure the people of Liangzhou and set their hearts at ease. And yet, though the hall is crowded with guests, the two generals themselves are nowhere to be seen. You find your way to the Buddha Hand's study, where the two of them sit facing one another at the desk, seemingly deep in discussion. You are still hesitating over whether to disturb them when the Buddha Hand looks up, drops his brush, and, with easy warmth, slips an arm around your shoulders, urging you to join them. General Zhang Yichao also inclines his head in greeting.
In this gathering, you have thousands of words in your heart, yet no idea where to begin. At this moment, you simply want to...
#Y[Share a cup of River All Red.] Thousands of words cannot compare to a single cup of wine. You cannot change this predestined karma recorded in the annals of history. All you want is to share a drunken reverie with the two generals and remember this very moment.#E
Hearing your suggestion, the Buddha's Hand laughs heartily, and General Zhang Yichao readily agrees.

My heart swells with gratitude. Where else under Heaven can one find such a kind soul as the Youxia-er—benevolent in heart, gentle in demeanor, and ever generous in action!

I compiled the Youxia-er's deeds into a book, which became a bestseller among merchants, spreading his virtuous name far and wide. A Swordsman from Well of Heaven, skeptical of such tales, questioned how someone neither affiliated with the Heaven's Gate nor a wealthy merchant could be so magnanimous. I answered truthfully: because he is virtuous.

Enclosed with this letter is the Youxia-er's charitable donation. When we meet again, let us dispense with formalities. The Wayfarer bows once more to the honorable Youxia-er.

zh:
我等时间，等了一辈子。 
等到手中的唐旗已暌违这片土地，近一个甲子。 
人言常道，五十而知天命。可我等的，并不是那个天命的安排。 
所以我与时间相争，哪怕背弃我的善良，滥用我的权术，牺牲……我的长兄。 
不，哪怕牺牲的是我。凉州可以无我，归义军可以无我， 
但那个誓心归国的愿望，还需要一个继任者。 
而今日，我便要等那个继任者到来。 
只是，我等的那个人，还存着赤子的热忱，和对我的敬重。 
长安的质子，不应是归义军领袖的软肋。 
故而，我告诉他真相，也告诉他龌龊。 
我希望他舍弃我，一如我舍弃兄长。 
  
如果权力的更迭都需要鲜血，那么就用我的血肉来为他造势。 
直到他凌驾我的旧部，取代我的威望。 
看着外面被他控制的亲兵，看着他压制那些不愿我归唐的声音。 
果然，他做得很好。 
我本以为，他来的时候，会把刀架在我的脖颈， 
可他却把刀递给了我—— 
我太熟悉这把刀，起初的那场送别，就是兄长将刀送予我， 
后来我又把它送还给兄长的儿子。 
而现在，这把刀又还至跟前。 
他说，他会带着归义军，等我回家。 
那一刻，我们洞谙彼此，我知道，此时、未来， 
不管千里、万里，我们还会站在彼此身旁。
en:
I have waited a lifetime—  
waiting until the Tang banner I once held has long since vanished from this land, almost sixty years gone.  
They say a man knows his destiny by fifty. But what I waited for was no simple fate ordained by heaven.  
So I wrestled with time itself—even if it meant forsaking my compassion, wielding power ruthlessly, sacrificing... my eldest brother.  
No, even if it meant sacrificing myself. Liangzhou could do without me. The Guiyi Army could do without me.  
But the sacred oath to reclaim our homeland still demands a torchbearer.  
And today, I wait for that successor to appear.  
Yet the one I await still carries the fire of innocence—and a deep respect for me.  
The hostage in Chang'an must never become a weakness for our cause.  
So I laid bare the truth before him—the noble and the sordid alike.  
I want him to abandon me, just as I abandoned my brother.  
  
If every passing of the torch must be bathed in blood, then let mine stain the path ahead—  
until he rises above my old allies, eclipsing even my own renown.  
I watch his loyal guards standing sentry outside, watch him silence the voices opposed to my return to Tang.  
He is proving himself worthy indeed.  
I once thought his arrival would come with a blade at my throat—  
but instead, he handed the blade into my hands.  
I know this blade too well. At our first farewell, it was my brother who gave it to me.  
Later, I passed it on to my brother's son.  
And now, it has come full circle—back into my grasp.  
He vows to lead the Guiyi Army, waiting for the day I come home.  
In that moment, we understood one another completely.  
From now on, through all the miles that lie ahead, no matter the distance, we will stand side by side.
